teile.einleitung: The New Stone Age, also called the Neolithic, is the last section of the Stone Age. During this time people became farmers, kept animals and lived in permanent villages. It began around 9500 BC in the Fertile Crescent and reached central Europe around 5500 BC.
wichtigste: The technical term for the New Stone Age is Neolithic.
It began first in the Fertile Crescent, around 9500 BC.
The farming way of life reached central Europe around 5500 BC.
What was new was that stones were ground and drilled through.
The glacier mummy Ötzi lived around 3300 BC and was found in 1991.
The cult site Göbekli Tepe, over 11,000 years old, stands in Turkey.
In central Europe, the Neolithic was followed by the Bronze Age.

abschnitte.titel: What is the New Stone Age?
abschnitte.text: The word **Neolithic** means “new Stone Age”. It followed the Old and Middle Stone Age. In the **Fertile Crescent**, an area in the Near East, it began around 9500 BC. The farming way of life reached central Europe around 5500 BC, and here it lasted until about 2200 BC, when the **Bronze Age** began.

The greatest change was the transition to **arable farming** and livestock breeding. People grew cereals such as emmer, einkorn and barley and kept sheep, goats, cattle and pigs. They became settled and lived in villages. That is why people speak of the **Neolithic Revolution**.

What was new was that stones were **ground** and drilled through. This produced smooth stone axes with which trees could be felled. People also invented **pottery**, that is, vessels of fired clay. Towards the end of the New Stone Age, the first objects of copper appeared.

abschnitte.titel: Ötzi, the man from the ice
abschnitte.text: In 1991, hikers in the **Ötztal Alps** on the border between Austria and Italy found a glacier mummy. The man, now called **Ötzi**, lived around 3300 BC. He wore clothing of fur and leather and had a copper axe, a bow and arrows with him. Today he is on display in a museum in Bolzano.

In present-day Turkey stands the cult site **Göbekli Tepe**, over 11,000 years old, with large, decorated stone pillars. It was built when people there had only just become settled. Later, people in Europe set up huge stone structures such as **Stonehenge** in England. In Switzerland too there are such stones, for example the menhirs of Yverdon-les-Bains.

abschnitte.titel: The New Stone Age in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland, people of the New Stone Age often lived in **pile-dwelling villages** on lake shores. Thanks to water and mud, wood, fabrics, baskets and even remains of bread were preserved there. Many of these sites are now UNESCO World Heritage Sites. At the Schnidejoch in the Bernese Oberland, the melting ice released pieces of equipment about as old as Ötzi.

begriffe.erklaerung: Technical word for the New Stone Age, means “new Stone Age”.
An area in the Near East where agriculture began.
Vessels and objects made of fired clay.
A large stone set upright in prehistoric times.

gewusst: Ötzi had over 60 tattoos on his skin.
Göbekli Tepe is about 6,000 years older than Stonehenge.
The arrowhead in Ötzi's shoulder shows that he was probably murdered.

teile.einleitung: With isotope analysis, researchers can read from old bones and teeth what a person ate and where they grew up. For this, it measures tiny differences between different forms of chemical elements.
wichtigste: Isotopes are forms of an element that differ slightly in weight.
The ratio of strontium-87 to strontium-86 in tooth enamel reveals origin.
Tooth enamel forms in childhood and does not change afterwards.
A high nitrogen-15 value shows a lot of animal protein in the diet.
Carbon isotopes can point to C4 plants such as millet or maize.
Usually the collagen in the bone is measured.

abschnitte.text: Many chemical elements exist in several forms, the **isotopes**. They behave almost the same but are of different weight. Through water and food they get into the body and are built into bones and teeth. In the laboratory, the ratio of the isotopes is measured with a **mass spectrometer**. From this, conclusions can be drawn about a person's life.

abschnitte.titel: Where did a person come from?
abschnitte.text: The rock of every region has its own ratio of **strontium-87 to strontium-86**. This gets into the body through water and food. The **tooth enamel** forms in childhood and is not rebuilt afterwards. So it stores the origin from childhood. Bones, by contrast, are constantly rebuilt and show rather the last years of life. If the value in the tooth does not match the place of the grave, the person had **moved in from elsewhere**. In addition, **oxygen isotopes** are measured, which depend on the drinking water and on the climate of the region of origin.

For studies of diet, the **collagen**, the most important protein of the bone, is extracted from the bone. With every step of the **food chain**, the share of **nitrogen-15** rises. Someone who ate a lot of meat, milk or fish has higher values than someone who ate almost only plants. Carbon isotopes show whether someone ate **C4 plants** such as millet or maize. In photosynthesis, these take up more heavy carbon-13 than C3 plants such as wheat.

abschnitte.titel: An example from the New Stone Age
abschnitte.text: Researchers studied skeletons of the **Linear Pottery culture**, an early farming culture in central Europe. Many women had strontium values that did not match the surroundings of their grave. Most men, by contrast, had local values. This suggests that women often moved to the settlement from other places. In this way, isotope analysis helps to detect migrations in a time without writing.

gewusst: Even after thousands of years, a tooth can reveal in which region a person lived as a child.
With isotope analysis, it was found that the man from the ice, Ötzi, grew up in South Tyrol.

teile.einleitung: The La Tène culture is the culture of the Celts in the later Iron Age. It is named after the find site La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel. It is known for flowing art, glass jewellery and new inventions.
wichtigste: The La Tène culture is linked with the Celts.
The Swedish archaeologist Hans Hildebrand suggested the name.
Celts made coloured, seamless bracelets of glass.
The fibula was a clothing pin, similar to a safety pin.
The rotary quern made grinding grain faster.
The Gundestrup cauldron from Denmark shows Celtic images of gods.

abschnitte.text: The Swedish archaeologist **Hans Hildebrand** divided the Iron Age into an earlier and a later phase. He named the earlier one after Hallstatt in Austria, the later one after **La Tène** in Switzerland. His names caught on in research. Greek and Roman writers called the peoples north of the Alps **Celts** or Gauls. Their culture largely corresponds to the La Tène finds.

The Celts made **bracelets of glass** that have no seam. The rings were drawn from hot glass and often coloured blue, brown or yellow. They held their clothes together with a **fibula**. It works similarly to a safety pin. Because the shape of fibulae often changed, they help researchers in **dating** finds.

In the La Tène period, the **rotary quern** spread. In it, an upper stone is turned on a lower one. This was much faster than rubbing on a flat grindstone. The Celts were also skilled smiths. They built large fortified settlements called **oppida** and struck coins of their own.

Celtic art shows interlaced tendrils, spirals and faces. Famous is the silver **Gundestrup cauldron**, which lay in a bog in Jutland in **Denmark**. It shows gods, warriors and animals in the Celtic style. On it and on other works of art, you can see the god **Cernunnos** with deer antlers. He usually sits cross-legged, surrounded by animals, and is regarded as a god of nature.

In the area of present-day Switzerland lived Celtic tribes such as the **Helvetii**. They had oppida, for example on the Engehalbinsel in Bern. In 58 BC, the Helvetii wanted to emigrate to Gaul. The Roman general Julius Caesar defeated them and sent them back. After that the area came under Roman rule.

gewusst: The name Helvetia for Switzerland goes back to the Celtic Helvetii.
The abbreviation CH stands for Confoederatio Helvetica, that is, the Helvetic Confederation.

teile.einleitung: The first farmers were people who no longer only hunted and gathered, but grew plants and kept animals themselves. They grew wheat and barley and kept sheep and goats. This new way of life began about 11,000 years ago in the Near East and changed the world for ever.
wichtigste: The first farmers grew cereals such as wheat and barley.
They kept sheep and goats, and later cattle and pigs too.
To make room for fields, they cleared the forest.
They cut the grain with a sickle and ground the kernels on stones to make flour.
They shaped pots from clay and made cloth from flax.
Goats and cows gave milk, sheep provided meat and wool.
The first farmers came to Switzerland about 7500 years ago.

abschnitte.text: The first farmers lived about 11,000 years ago in the **Fertile Crescent**, an area in the Near East. Wild cereals grew there, whose grains people gathered. In time they sowed the grains themselves and chose the best plants. In this way our first **crops** such as wheat and barley arose from wild plants.

Besides farming, people began **herding animals**. First they tamed sheep and goats, and later cattle and pigs. Goats and cows gave **milk**, and the sheep provided meat, skin and wool. Animals were also a kind of living store for bad times.

To make room for fields, farmers had to clear forest. For this they used **stone axes** with polished blades. They loosened the soil with digging sticks and hoes. At harvest they cut the grain with a **sickle** into which sharp flint blades were set.

Farmers ground the grains on a flat **grindstone** to make flour, from which they made porridge and flatbread. From **clay** they shaped pots and fired them in the fire so that they became hard. From the fibres of **flax** they spun thread and wove cloth. This created completely new trades and skills.

From the Near East, the farming way of life slowly spread across Europe. It reached central Europe around 5500 BC. In Switzerland, the first farmers often lived on lake shores in **pile-dwelling villages**. Thanks to the wet ground, even grains of cereal, remains of bread and pieces of cloth have been found there.

Because fields had to be tended, people became **settled** and built permanent houses. With stores of food, more people could be fed, and the population grew. At the same time, work in the field was hard, and a failed harvest could mean hunger. Almost everything we eat today goes back to these first farmers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Growing plants in fields.
Keeping and breeding animals.
A curved knife for cutting grain.
A plant whose fibres are used to make linen cloth.

gewusst: The first farmers were often smaller and less healthy than the hunters and gatherers before them, because their diet was less varied.
Wild cereal drops its grains as soon as it is ripe, so the farmers bred varieties whose grains stay on the ear.
Flour in the Stone Age often contained fine sand from the grindstone, which wore down the teeth.

teile.einleitung: Maize is today one of the most important crops in the world. It comes from Mexico and was bred there about 9,000 years ago from a wild grass. Only after the voyages of Columbus did it come to Europe.
wichtigste: The ancestor of maize is the wild grass teosinte.
Maize was bred in the valley of the Río Balsas in south-western Mexico.
Domestication began about 9,000 years ago.
Some of the oldest maize cobs come from the Guilá Naquitz cave.
Maize, beans and squash are called the “Three Sisters”.
Maize reached Europe at the end of the 15th century.

abschnitte.text: The ancestor of maize is **teosinte**, a wild grass from Mexico. It hardly resembles maize today and has only small, hard ears. Over many generations, people chose plants with larger grains. This is called **domestication**, that is, the taming of a wild plant. An important gene is called **tb1**. It ensures that maize forms only few side shoots.

Genetic studies show that the teosinte from the valley of the **Río Balsas** in south-western Mexico is closest to maize. There cultivation probably began about **9,000 years ago**. Some of the oldest known maize cobs come from the **Guilá Naquitz** cave in Oaxaca. They are about 6,200 years old and still very small.

Indigenous peoples of the Americas planted maize together with **beans** and **squash**. These three plants are called the **Three Sisters**. The maize serves the beans as a climbing frame. The beans fix nitrogen and so fertilise the soil. The large squash leaves shade the ground and keep it moist. This mixed cropping is also called **milpa**.

In Central America, maize is traditionally cooked with **lime** or **ash**. This process is called **nixtamalisation**. It makes the vitamin **niacin** available to the body and the dough workable, for example for tortillas. Anyone who eats maize as the main food without this process can fall ill with the deficiency disease **pellagra**.

**Christopher Columbus** brought maize to Spain at the end of the 15th century. From there it spread in Europe in the 16th century. In Switzerland, a lot of maize is grown today, mainly as feed for animals. In the St Gallen Rhine Valley, **Ribelmais** has a long tradition. From it, Ribel is cooked, an old farmers' dish.

gewusst: Maize can hardly sow itself any more without the help of humans, because the grains sit firmly on the cob.
Popcorn is produced because the water in the maize kernel turns to steam when heated and makes the kernel burst open.

teile.einleitung: The Copper Age lies between the New Stone Age and the Bronze Age. At that time people learned to obtain copper from rock and to make tools and jewellery from it. Stone tools, however, remained important.
wichtigste: The Copper Age is named after the metal copper.
The technical term is Chalcolithic, which means copper-stone age.
Copper is obtained by heating ore strongly in a fire.
Malachite is a green copper ore.
In the burial ground of Varna in Bulgaria, over 3,000 gold objects were found.
In eastern Switzerland, the Pfyn culture was already working copper.
Pure copper is soft, so stone tools remained important.

abschnitte.text: Another name for the Copper Age is **Chalcolithic**. The word comes from Greek: “chalkós” means copper and “líthos” stone. So it means **copper-stone age**. The name fits well, because besides the first copper implements, people went on using many tools made of stone.

Copper is mostly found in rock that is called **ore**. An important copper ore is the bright green **malachite**. It is assumed that people came across copper through such striking stones. In **smelting**, the ore is heated very strongly with charcoal. The metal then separates from the rock. Some of the oldest traces of this were found at **Belovode** in Serbia, from the time around 5000 BC.

In the burial ground of **Varna** in Bulgaria lay over 3,000 objects made of gold. They are about 6,500 years old. This makes the find one of the oldest gold treasures in the world. Some graves were furnished far more richly than others. This shows that there were already differences between poor and rich at that time.

In eastern Switzerland lived the people of the **Pfyn culture**, named after Pfyn in the canton of Thurgau. In their settlements, **crucibles made of clay** with copper remains were found. In them the metal was melted and cast. **Ötzi**, who died in the Alps about 5,300 years ago, also lived in the Copper Age. His axe has a blade of almost pure copper and a handle of **yew wood**.

Tools of pure copper are relatively **soft** and quickly become blunt. So copper did not yet entirely replace stone tools. Later, copper was mixed with tin. This produced the harder **bronze**. Only it largely replaced stone, and the Bronze Age began.

gewusst: Malachite is such a beautiful green that it is also used as a gemstone.
The Copper Age did not begin everywhere at the same time, in the Balkans much earlier than in central Europe.

teile.einleitung: In the last centuries before Christ, the Celts made coins of their own. There were coins of gold, silver and a mixture called potin. Many Celtic coins have also been found in the area of present-day Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Celts struck coins of gold, silver and potin.
Potin is a mixture of copper, tin and lead.
Rainbow cups are curved Celtic gold coins.
Quinarii were small silver coins modelled on Roman ones.
A horse is shown on many coins.
In 1890, large lumps of fused potin coins were found in Zurich.

abschnitte.text: Some Celtic gold coins are curved like small bowls. They are called **rainbow cups** (Regenbogenschüsselchen). After heavy rain, such coins sometimes came to light in fields. So people believed they had fallen down at the end of the **rainbow**. Many legends surround these coins.

In the 1st century BC, small silver coins, the **quinarii**, were common in the area of Switzerland. They followed the Roman coin system and made trade with Rome easier. For everyday use there was small change made of **potin**. This is a mixture of **copper, tin and lead**. Potin contains a lot of tin and so is easy to cast.

On the back of many Celtic coins a **horse** is shown. The motif goes back to **Greek models** that showed a horse and chariot. The Celts often depicted it greatly simplified and altered. Sometimes the horse consists only of balls and lines. In this way a quite distinct Celtic style arose.

In 1890, large lumps of fused potin coins were found in **Zurich** at what is now the Alpenquai. The biggest weighs about **59 kilograms**. It contains about **18,000 coins**. They were fused together in fire. Probably they were deposited as an **offering**. The find is among the most important Celtic coin finds in Switzerland.

gewusst: A single lump of coins from Zurich contains about 18,000 coins.
In the past, people believed that rainbow cups fell from the sky.

teile.einleitung: The Old Stone Age is the oldest and by far the longest part of human history. It began about 2.5 million years ago with the first stone tools and lasted until the end of the last Ice Age. During this time, all people lived as hunters and gatherers.
wichtigste: The technical term for the Old Stone Age is Palaeolithic.
The Old Stone Age began about 2.5 million years ago in Africa.
It is by far the longest part of the Stone Age.
In Europe it ended roughly with the end of the last Ice Age about 11,700 years ago.
The Old Stone Age was followed by the Middle Stone Age and then the New Stone Age.
In Europe, Neanderthals lived for a long time before Homo sapiens arrived.
In Switzerland, the caves of Wildkirchli and Kesslerloch are famous sites.

abschnitte.titel: What is the Old Stone Age?
abschnitte.text: The word **Palaeolithic** comes from Greek and means “old stone”. The Old Stone Age began when early humans in Africa made the first simple **stone tools** about 2.5 million years ago. It lasted until about 11,700 years ago, when the last Ice Age came to an end. This means it makes up well over 99 per cent of the whole of human history.

In the Old Stone Age there were several kinds of humans, for example **Homo erectus**, the Neanderthal and the modern human. The **Neanderthal** lived in Europe and western Asia and was well adapted to the cold. About 45,000 years ago, Homo sapiens came to Europe. A few thousand years later, the Neanderthals disappeared.

For long periods of the Old Stone Age, Europe was much colder than today. Large parts of Switzerland lay under thick **glaciers**. Mammoths, woolly rhinoceroses, reindeer and wild horses lived on the steppe. People hunted these animals, gathered plants and followed the herds.

The oldest tools were simply pebbles that had been chipped. Later, people made the **hand axe** and fine blades from flint. From bone and antler they made needles, harpoons and spear-throwers. The use of **fire** is also one of the great inventions of this time.

Towards the end of the Old Stone Age, the first works of art appeared. The cave paintings of **Lascaux** and Chauvet in France are famous. The **Venus of Willendorf** from Austria is a small stone figure of a woman, only about 11 centimetres tall and around 30,000 years old. People also wore jewellery made of shells and animal teeth.

abschnitte.titel: The Old Stone Age in Switzerland
abschnitte.text: The **Wildkirchli** cave in the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden is known for its stone tools and many bones of cave bears. In the **Kesslerloch** cave near Thayngen in canton Schaffhausen, a piece of reindeer antler with a reindeer carved into it was found. It is about 14,000 years old and is one of the most beautiful works of art from the Ice Age. At that time, people in the Swiss Plateau hunted mainly reindeer and wild horses.

begriffe.erklaerung: Technical word for the Old Stone Age, meaning “old stone”.
Large stone tool, worked on both sides, that you held in your hand.
A long cold period when glaciers covered large parts of the land.
A kind of human that lived in Europe until about 40,000 years ago.

gewusst: If you spread the whole of human history over one day, the Old Stone Age would last almost the whole day until just before midnight.
Most people today outside Africa carry a small piece of Neanderthal DNA in them.
Some cave paintings in France are over 30,000 years old.

teile.einleitung: When people became settled, several families lived close to one another, and so the first villages arose. They built permanent houses of wood and clay, often near water. One of the oldest known settlements is Çatalhöyük in present-day Turkey.
wichtigste: A village arose when several families lived close together.
In central Europe, the first farmers built their houses of wood and clay.
They covered the roofs with reeds or straw.
The large houses of the first farmers in central Europe are called longhouses.
Many houses had a hearth in the middle.
Villages liked to lie near water, for drinking and fishing.
Çatalhöyük in present-day Turkey is a very old settlement.

abschnitte.text: Hunters and gatherers moved around and lived in camps. When people began to lay out fields, they had to stay in one place. Several families built their houses close together, and so a **village** arose. Together they could help and protect each other better.

One of the oldest settlements in the world is **Çatalhöyük** in present-day Turkey. Several thousand people lived there from about 7400 BC. The houses of **mud brick** stood so close together that there were no alleys. People walked over the roofs and climbed down a ladder through an opening into the house.

In central Europe, the first farmers built large **longhouses** that could be up to 30 metres long. The frame was made of wooden posts, and the walls of wickerwork smeared with **clay**. They covered the roof with reeds or straw. A large family lived in a longhouse, sometimes with a storeroom and space for animals.

In the middle of many houses was a **hearth** for cooking and warmth. On a **loom**, people made cloth. Around the village, a fence of wood was sometimes built for protection. Villages liked to lie close to a stream or lake, for drinking and fishing.

In Switzerland, many early villages arose on the shores of lakes, the **pile-dwelling settlements**. The houses stood on wooden piles so that they stayed dry in floods. Remains of such villages were found on Lake Zurich, Lake Biel, Lake Constance and many other lakes. Since 2011 they have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

In the village, people could divide up the work. Some were especially skilled at pottery, others at weaving or at making stone axes. In time there were rules for living together, and **property** such as fields and livestock. Much later, some villages became the first towns.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small settlement in which several families live together.
A long house of the first farmers in central Europe, made of wood and clay.
A mixture of clay and sand used for walls and bricks.
A device for weaving threads into cloth.

gewusst: In Çatalhöyük, people often buried their dead directly under the floor of their houses.
A single longhouse needed dozens of large tree trunks.
Jericho in the West Bank is also among the oldest permanently inhabited places in the world.

teile.einleitung: The **Corded Ware culture** is a culture of the late New Stone Age in Europe. It existed from roughly 2800 to 2200 BC. It gets its name from clay vessels into which patterns were pressed with a **cord**.
wichtigste: The Corded Ware is dated to about 2800 to 2200 BC.
Typical are vessels with patterns that were impressed with a cord.
Because of the axes in graves, it is also called the Battle Axe culture.
In the grave, men usually lay on the right side, women on the left.
DNA shows a close relationship with the Yamnaya culture of the steppe.
It extended roughly from the Rhine to the Volga.
In Switzerland, it is known from lakeshore settlements such as on Lake Zurich.

abschnitte.text: The people of this culture made beakers and jugs of clay. Before firing the vessels, they pressed a twisted **cord** into the soft clay. This produced fine line patterns. After these decorations, researchers named the whole culture.

In many graves lay carefully ground **stone axes**. That is why the Corded Ware is also called the **Battle Axe culture**. The dead were mostly buried singly in graves with burial mounds, with their legs drawn up. Typical is this: **men** lay on the **right**, **women** on the **left** side. In Jutland and northern Germany, the north-western form is called the **Single Grave culture**.

By studying ancient **DNA**, researchers found out that the Corded Ware people were closely related to the **Yamnaya culture**. This lived in the steppes north of the Black Sea. This suggests that at that time many people moved from the east to central Europe. Famous are the graves of **Eulau** in Saxony-Anhalt: there parents were found with their children, the oldest genetically proven **nuclear family**.

The Corded Ware was widespread, roughly **from the Rhine to the Volga**. In **Switzerland**, it is especially well attested in **lakeshore settlements**, for example on **Lake Zurich**. There wood, implements and vessels were well preserved in the damp ground. The pile dwellings around the Alps are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gewusst: Wood from Swiss lakeshore settlements can often be dated to the exact year using tree rings.
The graves of Eulau were only recognised as a family through modern DNA studies.

teile.einleitung: The princely grave of Hochdorf is a richly furnished grave of a Celtic prince in Baden-Württemberg. It dates from the earlier Iron Age, the Hallstatt period. Because it was never robbed, many precious grave goods were preserved.
wichtigste: The princely grave lies in Hochdorf in Baden-Württemberg.
Jörg Biel led the excavation in 1978 and 1979.
A Greek bronze cauldron held about 500 litres.
According to analyses, it was filled with mead.
In the burial chamber hung 9 drinking horns.
The dead man was over 1.80 m tall.
The burial mound had a diameter of about 60 m.

abschnitte.text: The archaeologist **Jörg Biel** of the State Office for the Preservation of Monuments in Baden-Württemberg led the excavation of the grave in **1978 and 1979**. It became one of the best-known excavations in Germany. The grave dates from the **Hallstatt period** in the 6th century BC. Because it had never been robbed, the burial chamber was found almost untouched.

Over the grave lay a **burial mound** with a diameter of about **60 metres**. It was about six metres high and surrounded by a ring of stones. Today the mound has been reconstructed. Nearby, a museum shows the finds and a replica of the burial chamber.

In the burial chamber stood a huge **bronze cauldron** from a **Greek** workshop. It measures about a metre across and held about **500 litres**. Remains of pollen show that it was filled with **mead**, a drink made from honey. On its rim sit three lions. Two come from the Greek workshop, and the third was probably made as a replacement by a local craftsman in a different style.

abschnitte.titel: The prince and his grave goods
abschnitte.text: On the wall hung **nine drinking horns**. Eight come from aurochs, and the ninth, large one is made of iron. They are decorated with gold bands and point to feasting. The dead man lay on a bronze couch and wore gold jewellery. At **over 1.80 m**, he was very tall for his time. This might point to good nutrition among the upper class.

gewusst: Even the prince's shoes were decorated with thin sheets of gold.
In the grave, a four-wheeled wagon fitted with iron was also found.

teile.einleitung: Neanderthal 1 is the famous find of bones from the Neander Valley near Düsseldorf in Germany. It was discovered in 1856 and gave a whole human species its name: the Neanderthal.
wichtigste: The bones lay in the Kleine Feldhofer Grotte in the Neander Valley.
The teacher Johann Carl Fuhlrott recognised their importance.
William King suggested the name Homo neanderthalensis in 1864.
Rudolf Virchow thought the bones were altered by disease.
Since 1877 they have been kept in the Rhineland State Museum in Bonn.
The bones are about 40,000 years old.

abschnitte.text: In 1856, workers in the Neander Valley were quarrying **limestone**. In doing so they cleared out the **Kleine Feldhofer Grotte**, a cave named after a nearby farm. In the clay they found bones. At first they thought they were the bones of a cave bear. The cave itself was later completely destroyed by the quarry. The valley is named after the hymn writer **Joachim Neander**, who was a pastor in the 17th century.

The workers gave the bones to the teacher and naturalist **Johann Carl Fuhlrott** from Elberfeld. He saw that they came from a human being. At the same time they differed clearly from humans today: the skullcap was flat, and strong ridges lay above the eyes. Fuhlrott suspected that it was a very old human. This idea was new and disputed at the time.

The English geologist **William King** described the find and suggested the name **Homo neanderthalensis** in 1864. This is regarded as the official naming of the species. The famous doctor **Rudolf Virchow** was of a different opinion. He thought the features were consequences of **disease**. Because Virchow was so well known, it took a long time in the German-speaking world before the find was recognised as a separate form of human.

Since **1877**, the bones have been kept in the **Rhineland State Museum in Bonn**. In **1997 and 2000**, researchers searched for the buried find site again. In the old rubble of the quarry, they found stone tools and many further pieces of bone. Some fitted exactly onto the old skeleton. The pieces come from at least **three individuals**. With the **radiocarbon method**, an age of about 40,000 years was determined.

gewusst: A newly found piece of bone fitted exactly onto the thigh bone of the old skeleton after almost 150 years.
In the Neander Valley today stands a museum that tells the history of the Neanderthals.

teile.einleitung: A burial mound is a grave over which people have heaped earth and stones into a hill. Especially in the Hallstatt period, the earlier Iron Age, powerful families had themselves buried in large burial mounds.
wichtigste: A burial mound is also called a tumulus in technical language.
Many burial mounds are best preserved today in forests.
Rich dead people of the Hallstatt period were often given a four-wheeled wagon in the grave.
The princely grave of Hochdorf was discovered unrobbed in 1977.
The Magdalenenberg near Villingen is the largest Hallstatt-period burial mound in central Europe.
Rich burial mounds show that there was a powerful upper class.

abschnitte.text: Over the burial chamber, people heaped up a lot of earth and stones. This produced a round hill that could be seen from far away. Experts call it a **tumulus**, the Latin word for hill. A **menhir** is something different: a single, upright stone. Burial mounds exist from many periods, but especially many from the Bronze Age and the Iron Age.

On farmland, the hills were **ploughed flat** by the plough over centuries. That is why they can often hardly be recognised there. In the forest, the ground was not worked. There, many mounds were preserved as clear rises. In Switzerland, too, quite a few burial mounds from the Iron Age are found in forests.

In the **Hallstatt period**, rich dead people were often given a **four-wheeled wagon** in the grave. There were also horse harness, drinking vessels and jewellery. Some grave goods came as **imports** from the south, from the Mediterranean region. Only a few people received such a grave. Most graves were much simpler. This shows that there was a powerful **upper class**.

In 1977, the grave of a Celtic prince was discovered at **Hochdorf** in Baden-Württemberg. Grave robbers had spared it, so the furnishings were almost complete: gold jewellery, a large bronze cauldron and a cone-shaped **hat of birch bark**. Near Villingen in the Black Forest lies the **Magdalenenberg**. It is the largest Hallstatt-period burial mound in central Europe and has a diameter of over 100 metres. Around the main grave lay over a hundred further burials.

gewusst: The prince of Hochdorf wore a finely decorated hat made of birch bark.
In the Magdalenenberg, over a hundred later graves were found beside the main grave.

teile.einleitung: Fire was one of the most important discoveries of humankind. Stone Age people used it for warmth and cooking, as light and as protection from wild animals. According to what we know today, Homo erectus was probably the first kind of human to use fire.
wichtigste: Stone Age people needed fire for warmth and cooking.
Fire kept wild animals away.
People probably got their first fire from lightning.
Later they made fire with sparks from stones or by rubbing wood together quickly.
Tinder is the dry material that catches the sparks first.
Very old traces of used fire were found in the Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa.
For about 400,000 years, people have used fire often and regularly.

abschnitte.text: The first humans could not yet make fire. They probably got their first fire from **lightning** that set a tree or dry grass alight. They took burning branches with them and carefully tended the embers. According to what we know today, **Homo erectus** was probably the first kind of human to use fire.

In the **Wonderwerk Cave** in South Africa, burnt bones and plant ash about a million years old were found. From an old fire, **charcoal** and ash are left in the ground. From these, archaeologists can tell where hearths used to be. For about 400,000 years, people have used fire often and regularly.

Later, people learned to make fire themselves. If you strike a piece of flint against a mineral containing iron such as **pyrite**, sparks are produced. It also works without stones, by rubbing wood together very fast or twirling a stick in a small board until it glows. The sparks or embers are caught with **tinder**, for example dry grass or a tree fungus, the tinder fungus.

Cooked and roasted **meat** was easier to chew and digest. Many plants and roots also became edible through cooking. The heat also killed germs. Researchers think that cooked food helped the human brain to grow larger.

The fire gave warmth on cold nights and light in dark caves. It kept **wild animals** such as bears and big cats away. Around a **hearth**, stones were laid so that the fire did not spread and the heat was stored. People sat together at the fire, told stories and planned the hunt.

With fire, you could harden spear points made of wood. Later, the first farmers used it to fire clay pots and clear forests for their fields. Without fire, **metalworking** in the Bronze Age and Iron Age would not have been possible either. The glacier mummy Ötzi carried tinder fungus with him around 3300 BC to make fire.

begriffe.erklaerung: Dry, easily burning material that catches sparks.
The place where a fire is made, often ringed with stones.
The glowing remains of a fire from which it can be lit again.
A shiny mineral that makes sparks with flint.

gewusst: The tinder fungus is a fungus that grows on trees and was once used all over Europe to make fire.
From charcoal in old hearths, researchers can work out how old a site is.
Humans are the only living things that can kindle fire themselves.

teile.einleitung: The Out-of-Africa theory explains where we modern humans come from. According to it, Homo sapiens arose in Africa and spread from there across the whole world.
wichtigste: Homo sapiens arose in Africa and spread from there.
Larger groups left Africa about 70,000 to 50,000 years ago.
A jaw from the Misliya Cave shows earlier advances.
Humans reached Australia about 50,000 years ago or earlier.
Humans came to America over the land bridge Beringia.
Genetic diversity is greatest in Africa.
The opposing hypothesis is called the multiregional hypothesis.

abschnitte.text: According to the **Out-of-Africa theory**, modern humans, **Homo sapiens**, developed in Africa. From there they gradually settled the other continents. In doing so they largely replaced the other forms of human that lived there, such as the Neanderthals in Europe. The most important opposing idea is the **multiregional hypothesis**. It assumed that modern humans developed in several regions of the world in parallel from older forms of human.

Today it is mainly **genetic data** that support the origin in Africa. Genetic diversity is **greatest in Africa**. The longer people live in one place, the more differences accumulate in their genes. **Mitochondrial DNA** is passed on only by the mother. Calculations back in time lead to a woman who lived in Africa a long time ago. She is called **Mitochondrial Eve**. She was not the only human of her time, but her line has survived to this day.

Larger groups left Africa about **70,000 to 50,000 years ago**. All humans outside Africa today go back to them. According to one hypothesis, they crossed the strait of **Bab al-Mandab** at the southern end of the Red Sea. When sea level was low, it was only a few kilometres wide. But there were also earlier advances: an upper jaw about 180,000 years old from the **Misliya Cave** in Israel, described in 2018, belongs to a modern human.

Modern humans reached **Australia** about 50,000 years ago or even earlier. That was a great achievement. Even in the Ice Age, when sea level was lower, **open sea** remained between South-East Asia and Australia. People had to cross it with **boats or rafts**. What these boats looked like is not known, because they have not been preserved.

In the Ice Age, a lot of water was locked up in ice, so sea level was lower. Between **Siberia and Alaska**, a broad land bridge arose, called **Beringia**. Where the Bering Strait lies today, there was dry land at that time. Over this bridge, people reached **America**. From there they spread as far as the southern tip of South America.

gewusst: People outside Africa carry a small share of Neanderthal genes in them.
The oldest known fossils of Homo sapiens come from Morocco and are about 300,000 years old.

teile.einleitung: Jericho is a city in the Jordan Valley and is regarded as one of the oldest permanently inhabited places in the world. Even in the New Stone Age, people there built a tower and a wall of stone.
wichtigste: Jericho lies about 250 metres below sea level.
It is regarded as the lowest-lying city in the world.
People have lived at the site for over 10,000 years.
Around 8000 BC, a stone tower about 8.5 metres high was built.
Kathleen Kenyon dug at Jericho from 1952 to 1958.
The settlement mound Tell es-Sultan has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2023.

abschnitte.text: Jericho lies in the **West Bank** near the Jordan and the Dead Sea. The city is administered by the Palestinian Authority. It lies about **250 metres below sea level** and is regarded as the lowest-lying city in the world. The area is very dry. But the strong spring **Ain es-Sultan** still supplies a lot of water today and makes the oasis fertile. That is why people could live here permanently very early.

Around 8000 BC, the inhabitants built a round **tower** of stone. It is still preserved to a height of about 8.5 metres and has a staircase inside. It is regarded as one of the oldest stone structures in the world. Around the settlement ran a **stone wall** with a ditch in front of it. It too is among the oldest walls in the world. What exactly the tower and wall were for is still debated.

The people of New Stone Age Jericho kept some **skulls** of their dead. On them they modelled faces of **plaster** and inserted shells as eyes. This produced lifelike-looking heads. Probably they honoured their **ancestors** in this way.

Ancient Jericho lies in the **Tell es-Sultan**. A “tell” is a mound that has arisen from the remains of many settlements built on top of one another. The British archaeologist **Kathleen Kenyon** studied it from 1952 to 1958. In doing so she discovered buildings from the New Stone Age. Since 2023, Tell es-Sultan has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: The tower of Jericho is thousands of years older than the pyramids in Egypt.
Jericho is at once one of the oldest and the lowest-lying city in the world.

teile.einleitung: **Ankylosaurus** was a dinosaur with armour made of bony plates. It lived at the end of the Cretaceous in North America. On its tail it carried a heavy club made of bone.
wichtigste: Ankylosaurus lived about 68 to 66 million years ago at the end of the Cretaceous.
Its fossils come from the west of North America.
It was about 6 to 9 metres long, often estimated at around 8 metres.
Its back was covered with hard bony plates and bumps.
It was a plant eater and ate low-growing plants.
The name means “stiffened lizard”.

abschnitte.text: The back of Ankylosaurus was covered with many **bony plates** and bumps. These plates grew in the skin and formed a solid **armour**. Parts of the head were protected too. So it was well armed against the bites of meat-eating dinosaurs. The name **Ankylosaurus** means “stiffened lizard”, because many of its bones were firmly fused together.

The body of Ankylosaurus was **broad and low** and lay close to the ground. It stood on four short, strong legs. So it was hard to knock over. With its heavy body, it was probably **rather slow**. But it did not need to run away, because its armour protected it.

At the end of its tail, Ankylosaurus carried a large **club** made of fused bones. Many researchers think it could swing it with great force. So it could probably defend itself against attackers. But nobody knows for sure, because behaviour can only be worked out from the bones.

Ankylosaurus was a **plant eater**. Because it was built so low, it ate **plants close to the ground**. It lived about **68 to 66 million years ago** at the end of the **Cretaceous**. Its fossils have been found in the west of **North America**. Tyrannosaurus rex lived there at the same time. Depending on the estimate, an Ankylosaurus was about **6 to 9 metres** long.

gewusst: Ankylosaurus was one of the last dinosaurs to live before the great extinction.
Complete skeletons of Ankylosaurus are very rare. It is known mainly from skulls, pieces of armour and tail clubs.

teile.einleitung: **Diplodocus** was one of the longest dinosaurs. It had a long neck, an even longer tail and ate plants. It lived in the Jurassic in North America.
wichtigste: In Diplodocus, the neck and tail were especially long.
It grew to about 25 metres long.
Its teeth looked like thin pencils.
The name Diplodocus means “double beam”.
It lived on land and carried its tail in the air.
The famous cast in the Natural History Museum in London is called “Dippy”.

abschnitte.text: **Diplodocus** belongs to the **long-necked dinosaurs**, which are also called sauropods. It grew to about **25 metres** long, which is longer than two buses one behind the other. Most of that was the long neck and the even longer tail. Despite its length, it was more slenderly built than many other long-necked dinosaurs.

abschnitte.titel: A plant eater with pencil teeth
abschnitte.text: Its teeth were as thin as **pencils** and sat at the front of the mouth. With them it stripped leaves from plants. It could hardly chew with them, and simply swallowed its food. With its long neck it reached many plants without having to walk far.

The name Diplodocus means “**double beam**”. It refers to special bones under its tail that have a double shape. Researchers think it could swing the thin tip of its tail like a **whip**. Fossilised footprints show no drag marks of a tail. So it carried it in the air above the ground.

abschnitte.titel: On land and in the museum
abschnitte.text: In the past, people thought such large animals must have lived in water. Today we know that Diplodocus lived **on land**. Best known is the cast “**Dippy**”. For many years it stood in the entrance hall of the Natural History Museum in London. Copies of the same skeleton also stand in other museums around the world.

gewusst: The tail of Diplodocus was made up of about 80 vertebrae.
Because many casts of one Diplodocus skeleton were sent out, it is one of the best-known dinosaurs in the world.

teile.einleitung: The Lascaux Cave in France is one of the most famous painted caves in the world. Its walls show horses, aurochs and deer that were painted about 17,000 years ago.
wichtigste: Lascaux lies near Montignac in the Dordogne in south-western France.
The pictures are about 17,000 years old.
Horses are shown most often.
The most famous room is called the Hall of the Bulls.
The real cave has been closed to visitors since 1963.
The newest replica, Lascaux IV, opened in 2016.

abschnitte.text: Lascaux lies near **Montignac** in the **Dordogne** in the south-west of France. In this area there are especially many sites from the **Old Stone Age**. The pictures in Lascaux were painted about 17,000 years ago. At that time it was much colder in Europe than today, and animals such as wild horses and aurochs lived there.

The most famous room is called the **Hall of the Bulls**. On wall and ceiling, large **aurochs**, horses and deer are painted. The aurochs was a large wild ox that is extinct today. One painted bull is over 5 metres long. Animal pictures this big are very rare in caves.

In Lascaux, **wild horses** are shown most often. There are also aurochs, ibex, bison and **deer**. A row of deer heads with large antlers is especially well known. In the deep **shaft** of the cave you see a bison that has been hit by a spear. Next to it lies a person with a bird's head. What this scene means, nobody knows for sure.

After the discovery, very many visitors came. Their **breath** brought moisture into the cave, and **mould** formed. The pictures were damaged, so the cave was closed in 1963. Today visitors can look at an exact **replica**. The newest is called **Lascaux IV** and opened in 2016. Lascaux, together with further sites in the Vézère valley, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

gewusst: One painted bull in Lascaux is over 5 metres long.
There are several replicas of Lascaux, so that the real pictures stay protected.

teile.einleitung: The Celts were many peoples and tribes who lived in large parts of Europe over 2,000 years ago. They had related languages, a similar art and shared customs, but never a common state of their own. Celts also lived in the area of present-day Switzerland, for example the Helvetii.
wichtigste: Greek writers called the peoples north of the Alps “Keltoi”.
The Romans called the Celts in present-day France Gauls.
Among the Celts, the druids were priests, judges and teachers.
The Celts passed on their religious knowledge mainly by word of mouth.
Around 387 BC, a Celtic army under Brennus conquered the city of Rome.
The Celts often lived in large fortified settlements, the oppida.
Breton, Irish and Welsh are Celtic languages that are still spoken today.

abschnitte.text: The name comes from the Greeks, who called the peoples north of the Alps **Keltoi**. The Romans called the Celts in present-day France **Gauls**. The Celts lived in many separate tribes that often quarrelled with one another. Among them were, for example, the Helvetii on the Plateau of present-day Switzerland.

The heyday of the Celts was the **Iron Age**, roughly from 800 BC until the conquest by the Romans. The earlier Iron Age is called the Hallstatt period, the later one the **La Tène period**. The La Tène period is named after the find site La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel, that is, after a place in Switzerland. Celts lived from Spain and France across southern Germany and the Alps to Bohemia and the British Isles.

Around 387 BC, a Celtic army under **Brennus** defeated the Romans and conquered the city of Rome. Other Celts travelled as far as Greece and on to Asia Minor. There the **Galatians** settled in central Anatolia in present-day Turkey. Later the Romans grew ever stronger, and Julius Caesar conquered the whole of Gaul between 58 and 50 BC.

The **druids** were priests, judges and teachers all in one. According to Caesar, their training lasted up to 20 years, and they were exempt from military service and from taxes. They learned everything by heart, because religious knowledge was passed on mainly by word of mouth. The Celts worshipped many gods and made offerings to them, often at springs, lakes and rivers.

The Celts built large fortified settlements called **oppida**, for example on the Engehalbinsel in Bern or on the Mont Vully. They were skilled smiths and made weapons, tools and magnificent jewellery such as the neck ring called the **torque**. In the late La Tène period, they struck coins of gold, silver and potin, a mixture of copper, tin and lead. The **Coligny calendar** on a bronze tablet from France shows that they divided up time precisely.

Celtic languages are still spoken today, for example **Breton** in France, Irish, Welsh and Scottish Gaelic. Many place and river names have Celtic roots, in Switzerland for example Thun, Solothurn or Winterthur. The Latin name for Switzerland, **Confoederatio Helvetica**, recalls the Celtic Helvetii. The well-known comics about Asterix are also set among the Gauls.

begriffe.erklaerung: A Celtic priest, judge and teacher who knew a great deal of knowledge by heart.
A large settlement of the Celts protected by walls and ramparts, similar to a town.
What the Romans called the Celts in the area of present-day France.
The later Iron Age, named after the find site La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel.
A thick, open neck ring of metal that distinguished Celts wore.

gewusst: The whole later Iron Age of Europe is named after a find site in Switzerland, La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel.
According to Caesar, the druids were not allowed to write down their knowledge, although they knew Greek writing for other things.
The abbreviation CH on Swiss cars stands for Confoederatio Helvetica and so recalls a Celtic tribe.

teile.einleitung: Among the dinosaurs there were plant eaters, meat eaters and probably also omnivores. Their teeth, their body build and their fossilised dung reveal what they ate.
wichtigste: Most dinosaur species ate plants.
Meat eaters had sharp teeth with small serrations.
Many plant eaters had a large belly for long digestion.
They ate ferns, horsetails and conifers.
Some swallowed stones to break up their food.
For protection, plant eaters had horns, armour or lived in herds.
Omnivores eat plants and meat.

abschnitte.text: Meat-eating dinosaurs had **pointed, curved teeth** with small **serrations**, similar to a steak knife. With them they could tear meat. Many ran on two strong hind legs and had sharp claws. The best-known meat eater is **Tyrannosaurus rex**. But there were far fewer species of meat eaters than of plant eaters.

Most dinosaur species were **plant eaters**. At that time, mainly **ferns**, **horsetails** and **conifers** grew. Grass as we know it today was still rare for a long time. Plants are hard to digest. So many plant eaters had a long gut and a very **large belly**. Some swallowed **stones** that helped to grind hard plants in the stomach. Chickens do something similar today.

Plant eaters had to protect themselves from the meat eaters. Some had **horns**, like Triceratops. Others wore **armour** of bony plates, like Ankylosaurus. Still others lived in large **herds**. In a group they were safer, because many eyes spot danger sooner. The huge long-necked saurians were also so big that hardly any predator could attack them.

How do we know what a dinosaur ate? The **teeth** give important clues. Fossilised dung, a **coprolite**, also helps. In it you find remains of bones or plants. In this way you can see what the animal ate last. Some dinosaurs were probably **omnivores**. They ate both plants and meat, like bears, for example, today.

gewusst: The teeth of many dinosaurs kept growing throughout life; a broken tooth was simply replaced.
Birds are the descendants of the dinosaurs today, and among them too there are plant eaters, meat eaters and omnivores.

teile.einleitung: A dinosaur skeleton in a museum is an impressive sight. But how does it get there, and what is it made of? Here you can find out how researchers put a skeleton together and which dinosaurs are easy to recognise from their skeletons.
wichtigste: The skeleton is the framework of bones in a body.
You can look at dinosaur skeletons in a museum.
Many skeletons in museums are made of casts.
A metal frame holds a large skeleton upright.
Missing bones are filled in with replicas.
Tyrannosaurus had short arms, Triceratops three horns and Stegosaurus plates on its back.

abschnitte.text: The **skeleton** is made up of many bones. It gives the body support and shape. With dinosaurs, often only the hard bones and teeth were preserved, because they turned to stone. From them, researchers can tell how big an animal was and how it moved.

Natural history museums put dinosaur skeletons on display. Real fossilised bones are very heavy and valuable. So light **casts** that look exactly the same are often shown. A **metal frame** carries the bones so that the skeleton can stand in a lifelike pose. In Switzerland you can see dinosaurs, for example, at the Saurier Museum Aathal in canton Zurich or at the Saurier Museum Frick in Aargau.

A completely whole skeleton is almost never found. Missing bones are filled in as **replicas**, modelled on related animals. Good museums show which parts are real and which are rebuilt. Sometimes a skeleton is later mounted again in a new way, because researchers have found out more about how the animals held themselves.

Some dinosaurs can be recognised straight away from the skeleton. **Tyrannosaurus** was a huge meat-eating dinosaur with very short arms. **Triceratops** means “three-horned face”: it had two long horns above the eyes and one on the nose. **Stegosaurus** carried two rows of large bony plates on its back and spikes on its tail. **Diplodocus** and **Brachiosaurus** were long-necked dinosaurs that ate plants.

gewusst: A cast of a Diplodocus stands in several museums around the world, because many copies were made of the same skeleton.
Mounting a large dinosaur skeleton can take weeks or even months.

teile.einleitung: The Mousterian is a culture of the Middle Palaeolithic. It is named after a find site in France and is linked mainly with the Neanderthals, but early modern humans also made such tools.
wichtigste: Gabriel de Mortillet introduced the term in 1872.
The name comes from the find site Le Moustier in the Dordogne.
Typical is the Levallois technique with a prepared core.
Scrapers are especially common.
François Bordes divided the Mousterian into variants.
Early Homo sapiens also made Mousterian tools.

abschnitte.text: The French researcher **Gabriel de Mortillet** introduced the term in 1872. He named the culture after the find site **Le Moustier** in the Dordogne in south-western France. Mortillet divided the Old Stone Age according to typical find sites. The Mousterian belongs to the **Middle Palaeolithic**. It ended about 40,000 years ago. In Switzerland too, finds from this time are known, for example from the cave of **Cotencher** in the canton of Neuchâtel.

Typical of the Mousterian is the **Levallois technique**. In it, a stone, the **core**, was first carefully prepared. Then, with one targeted blow, a flake of planned shape was struck off. This required a lot of practice and **forward thinking**. You had to know beforehand what the finished piece should look like. From the flakes, points and other implements were made.

Most common are **scrapers** in many forms: single, double or curved. With them, for example, pelts and wood were worked. On some tools, remains of **bitumen** and other natural adhesives were found. They show that points were fixed to handles or shafts. This is called **hafting**. In a late form, the “Mousterian of Acheulean tradition”, there are small, **heart-shaped hand axes**.

The researcher **François Bordes** arranged the finds with a statistical method. He counted how often certain tool types occurred. In this way he distinguished several variants, for example the **Charentian type** and the **Denticulate type** with toothed pieces. A subgroup of the Charentian is the **Quina type** with thick, curved scrapers. Why these differences existed is still debated today.

In Europe, the tools of the Mousterian mostly come from **Neanderthals**. In the caves of **Qafzeh** and **Skhul** in Israel, however, they were found together with remains of early **Homo sapiens**. This shows that a culture cannot be assigned rigidly to a single form of human. Different groups of people could use similar techniques.

gewusst: The Levallois technique is named after a suburb of Paris where such stone tools were found.
The adhesive remains on Mousterian tools are among the oldest evidence that humans built tools from several parts.

teile.einleitung: A coin is a small piece of metal with a fixed value. The first coins arose about 2,600 years ago in Lydia, in present-day Turkey. The Celts in Switzerland, too, already made coins.
wichtigste: Before coins, people exchanged goods.
The first coins appeared around 600 BC in the kingdom of Lydia.
They consisted of a mixture of gold and silver.
The picture was impressed with a die and hammer.
The Celts imitated Greek gold coins.
Potin coins were cast in moulds.

abschnitte.text: In earlier times there was no money. Whoever needed something gave something else for it. For example, people exchanged cereal for a tool. This is called **barter**. It was often tiresome: not everyone wanted just what you could offer. And you cannot put a cow in your pocket. Coins, by contrast, are **small and light**, and you can carry them and count them.

The first coins arose around **600 BC** in the kingdom of **Lydia**. This country lay in the west of present-day **Turkey**. The coins consisted of a natural mixture of **gold and silver**. Metal is valuable and lasts a very long time. Soon the Greeks took over the idea, and later the Romans too. In this way coins spread in many countries around the Mediterranean.

First a small piece of metal was made, the **blank**. It was placed between two **dies** with cut pictures. Then it was struck hard with a **hammer**. In this way the picture was pressed into the metal. This is called **striking**. Today large machines do this. In Switzerland, the mint **Swissmint** in Bern strikes the francs and rappen.

The **Celts** got to know coins through trade. They knew gold coins of a Greek king and made coins of their own after this model. There were also **potin coins**. Potin is a mixture of copper, tin and lead. These coins were not struck but **cast in moulds**. In **Zurich**, in 1890, a large lump of many potin coins baked together was found, the Zurich potin lump.

gewusst: The Greek models of the Celtic gold coins came from King Philip II of Macedon, the father of Alexander the Great.
The Zurich potin lump consists of thousands of coins that have fused together.

teile.einleitung: The three-age system divides prehistory into the Stone Age, the Bronze Age and the Iron Age. It arranges the periods according to the material from which people made their tools and weapons. It was developed in the 19th century in Denmark.
wichtigste: The three-age system distinguishes the Stone Age, the Bronze Age and the Iron Age.
Christian Jürgensen Thomsen developed it at the collection of antiquities in Copenhagen.
It was published in 1836 in the “Guide to Northern Antiquities”.
Thomsen relied on objects that were found together.
Jens Jacob Asmussen Worsaae confirmed the system with excavations.
In 1865, John Lubbock divided the Stone Age into the Palaeolithic and the Neolithic.

abschnitte.text: **Christian Jürgensen Thomsen** put the holdings of the royal **collection of antiquities** in Copenhagen in order. The Danish National Museum later grew out of it. He sorted the finds by the material of weapons and tools: stone, bronze and iron. His system appeared in **1836** in the “Guide to Northern Antiquities”. A German translation followed as early as 1837.

Thomsen based his sequence especially on **closed finds**. These are objects that lay together in a grave or a hoard. He paid attention to which things regularly occurred together. In this way he could form groups and explain which period came before which.

Thomsen's pupil **Jens Jacob Asmussen Worsaae** showed in excavations that finds of stone, bronze and iron lay on top of each other in this order. He is regarded as one of the first professional archaeologists. In 1865, the Englishman **John Lubbock**, in his book “Prehistoric Times”, distinguished the Old Stone Age, the **Palaeolithic**, from the New Stone Age, the **Neolithic**. These terms are still used today.

abschnitte.titel: An old idea, and the limits of the system
abschnitte.text: The Roman poet **Lucretius** had already described a sequence of stone, bronze and iron in his poem “De rerum natura”. Thomsen turned this into a scientific system of order. But it does not fit everywhere. In Africa south of the Sahara, the Stone Age was followed directly by the **Iron Age** in many places. In America, there was no iron smelting before the arrival of the Europeans.

gewusst: Even in Swiss museums, finds from prehistory are still arranged by Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age.
Thomsen was not a trained archaeologist, but came from a merchant family.

teile.einleitung: A hand stencil is the outline of a hand on a cave wall. People in prehistoric times placed their hand against the rock and blew paint around it. Such hands are among the oldest pictures of humankind.
wichtigste: In many caves you can find outlines and prints of human hands.
For a hand stencil, paint is blown around the hand.
A hollow bird bone, for example, served as a tube.
For a positive hand print, the painted hand is pressed against the wall.
Many hands are sprayed with red ochre, others with black.
Small hands show that children were there too.

abschnitte.text: For a **hand stencil**, you place your hand against the wall and blow paint around it. Where the hand lay, the wall stays free. This produces a light outline. For a **positive hand print**, you dip your hand in paint and press it against the wall. In many caves there are both kinds, often beside pictures of animals.

As paint, people mainly used **ochre**, a red or yellow earth. For black they took charcoal or dark minerals. The paint was mixed with water. Then it was blown through a **hollow bone**, such as a bird bone, or through a plant stalk. Some people probably blew the paint straight from the mouth.

The most famous site is the **Cueva de las Manos**, the “Cave of the Hands”, in Patagonia in **Argentina**. There are hundreds of hands on the rock wall. In the cave of **Gargas** in France, many hands look as if fingers were missing. Perhaps the fingers were just bent over, perhaps it was a kind of sign. Nobody knows exactly.

Some hands are so small that they must come from **children** or teenagers. So children were in the caves too. Why people put their hands on the walls is not certain. Perhaps it was a sign meaning “I was here”, perhaps it had a religious meaning.

gewusst: Hand prints are found on almost every continent, from Europe to Australia.
In the Cueva de las Manos there are so many hands that the wall looks almost as if it were painted in colour.

teile.einleitung: The cave bear was a large bear that lived in Europe during the Ice Age. Its bones are found in many caves, including in Switzerland, for example in the Drachenloch and in the Wildkirchli.
wichtigste: The cave bear was bigger and stronger than most brown bears today.
It ate mainly plants.
It lived at the same time as Stone Age people.
It died out in the last Ice Age, about 25,000 years ago.
In Switzerland, bones were found in the Drachenloch and in the Wildkirchli.
In the past, its skulls were taken for dragon skulls.

abschnitte.text: The cave bear is called **Ursus spelaeus** in science. “Ursus” means bear and “spelaeus” means “living in caves”. It was heavier and stronger than most **brown bears** today. Even so, it ate mainly **plants**. This is shown by studies of its teeth and bones.

Cave bears spent their **winter rest** in caves. Weak and old animals often did not survive the winter. So over thousands of years many bones piled up. On the walls of many caves you can still see **scratch marks** from their claws today. Cave bears and **Stone Age people** lived in Europe at the same time and sometimes used the same caves.

High above **Vättis** in the canton of St Gallen lies the **Drachenloch** (“dragon's hole”). Many cave bear bones were found there. In the **Wildkirchli** in the Alpstein in Appenzell Innerrhoden, too, cave bear bones came to light. Tools of Stone Age people were also found there. These caves lie high in the mountains and show that the bears also lived in the mountains.

In the past, people did not know the cave bear. So the large skulls were interpreted as the remains of **dragons**. That is why some caves have names such as Drachenloch or Drachenhöhle (“dragon cave”). The cave bear died out during the **last Ice Age**, about 25,000 years ago. Exactly why is still being researched. Probably cold, less food and humans played a part.

gewusst: The Drachenloch above Vättis got its name from bear skulls that were taken for dragon skulls.
Although it was so big, the cave bear lived mainly on plants.

teile.einleitung: Hunter-gatherers are people who live from hunting and from wild-growing plants. Throughout the whole Old Stone Age, all people lived like this, that is, during over 99 per cent of human history. They roamed in small groups and followed the animals and the ripe plants.
wichtigste: Hunter-gatherers gathered berries, nuts and other plants.
They often moved on because they followed the animals and ripe plants.
People without a fixed home are called nomads.
Important weapons were the spear and the spear-thrower.
In Ice Age central Europe, they hunted reindeer and wild horses especially often.
Of a killed animal, they used almost everything.
The dog was the first animal helper of humans.

abschnitte.text: People of the Stone Age **gathered** berries, nuts, mushrooms, roots, seeds and herbs. They knew exactly which plants were edible and which were poisonous. Birds' eggs, honey, mussels and snails also belonged on the menu. Often gathering was even more important for nutrition than hunting.

The most important weapon of the hunters was the **spear**. With the **spear-thrower**, a stick with a hook, spears could be thrown further and harder. Towards the end of the Old Stone Age, the bow and arrow were added. In Ice Age central Europe, people hunted **reindeer** and wild horses especially often.

Of a killed animal, the hunters used almost everything. They ate the meat, and from the fur they made clothes and tents. From bone and antler they carved needles, harpoons and tools. Sinews served as thread, and fat burned in lamps.

Hunter-gatherers had no fixed home. They are called **nomads**, and their way of life is nomadic. They followed the herds of animals and the plants that ripened according to the season. They lived in small **groups**, mostly of a few dozen people. Everyone had to help, and the food was shared.

The first domestic animal of humans was the **dog**. It descends from the wolf and was tamed more than 15,000 years ago, long before all other domestic animals. Dogs helped with hunting, guarded the camp and kept people warm at night. In the Kesslerloch near Thayngen, too, very old dog bones were found.

With the invention of farming, most people became settled. But some peoples still live wholly or partly as hunter-gatherers today. These include the **San** in the Kalahari in southern Africa and the Hadza in Tanzania. Researchers learn a lot from them about life in the Stone Age.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who has no fixed home and moves around.
A stick with a hook with which spears can be thrown further.
A species of deer of the cold regions that also lived in Switzerland in the Ice Age.
The taming and breeding of wild animals into domestic animals.

gewusst: Hunter-gatherers often had to work only a few hours a day for their food.
On Lake Neuchâtel, camp sites of reindeer hunters about 15,000 years old were found.
People of the Stone Age knew hundreds of plants and knew what they could be used for.

teile.einleitung: The Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago from dust and rock that circled the young Sun. At the beginning it was a glowing hot ball full of volcanoes and liquid lava. Only after a long cooling did seas form, and finally the first life.
wichtigste: The Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago.
The Sun came first, and the Earth formed from dust and rock around it.
At the beginning the Earth was glowing hot and had very many volcanoes.
The Moon probably formed in a huge collision.
As the Earth cooled and it rained for a long time, the seas formed.
The first life arose in the water and was tiny.
The Earth is the third planet from the Sun and almost a sphere.

abschnitte.text: First the **Sun** formed from a huge cloud of gas and dust. Around it, a flat disc of dust and rock was left over. In it, small grains stuck together and became ever larger lumps. From such lumps, the **Earth** grew over a few million years.

The young Earth was glowing hot. Lumps of rock from space constantly crashed into it, and its surface was partly a sea of **lava**. Lava is liquid, hot rock. Heavy materials such as iron sank inwards and formed the **Earth's core**, while lighter rocks stayed on top.

According to researchers today, the young Earth collided with another heavenly body. It was about as big as Mars and is called **Theia**. In the huge collision, a lot of material was flung into space. From it the **Moon** formed.

The many **volcanoes** gave off gases and water vapour, and from them a first atmosphere formed. As the Earth slowly cooled, the water vapour turned into clouds, and it rained for a very long time. So the hollows filled with water, and the **seas** formed. Some of the water probably also came to Earth with comets and asteroids.

The Earth is the third **planet** from the Sun. It is almost a sphere, but slightly flattened at the poles, and has a diameter of about 12,700 kilometres. Deep inside it is very hot, in the core about as hot as the surface of the Sun. Above lie the **mantle** and the thin crust on which we live.

In the seas, the first **life** arose at least 3.5 billion years ago. The first living things were tiny and consisted of just a single cell. They lived in the water because it protected them from the strong radiation of the Sun. It then took billions more years until the first plants and animals on land.

begriffe.erklaerung: Liquid, hot rock that comes out of volcanoes.
The innermost part of the Earth, mainly made of iron and nickel.
A large heavenly body that orbits a star.
A large connected mass of land, for example Europe or Africa.

gewusst: The oldest known mineral grains on Earth come from Australia and are about 4.4 billion years old.
Shortly after it formed, the Moon was much closer to the Earth than today and looked huge in the sky.
A day on the young Earth lasted only a few hours, because it spun much faster.

teile.einleitung: **Ammonites** were sea animals with a spiral shell. They lived in the oceans for many millions of years and are now extinct. Their fossilised shells are among the best-known fossils, in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: Ammonites belonged to the cephalopods, like squid and octopuses today.
Their shell was usually coiled into a flat spiral.
Inside, the shell was divided into many chambers.
The animal lived in the front chamber, the living chamber.
The name comes from the Egyptian god Amun, who was shown with ram's horns.
Ammonites are often found in the Jura.
The largest ammonites grew to over 1.5 metres.

abschnitte.text: Ammonites belonged to the **cephalopods**. This group of animals today includes squid and octopuses. Like these, ammonites had **tentacles** with which they grabbed food. Unlike a squid, however, they had a hard **shell**. The animal alive today that looks most like them is the **pearly nautilus**, also called the **nautilus**. It also has a chambered spiral shell.

The shell of an ammonite was usually coiled into a flat **spiral**. It is a little like a snail shell. Inside, it was divided into many **chambers**, separated by thin walls. The rear chambers contained gas and liquid and helped the animal to **float** in the water. The animal itself sat in the large **living chamber** at the front, by the opening, and stretched its tentacles out from there.

The name goes back to the Egyptian god **Amun**, whom the Greeks called **Ammon**. He was shown with curved **ram's horns**. The coiled shells reminded people of these horns. That is why fossilised ammonites are called **Ammonshörner** (“horns of Ammon”) in German.

In Switzerland, ammonites are found especially often in the **Jura**. Its limestone rocks formed on the bed of a sea. A whole geological period is even named after this mountain range, the **Jurassic**. Because the shapes of ammonites changed quickly, they help experts to work out the age of layers of rock. That is why they are called **index fossils**.

Most ammonites were a few centimetres across. But there were giants too. The largest known ammonite was found in 1895 near **Seppenrade** in Germany. Its shell measures about **1.74 metres**. At the end of the **Cretaceous**, about 66 million years ago, the ammonites died out, at the same time as the dinosaurs.

gewusst: Ammonites filled the seas for over 300 million years.
Some ammonites shimmer in rainbow colours because their shell was made of mother-of-pearl.

teile.einleitung: Homo erectus is an extinct human species that lived for about two million years. It was one of the first humans to leave Africa and reach as far as Asia.
wichtigste: The name Homo erectus means “upright human”.
Eugène Dubois found the first fossils on Java in 1891.
Finds near Zhoukoudian in China became known as “Peking Man”.
In Dmanisi in Georgia, fossils about 1.8 million years old were found.
Homo erectus used fire about a million years ago.
Adults were about 1.45 to 1.80 metres tall.

abschnitte.text: The Latin word “erectus” comes from “erigere”, which means to set upright. The name stresses the **upright build of the body**. Adult Homo erectus were about 1.45 to 1.80 metres tall and weighed 50 to 60 kilograms. Their body already closely resembled that of humans today. The species lived for about **2 million years**. The most recent finds are about 110,000 years old.

The German zoologist **Ernst Haeckel** had suspected a link between ape and human and called it “Pithecanthropus”. The Dutch doctor **Eugène Dubois** therefore travelled deliberately to South-East Asia. In 1891, he found a skullcap near **Trinil** on the island of **Java**, and later a thigh bone. At first he named the species Pithecanthropus erectus. For a long time people spoke of “Java Man”.

In the 1920s, further fossils were found in the cave of **Zhoukoudian** near Beijing. Davidson Black at first named them Sinanthropus pekinensis, and they became known as **Peking Man**. In **Dmanisi** in Georgia, a lower jaw and several skulls were found from 1991 onwards. They are about 1.8 million years old and are among the oldest human finds outside Africa.

In the **Wonderwerk Cave** in South Africa, traces of fire about a million years old were found. They are attributed to Homo erectus. Fire helped with **cooking**, keeping warm and protection from wild animals. Homo erectus also made **hand axes**, stone tools worked on both sides. This made it very adaptable and able to live in many regions.

gewusst: Dubois searched deliberately for a fossil that, according to a theory, had to exist, and indeed found it.
Homo erectus existed for much longer than modern humans have so far.

teile.einleitung: A rescue excavation is an excavation that is carried out before a find site is destroyed, for example by building work. Today most excavations in central Europe are rescue excavations, in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: Rescue excavations take place before a find site is destroyed.
Most excavations in central Europe are rescue excavations.
The Convention of Malta of 1992 protects the archaeological heritage.
It gives preference to preserving the find site in the ground.
Under the polluter-pays principle, developers contribute to the costs.
In Switzerland, such finds belong to the canton.

abschnitte.titel: Digging before it is too late
abschnitte.text: When a find site is threatened with loss through **building projects**, **erosion** or agriculture, it is excavated beforehand. This is called a **rescue excavation**. In it, everything is exactly **documented**: drawn, photographed and measured. The finds go to the museum or to the archaeology store. The find site itself often disappears for ever afterwards. That is why the work has to be very careful.

In 1992, the **European Convention on the Protection of the Archaeological Heritage** was signed in **Valletta** on Malta. It is called the **Convention of Malta** for short. It demands that archaeological questions be included early in **spatial planning**. Ideally a find site should stay untouched **in the ground**, in Latin **in situ**. For every excavation destroys the evidence, even if it documents it. Sometimes building plans can be adapted for this.

Rescue excavations cost a lot of money. Under the **polluter-pays principle**, developers whose projects endanger find sites contribute to the costs. They bear part of the costs of investigation and documentation. In Switzerland, ownerless antiquities of scientific value belong, under **Article 724 of the Civil Code**, to the **canton** in which they were found. That is why the **cantonal archaeological services** are responsible for excavations.

In the **1980s**, the **A5** motorway was built on Lake Neuchâtel. For this, the lakeshore at Hauterive was filled in. Beforehand, the find site **Hauterive-Champréveyres** was excavated.
