Camps of reindeer hunters of the late Old Stone Age and settlements from the Bronze Age were found. In **Zurich**, the **Opéra car park** was built in 2010 and 2011 under the **Sechseläutenplatz**. Beforehand, the city archaeology service studied the remains of New Stone Age **lakeshore settlements** over a large area.

gewusst: Many famous finds in Switzerland only came to light because building took place and people had to dig beforehand.
In the excavation for the Opéra car park, thousands of finds from the pile-dwelling period were recovered.

teile.einleitung: Ötzi's copper axe is one of the most famous tools of prehistory. Ötzi was carrying it when he died in the Alps about 5,300 years ago. What is special: the whole axe with its wooden handle is preserved.
wichtigste: The blade of Ötzi's axe is made of almost pure copper.
The handle is made of tough yew wood.
The blade was fixed with birch pitch and leather straps.
The copper comes from Tuscany in Italy.
Ötzi lived in the Copper Age.
With Ötzi's axe, the wooden handle is completely preserved, which is very rare.

abschnitte.text: Ötzi was found in 1991 in the **Ötztal Alps** on the border between Italy and Austria. The ice had preserved his body and his equipment over thousands of years. His equipment included an **axe**. Ötzi lived in the **Copper Age**, when the first tools of copper appeared. Today he can be seen in the Archaeological Museum in Bolzano.

The blade is made of almost pure **copper**. Fresh copper shines **reddish** like a new coin. The handle is made of **yew wood**, which is tough and does not break easily. The blade sat in a notch in the wood. It was glued in place with **birch pitch**, a natural adhesive, and tied on with **leather straps**.

abschnitte.titel: Where did the copper come from?
abschnitte.text: Researchers studied the metal closely. It comes from **Tuscany** in Italy, so from far away. This shows that people at that time exchanged goods over great distances. A copper axe was valuable, and not everyone owned one.

The axe was used to fell trees and chop **wood**. Perhaps Ötzi also needed it to carve his bow. From this period, mostly only blades without handles are otherwise found, because wood rots in the ground. With Ötzi's axe, the **wooden handle** was preserved completely. That is why we know exactly how such axes were built.

If copper lies outside for a long time, it gets a **green layer**. This is called **patina**. This layer protects the metal underneath. That is why many church roofs and monuments made of copper are green. Ötzi's copper axe, too, is no longer shiny red.

gewusst: Besides the copper axe, Ötzi also carried a dagger with a flint blade.
The blade of the axe is only about 10 centimetres long, the whole handle about 60 centimetres.

teile.einleitung: Dendrochronology is a method for working out the age of wood. It reads the annual rings of a tree like a calendar. In this way researchers find out when a tree was felled, for example for a pile dwelling or an old roof beam.
wichtigste: Dendrochronology dates wood using the annual rings.
The word comes from the Greek “dendron” for tree.
In central Europe a tree forms exactly one annual ring each year.
The weather decides how wide an annual ring becomes.
The American astronomer Andrew Ellicott Douglass is regarded as its founder.
The Hohenheim tree-ring calendar reaches back over 12,000 years.
If the bark edge is preserved, the exact year of felling is known.

abschnitte.text: A tree grows not only in height but also in width. In spring it forms pale, loose **earlywood**, and in late summer darker, denser **latewood**. Together they make one **annual ring**. The sharp change to the next earlywood makes the boundary between two years visible. So anyone who counts the rings knows how old a tree is.

Not every annual ring is equally wide. In warm, wet years a tree grows more than in cold or dry ones. This produces a typical **pattern** of wide and narrow rings. Trees in the same area show a similar pattern in the same years. This is exactly what dendrochronology uses: you compare the pattern of a piece of wood with a known series.

Researchers link the patterns of living trees, old beams and timbers from river gravel. Where two series overlap, they can be joined together. This produces a **tree-ring calendar**. The Hohenheim tree-ring calendar from southern Germany reaches back without a gap for over 12,000 years, to the time after the last Ice Age. The method was founded at the beginning of the 20th century by **Andrew Ellicott Douglass**, who was actually looking for traces of solar activity.

abschnitte.titel: Working out the year of felling
abschnitte.text: The last ring directly under the bark is called the **bark edge**. If it is preserved, the year of felling can be worked out to the exact year. If it is missing, you can only give the earliest possible year of felling. For oaks, an estimate helps: they have a fairly constant number of pale **sapwood rings**. If some of these are preserved, the missing rings are added statistically.

A sample is taken from a living tree with an **increment borer**. This hollow tool pulls a thin rod of wood out as far as the middle of the trunk, and the tree survives the small intervention. The method helps in archaeology, for example with the pile dwellings on Swiss lakes, whose piles could often be dated very precisely. Old houses, churches and bridges can also be dated this way.

gewusst: With tree rings you can sometimes work out not only the year but even the season in which a tree was felled.
The annual rings also reveal what the weather was like thousands of years ago.

teile.einleitung: **Bipedalism** is the technical term for walking on two legs. Humans are the only living primates that move around like this all the time. Many parts of our skeleton show how well we are built for it.
wichtigste: The word comes from Latin: “bi” means two, “pes” means foot.
Upright walking freed the hands for carrying and making things.
In humans, the foramen magnum lies far down in the middle of the base of the skull.
Seen from the side, the spine has a double S shape.
The pelvis is short and broad like a bowl.
The foot has an arch and a big toe pointing forwards.
Sahelanthropus from Chad is thought to be a possible early biped.

abschnitte.text: Most mammals walk on four legs. Great apes such as chimpanzees can stand upright for a short while, but mostly walk on all fours. Only humans walk upright all the time. This way of walking is called **bipedalism**, from the Latin words **bi** for two and **pes** for foot. A big advantage: the **hands** become free. This made it possible to carry food, children or tools.

In the skull there is an opening through which the spinal cord passes: the **foramen magnum**. In humans it lies far down in the middle of the base of the skull. This way the head sits balanced on the upright spine. The **spine** itself, seen from the side, has a **double S shape**. It absorbs shocks when walking and brings the body's centre of gravity over the feet.

The human **pelvis** is shorter and broader than a chimpanzee's. It has the shape of a **bowl** and supports the organs from below. It also provides room for muscles that keep the body stable when walking. The human **foot** has an **arch** that works like a spring. The big toe points forwards and pushes off when walking. Chimpanzees, by contrast, can grip with their feet.

When upright walking arose is studied using fossils. One possible early biped is **Sahelanthropus tchadensis** from Chad, about 7 million years old. Its skull, nicknamed **Toumaï**, was found in 2001. The position of the foramen magnum points to upright walking, but this is disputed. **Australopithecus afarensis**, to which the famous skeleton Lucy belongs, certainly walked upright.

Why our ancestors walked upright has not been finally settled. There are several **hypotheses**. One says that in the hot **savannah** the body presents less surface to the midday sun. The sun then hits mainly the head and shoulders, and higher up there is more cooling wind. Other researchers stress that on two legs you can walk long distances using little energy. Probably several reasons worked together.

gewusst: Our foot arch is still flat in small children and only forms properly when they learn to walk.
Humans cannot run particularly fast, but can keep running over very long distances.

teile.einleitung: About 66 million years ago, the dinosaurs disappeared from the Earth almost overnight. The main cause was a huge asteroid that struck in Mexico. Together with the dinosaurs, about three out of four kinds of animals and plants died out.
wichtigste: The dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago.
An asteroid about 10 to 15 kilometres across struck the Earth.
The crater lies in present-day Mexico on the Yucatán Peninsula.
Dust darkened the sky, and the Earth turned cold.
About three out of four kinds of animals and plants died out.
Huge volcanic eruptions probably played a part too.
Small mammals, crocodiles and the ancestors of birds survived.

abschnitte.text: An **asteroid** is a lump of rock in space. About 66 million years ago, a lump like this, about 10 to 15 kilometres across, hit the Earth. It struck in the area of present-day Mexico and left behind the **Chicxulub crater**, about 180 kilometres across. Today the crater lies hidden beneath the Yucatán Peninsula and the sea.

The impact flung huge amounts of dust, soot and rock into the air. There were gigantic waves called **tsunamis**, and huge forest fires. The dust darkened the sky, and for months hardly any sunlight got through. So it turned cold, and plants could no longer grow properly.

Without sunlight, many plants died. After that, the large **plant eaters** also found too little food, and the meat eaters went hungry with them. So about three out of four species died out, including all the large dinosaurs, the flying reptiles and many marine reptiles. The **ammonites**, sea animals with snail-like shells, disappeared too.

At about the same time, there were huge **volcanic eruptions** in India. Enormous amounts of lava flowed out, now known as the Deccan Traps. The volcanoes' gases changed the climate even more. Many researchers think that the asteroid and the volcanoes together made the disaster so terrible.

The survivors were mainly small animals that needed little food or could hide. They included small **mammals**, crocodiles, turtles, lizards and snakes. Some birds survived too, and birds are in fact the descendants of the dinosaurs. After the extinction, mammals spread widely, and much later humans arose from them too.

In 1980, the physicist Luis Alvarez and his son Walter discovered a thin layer of rock with a lot of **iridium**. This metal is rare on Earth, but common in asteroids. The layer is found worldwide at the boundary between the Cretaceous and the Palaeogene. Later, the matching crater was found in Mexico.

begriffe.erklaerung: A lump of rock that orbits the Sun.
A large, round hollow made by an impact.
An event in which very many species disappear in a short time.
A rare metal that points to an impact from space.

gewusst: The birds that chirp in your garden today are the last living dinosaurs.
The asteroid was so fast that it crossed the Earth's atmosphere in a few seconds.
The dinosaurs lived on Earth for about 165 million years, humans only for about 300,000 years.

teile.einleitung: People of the Old Stone Age who sought shelter in caves or under rock overhangs are often called cave dwellers. They used caves as protection from the cold, but often lived in tents too. In Switzerland, the Kesslerloch cave near Thayngen is a famous find site.
wichtigste: People of the Stone Age used caves as protection from the cold.
When there was no cave, they often lived in tents.
They made their clothes from animal skins and sewed with needles made of bone.
They slept on furs on the ground.
The Neanderthals are named after a valley in Germany.
The cave bear hibernated in caves.
In the Kesslerloch near Thayngen SH, the famous drawing of a reindeer was found.

abschnitte.text: In the Ice Age it was much colder in Europe than today. People used **caves** and rock overhangs as protection from cold, rain and wind. Mostly they lived in the bright entrance area, not deep in the dark. When there was no cave, they built **tents** from wooden poles and animal hides.

Stone Age people made their clothes from **animal skins** and leather. With needles made of **bone** that had an eye, they sewed the pieces together with animal sinews. They slept on furs on the ground, close to the warming fire. As jewellery, they liked to wear shells and pierced animal teeth.

The **Neanderthals** are named after the Neander Valley near Düsseldorf in Germany, where their bones were found in 1856. They lived in Europe for a long time and were strongly built and well adapted to the cold. They made good stone tools, used fire and cared for the sick. About 40,000 years ago they died out.

In many caves the **cave bear** also lived, a large animal of the Ice Age. It hibernated there. Some animals died during hibernation, which is why you often find many bear bones in caves. The cave bear was bigger than a brown bear today and ate mainly plants.

A famous cave in Switzerland is the **Kesslerloch** near Thayngen in the canton of Schaffhausen. Reindeer hunters lived there about 14,000 years ago. Thousands of stone tools and bones of prey animals were found. Especially well known is a piece of reindeer antler with the engraved drawing of a **reindeer** that seems to be grazing.

In some caves, people left magnificent **cave paintings**. In the cave of **Lascaux** in France, horses, deer and bulls are painted. They made the colours from coloured earth, charcoal and fat. Light was provided by torches and small stone lamps in which animal fat burned.

begriffe.erklaerung: A picture that Stone Age people painted on a cave wall.
A rock overhang under which people sought shelter.
A species of human that lived in Europe until about 40,000 years ago.
A large bear of the Ice Age that spent the winter in caves.

gewusst: People of the Stone Age lived much more often in the open air than deep in caves.
In the Wildkirchli in the Alpstein, hundreds of cave bear bones were found.
Many cave paintings lie so deep in the mountain that you could only see them with a lamp.

teile.einleitung: **Sabre-toothed cats** were large big cats with huge canine teeth. The best known is **Smilodon**, which lived in the Ice Age in America. Today all sabre-toothed cats are extinct.
wichtigste: Sabre-toothed cats had very long canine teeth.
The best-known sabre-toothed cat is called Smilodon.
Smilodon lived in the Ice Age in America.
It hunted large plant eaters.
Smilodon had a short tail.
Many animals got stuck in sticky tar pits.
The sabre-toothed cat is extinct.

abschnitte.text: The special feature of the sabre-toothed cat was its **very long canine teeth** in the upper jaw. In the largest Smilodon species they were over 20 centimetres long. The teeth stuck out of the mouth like curved sabres. To use them, the cat could open its mouth very wide.

**Smilodon** was about as big as a lion, but more stockily built. It had strong forelegs and a **short tail**. It hunted **large plant eaters**, for example bison or young mammoths. Probably it grabbed its prey with its forelegs and then bit with the long teeth. Fast, long chases were probably not its strength.

In **Los Angeles** there are the **La Brea** tar pits. There sticky asphalt wells up out of the ground. In the Ice Age, animals got **stuck** in it. Predators that wanted to eat them also fell in. In this way, thousands of Smilodon bones were preserved. Today they are **fossils** and show us what these cats looked like.

Smilodon lived in **North and South America**. At the end of the last Ice Age, about 10,000 years ago, it **died out**. Many of its prey animals also disappeared then. Smilodon is only distantly related to tigers or lions today. There were also other sabre-toothed cats that formerly lived in Europe.

gewusst: Smilodon is the official state fossil of California.
Sabre-toothed cats were not tigers, although they are often called “sabre-toothed tigers”.

teile.einleitung: Fire was vital for people in prehistoric times. But how do you make a fire without matches? With friction, embers and dry tinder it was possible even in the Stone Age.
wichtigste: If you rub two pieces of wood together quickly, heat is produced.
In fire drilling, a wooden stick is twirled quickly in a board.
With a bow, the drill stick turns faster.
From the embers, a flame is made with dry tinder.
You blow carefully into the embers so that they burst into flame.
Ötzi carried the tinder fungus with him for making fire.

abschnitte.text: Fire gave people **warmth** and **light** at night. It protected them from wild animals, and you could cook food with it. Cooked food is easier to chew and digest. So making and tending fire was one of the most important skills of prehistoric times.

If you rub two pieces of wood together quickly, **heat** is produced. If it gets hot enough, **embers** form. In **fire drilling**, a wooden stick is twirled quickly in a hollow in a wooden board. It goes faster with a **bow**: the string is wrapped round the stick, and when you pull the bow back and forth, the stick turns quickly. It is important that the wood is completely **dry**, because wet wood does not get hot enough.

The small ember on its own is not yet a fire. You place it in **tinder**, that is, very dry, fine material such as grass or tree bast. Then you **blow** carefully into it. This gives the ember more air, and a **flame** appears. After that you add thin twigs and then larger wood bit by bit.

The glacier mummy **Ötzi** had pieces of **tinder fungus** with him. This tree fungus keeps smouldering well when a spark or ember falls into it. Another way to make fire was **striking fire**: if you strike flint against a mineral containing iron such as pyrite, sparks are produced. These are caught with tinder.

gewusst: The tinder fungus gave the German word “Zunder” (tinder) its name.
Humans used fire long before they could kindle it themselves, for example after lightning strikes.

teile.einleitung: Even in the Old Stone Age, people liked to adorn themselves. They made necklaces from shells, animal teeth and snail shells. Jewellery probably also showed who someone was and which group they belonged to.
wichtigste: For necklaces, people drilled holes in shells and threaded them.
Fox teeth were popular jewellery.
Empty snail shells were used as beads.
Beautiful beads were carved from ivory.
The string was often a thin leather strap.
Some sewed many small beads onto their clothes.

abschnitte.text: People collected **shells** and empty **snail shells**. With a pointed stone, they **drilled** a small hole in them. Then they **threaded** the pieces onto a string. This string was often a thin **leather strap** made of animal skin. In this way necklaces and bracelets were made.

**Animal teeth** were popular too. Especially often, people of the Old Stone Age wore **fox teeth**. They pierced the tooth root and hung the teeth on a string. Teeth of large animals could perhaps also show that someone was a good hunter.

In the Ice Age, people carved **beads** from **ivory**, that is, from the tusks of mammoths. That was a lot of work, because each bead was cut, drilled and ground individually. Some people **sewed** many small beads onto their clothes. Graves were found in which thousands of such beads lay.

**Sea shells** were found at places far from the sea. This shows that people **exchanged** such things or brought them along on long journeys. They probably wore jewellery in order to **adorn themselves** and to show who they were and which group they belonged to.

gewusst: Some pierced snail shells from Africa are more than 70,000 years old and are among the oldest known jewellery.
Even the Neanderthals probably wore jewellery of feathers, shells or claws.

teile.einleitung: Homo floresiensis was a very small human species that lived on the Indonesian island of Flores. Because it was only about one metre tall, it was given the nickname “hobbit”.
wichtigste: Homo floresiensis was found on the island of Flores in Indonesia.
The first skull, LB1, was excavated in 2003 in the Liang Bua cave.
It was only about one metre tall.
Its brain, at about 400 cubic centimetres, was about as large as that of a chimpanzee.
According to current dating, the bones are about 100,000 to 60,000 years old.
Many explain its small size by island dwarfism.

abschnitte.text: The island of **Flores** belongs to the Lesser Sunda Islands in Indonesia. In the west of the island lies the limestone cave **Liang Bua**, whose name means roughly “cool cave”. There a team under the Australian archaeologist **Mike Morwood** dug together with Indonesian colleagues such as Radien Soejono and Thomas Sutikna. In September 2003, the skull **LB1** came to light. The description appeared in 2004 in the journal “Nature”.

The skeleton LB1 and further bones show a body height of about **one metre**. So Homo floresiensis was smaller than most eight-year-old children today. Its **brain**, at about 380 to 430 cubic centimetres, was about as large as that of a chimpanzee. The media gave it the nickname **hobbit**, after the small characters in the books of J. R. R. Tolkien.

On islands with little food, some animal species become smaller over many generations. This is called **island dwarfism**. Many experts think the same happened with these humans. Besides the bones, remains of **dwarf elephants** of the genus Stegodon were found. There were also many rodents, a giant marabou stork and **Komodo dragons**. These animals lived on the island at the same time.

At first the bones were thought to be only about 18,000 years old. A **redating** in 2016, however, gave an age of about 100,000 to 60,000 years. Where the ancestors of Homo floresiensis came from and how they reached the island is still being researched.

gewusst: On Flores, small humans lived together with dwarf elephants and Komodo dragons.
The name of the Liang Bua cave means roughly “cool cave”.

teile.einleitung: Mary Anning was a fossil collector from England. Even as a child, she found fossilised marine reptiles on the coast at Lyme Regis. Although she was never allowed to study, she became an important pioneer of fossil research.
wichtigste: Mary Anning lived from 1799 to 1847 in Lyme Regis on the south coast of England.
She searched the cliffs by the sea for fossils.
Around 1811, with her brother Joseph, she found the skeleton of an ichthyosaur.
In 1823, she found the first complete skeleton of a plesiosaur.
In 1828, she discovered a pterosaur, later called Dimorphodon.
Her family was poor, so she sold many finds.
As a woman, she was given little honour at the time.

abschnitte.text: **Mary Anning** was born in 1799 and died in 1847. So she lived almost entirely in the **19th century**. Her home was **Lyme Regis** on the south coast of **England**. The cliffs there consist of rock from the **Jurassic**. In storms they crumble, and again and again fossils come to light. But searching was dangerous, because rocks could fall.

Even as a child, Mary searched for fossils with her father and her brother. Around **1811**, Mary and her brother **Joseph** found the skeleton of an **Ichthyosaurus**. This is an **ichthyosaur**, a marine reptile that looked similar to a dolphin. The find made the young Mary known.

In **1823**, Mary Anning found the first complete skeleton of a **plesiosaur**. These marine reptiles had a long neck and four flippers. In 1828, she discovered the skeleton of a **pterosaur** that was later called **Dimorphodon**. It was the first such find in Britain. Mary also recognised that some stones are fossilised droppings of saurians.

Mary's family was **poor**. She sold fossils to collectors and researchers in order to earn money. At that time, women were not allowed into **scientific societies**. Often others got the fame for her finds. Mary learned everything herself and knew a great deal about fossils. Today she is regarded as an important **pioneer of palaeontology**, the science of fossils.

gewusst: The English tongue twister “She sells seashells by the seashore” is said to recall Mary Anning.
The coast near Lyme Regis is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site as the “Jurassic Coast”.

teile.einleitung: A dugout canoe is a boat hollowed out of a single tree trunk. It is among the oldest boats in the world. Many old dugout canoes have been found in Swiss lakes too.
wichtigste: A dugout canoe is a boat made from a single tree trunk.
In the New Stone Age, the trunk was hollowed out with stone axes.
Many dugout canoes in Switzerland are made of oak.
The dugout was moved forwards with a paddle.
The dugout from Pesse in the Netherlands is about 10,000 years old.
In the mud of lakes and bogs, wood hardly rots.

abschnitte.text: A **dugout canoe** is made from a single **tree trunk**. In the New Stone Age, the wood was chipped out piece by piece with **stone axes** of polished stone. Sometimes fire was used to help, so that the wood could be removed more easily. Many dugouts in Switzerland are made of **oak**, because oak is hard and lasts a long time in water. Some are also made of lime wood.

The dugout was moved with a wooden **paddle**. Some paddles were found together with the boats. The **pile dwellers** on the Swiss lakes used their dugouts for **fishing** and for **transport**. They went out onto the lake and brought goods to the other shore. So the lakes were more like routes of connection than obstacles.

On **Lake Biel**, **Lake Zurich** and other lakes, old dugouts have been found. They also came to light in **bogs**. There is a reason why they were preserved for so long: in wet mud, there is no air. So the wood rots there only very slowly. With the annual rings in the wood, it is often possible to work out when the tree was felled.

The oldest known dugout comes from **Pesse** in the **Netherlands**. It was built around 8000 BC and is therefore about **10,000 years** old. Dugouts existed all over the world. In some regions they are still built and used today.

gewusst: Depending on the tree trunk, a dugout can be over ten metres long.
In Europe, dugouts were built not only in the Stone Age, but into the Middle Ages and beyond.

teile.einleitung: Not all dinosaurs were huge. There were gigantic long-necked dinosaurs as long as several buses, but also small species that were hardly bigger than a chicken.
wichtigste: The largest dinosaurs were long-necked dinosaurs, the sauropods.
Argentinosaurus was probably about 30 to 35 metres long.
The largest sauropods weighed about as much as ten elephants.
A Tyrannosaurus rex was about 12 metres long and weighed 8 to 9 tonnes.
Compsognathus was only about the size of a chicken.
Researchers estimate size from fossilised bones.

abschnitte.titel: The giants with the long neck
abschnitte.text: The very largest dinosaurs belonged to the **sauropods**. They had a long neck, a long tail and four pillar-like legs. **Argentinosaurus** from South America was probably 30 to 35 metres long. That is as long as three buses one behind the other. The largest sauropods probably weighed 50 to 70 tonnes. No other land animal ever grew so big.

**Tyrannosaurus rex** was one of the largest meat-eating dinosaurs. The largest animals found were about 12 metres long, as long as a bus. A fully grown T. rex weighed about 8 to 9 tonnes. That is roughly as much as a large elephant. By comparison, an African elephant weighs about 6 tonnes.

There were tiny dinosaurs too. **Compsognathus** was only about 1 metre long, and a large part of that was tail. It weighed only a few kilograms and was about the size of a chicken. Small dinosaurs were often nimble hunters that caught insects and small animals.

Nobody has seen a living dinosaur. So researchers measure **fossilised bones**. From the length and thickness of the bones, they estimate how big and heavy an animal was. Often only single bones are found. That is why the figures are **estimates** and can change with new finds.

The heaviest animal still lives today: the **blue whale**. It can weigh well over 100 tonnes and so is heavier than almost all dinosaurs. Such a huge body is only possible in water, because the water helps to carry the weight.

gewusst: A blue whale is heavier than the largest dinosaurs known.
Some dinosaurs were smaller than a dog.

teile.einleitung: **Australopithecus afarensis** is a species of early human ancestors from East Africa. The most famous fossil of this species is **Lucy**. Her bones show that our ancestors already walked upright long before their brains grew large.
wichtigste: Lucy was found in 1974 at Hadar in Ethiopia by a team led by Donald Johanson.
Her name comes from the Beatles song “Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds”.
Her skeleton has the catalogue number AL 288-1, and about 40 per cent of it is preserved.
Pelvis and legs show upright walking on two legs.
The brain, at about 400 to 500 cm³, was hardly larger than a chimpanzee's.
In 1975 the “First Family” was found, and in 2000 the Dikika child “Selam”.
The original of Lucy is in the National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa.

abschnitte.text: In 1974, a team led by the American researcher **Donald Johanson** found many bones of a single being at **Hadar** in Ethiopia. Johanson discovered the first pieces together with his student Tom Gray. That evening the Beatles song “Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds” was playing in the camp. This is how the skeleton got the nickname **Lucy**. Officially it is called **AL 288-1**, after site 288 in the Afar region.

Several hundred pieces of bone were found from Lucy. They make up about **40 per cent** of a skeleton, an exceptional amount for such an old fossil. Lucy lived about **3.2 million years ago** and was only a little over a metre tall. The **original** belongs to Ethiopia and is in the **National Museum in Addis Ababa**. Usually a cast is displayed. From 2007 to 2013 the original travelled around the USA.

The pelvis, thigh bone and knee joint of Australopithecus afarensis are adapted to **upright walking**. But long arms and curved fingers show that these early humans could also **climb** well. The **brain**, at about **400 to 500 cm³**, was hardly larger than a chimpanzee's. So upright walking arose before the brain grew a lot. Fossilised footprints from **Laetoli** in Tanzania probably also come from this species.

In 1975, bones of at least **13 individuals**, adults and children, were discovered at Hadar at site AL 333. Experts call this find the **First Family**. In 2000, the skeleton of a child about three years old was found at **Dikika** in Ethiopia. The **Dikika child**, also called **Selam**, is about 3.3 million years old. It is one of the most complete child skeletons of an early human ancestor.

Johanson gave the species the name **Australopithecus afarensis** in 1978, together with **Tim White** and **Yves Coppens**. Australopithecus means “southern ape”, and afarensis refers to the **Afar** region. The species lived over a long period, from about 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago. It does not belong directly to the genus Homo, but is closely related to our ancestors.

gewusst: In Ethiopia, Lucy is also called “Dinknesh”, which means “you are wonderful” in Amharic.
The footprints at Laetoli are about 3.6 million years old.

teile.einleitung: Lucy is one of the most famous fossils in the world. The skeleton of a female early human ancestor is about 3.2 million years old. It was found in 1974 in Ethiopia and shows that our ancestors walked upright very early.
wichtigste: Lucy was found in November 1974 near Hadar in Ethiopia.
The skeleton is about 3.2 million years old.
Lucy belongs to the species Australopithecus afarensis.
She was found by Donald Johanson and his student Tom Gray.
About 40 per cent of Lucy's bones were found.
She was about 1.1 metres tall.
In Ethiopia she is called Dinkinesh, which means roughly “you are wonderful”.

abschnitte.text: In November 1974, a research team was searching for fossils near **Hadar** in north-eastern **Ethiopia**. The expedition was led by the American researcher **Donald Johanson**. Together with his student **Tom Gray**, he discovered the first bones. Little by little, about **40 per cent** of the skeleton came to light. For such an old fossil, that is an exceptional amount.

On the evening after the find, the song “Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds” by the **Beatles** played in the camp again and again. That is how the skeleton got its nickname. In Ethiopia it is called **Dinkinesh** in Amharic. That means roughly “you are wonderful”.

Lucy belongs to the species **Australopithecus afarensis**. This is an **early human ancestor** from East Africa. The species name refers to the Afar region, where she was found. Lucy was only about **1.1 metres** tall and weighed about 29 kilograms. Her pelvis and leg bones show that she walked **upright on two legs**. Her brain, however, was still about as small as a chimpanzee's.

Such a great age is hard to measure directly on bones. So researchers studied **volcanic ash** in the layers near the find. With physical methods, it can be determined when this ash was formed. This gave an age of about **3.2 million years**.

The original bones lie well protected in the **National Museum** in **Addis Ababa**, the capital of Ethiopia. Visitors there mostly see a **cast**, that is, an exact replica. Lucy has greatly shaped knowledge about the development of humans. To this day she is one of the most important fossils in research.

gewusst: Lucy was smaller than most ten-year-old children today.
East Africa is regarded as the region where many of the oldest ancestors of humans lived.

teile.einleitung: The Heuneburg is a Celtic princely seat on the upper Danube in Baden-Württemberg. Around 600 BC it was one of the earliest town-like settlements north of the Alps.
wichtigste: The Heuneburg lies above the Danube near Herbertingen-Hundersingen.
Around 600 BC it had a wall of mud bricks on a stone base.
At its peak, an estimated 4,000 people lived in the centre.
The outer settlement was about 100 hectares in size.
Nearby lies the large burial mound Hohmichele.
Some link the Heuneburg with the town of Pyrene in Herodotus.

abschnitte.text: The **Heuneburg** lies on a spur of the mountain above the upper **Danube**, near Herbertingen-Hundersingen. The river was an important **route** for trade and travel. The actual fort on the plateau covered only about three hectares. Outside it stretched a much larger **outer settlement** of about 100 hectares.

abschnitte.titel: A wall like in the south
abschnitte.text: Around 600 BC, the Heuneburg got an unusual wall. It consisted of air-dried **mud bricks** on a stone base. Such walls were common in the **Mediterranean region**, but north of the Alps they are unique. The wall shows that people here had contact with cultures in the south and knew their building skills.

With fort, outer fort and outer settlement, the Heuneburg was one of the earliest **town-like settlements** north of the Alps. At its peak, an estimated **4,000 people** lived in the centre. Including the surrounding area, about 17,000 people are assumed. The Greek historian **Herodotus** mentions in the 5th century BC a Celtic town **Pyrene** near the sources of the Danube. Whether the Heuneburg was meant is not certain, however.

abschnitte.titel: Burial mounds and the princess's grave
abschnitte.text: Large burial mounds belong to the surroundings of the princely seat. The **Hohmichele** lies in the forest near Altheim-Heiligkreuztal and is among the largest preserved burial mounds in central Europe. In 2010, the grave of a rich woman was discovered at the **Bettelbühl**. The burial chamber was recovered whole as a **block of earth** weighing tonnes and taken to the laboratory on a heavy transporter. There, specialists were able to uncover the jewellery in peace.

gewusst: The mud-brick wall of the Heuneburg is unique north of the Alps.
A whole grave was driven to the laboratory on a lorry as a huge block of earth.

teile.einleitung: Giant sloths were huge relatives of today's sloths. They lived in the Ice Age in America. The best known is **Megatherium** from South America, which could grow as big as an elephant.
wichtigste: Megatherium was as big as an elephant and weighed several tonnes.
It lived in South America.
Giant sloths ate leaves, twigs and other plants.
They could support themselves on their hind legs and tail and rear up.
On their forefeet they had large, powerful claws.
Unlike today's sloths, they lived on the ground.
Charles Darwin found bones of giant sloths in Argentina.

abschnitte.text: Today's sloths are small and hang slowly in the trees. Their extinct relatives, by contrast, were enormous. **Megatherium** weighed several tonnes, about as much as an elephant. When it reared up, it was much taller than a human. For life in the trees it was far too heavy, so it walked on the **ground**.

Giant sloths were **plant eaters**. To reach high leaves, they stood on their **hind legs**. In doing so they supported themselves on their thick, powerful tail like on a stool. With the forelegs, they then pulled branches towards them and plucked off leaves and twigs.

On the forefeet, the giant sloth had long, curved **claws**. With them it could grasp branches and bend them down. The claws were so large that the animal probably did not walk flat on the soles of its feet, but rather on the sides of its feet. The claws probably also helped to defend itself against predators.

Megatherium lived in **South America**, for example in present-day Argentina. Many bones have been found there. Other kinds of giant sloths also existed in Central and North America. At the end of the last Ice Age, the giant sloths died out. Whether the climate or also hunting by humans was mainly to blame is still being researched.

The researcher **Charles Darwin** travelled round the world in the 1830s on the ship **Beagle**. In Argentina he dug up bones of giant sloths. He wondered that these extinct giants resembled the small sloths of today. Such observations later helped him with his thoughts about the development of species.

gewusst: Megatherium is among the largest mammals that ever lived on land in South America.
Today's sloths are close relatives of the anteaters.

teile.einleitung: Pteranodon was a large pterosaur from the Cretaceous. It soared over the sea on huge wings and caught fish. Although it lived at the time of the dinosaurs, it was not a dinosaur itself.
wichtigste: Pteranodon was a pterosaur and could fly.
Its name means “wing without a tooth”.
It had no teeth in its beak.
At the back of its head, it bore a long bone crest.
The wings consisted of skin.
Large animals had a wingspan of 6 to 7 metres.
Most fossils come from Kansas in North America.

abschnitte.text: Pteranodon belongs to the **pterosaurs**, which are also called pterodactyls. They were reptiles that could fly. But they were not dinosaurs. Pteranodon lived in the late **Cretaceous**. Large animals had a **wingspan** of about 6 to 7 metres. That is wider than a car is long. Even so, its body was light, because its bones were hollow.

The wings of Pteranodon were a thin **flight membrane**. It was stretched on a **very long finger**. With these wings, Pteranodon probably often soared through the air for a long time without flapping much. On the ground it walked on **all fours**. This is shown by fossilised footprints of pterosaurs. In doing so, it supported itself on the folded wings.

The name **Pteranodon** means “wing without a tooth”. Its long beak was in fact **toothless**. Pteranodon flew over the sea and caught mainly **fish**. In some fossils, even fish remains were found. At the back of the head, a long **bone crest** stuck out backwards. In some animals, probably the males, it was especially large.

Most Pteranodon fossils come from **North America**, above all from the US state of **Kansas**. Today Kansas lies in the middle of the country. In the Cretaceous, however, a shallow **sea** covered large parts of North America. In the deposits of this sea, over a thousand Pteranodon fossils were found. This makes it one of the best-known pterosaurs.

gewusst: Pteranodon was one of the first pterosaurs to be found in North America.
The crest may have helped Pteranodon to hold its direction in flight, but this is not certain.

teile.einleitung: A dinosaur trackway is a series of fossilised footprints. In Switzerland, such trackways are even found high up in the Alps. They show that more than 200 million years ago, dinosaurs walked along the water there.
wichtigste: The dinosaur trackways of Vieux-Emosson are in the canton of Valais.
They were discovered in 1976 and lie at about 2400 metres.
The rocks were lifted when the Alps formed.
There are also trackways in the Val dal Diavel in the Swiss National Park.
More than 200 footprints were mapped there.
On the Tinzenhorn in Parc Ela, Rico Stecher found traces of sauropods.

abschnitte.text: Above the Emosson reservoir in the **canton of Valais**, near the border with France, lie famous dinosaur trackways. In late summer **1976**, melting firn snow uncovered the tracks, and they were discovered by chance. They lie on tilted slabs of rock at about **2400 metres** above sea level. The footprints are over 230 million years old.

The tracks were once made in soft mud on coasts, that is, at sea level. After that they were covered by new layers and turned to stone. When the **Alps formed**, these layers of rock were lifted over millions of years and tilted. That is why dinosaur trackways are found today on steep rock faces high in the mountains.

In the **Val dal Diavel** in the Swiss National Park in the Grisons, geologists discovered a slab of rock with trackways in 1961. On this slab, about 220 million years old, researchers mapped **more than 200** footprints. They come from plant-eating **prosauropods**. Because of falling rocks, the slab is closed off, but the larger footprints can be seen with good **binoculars** from the Chamanna Cluozza.

On the **Tinzenhorn** in Parc Ela in the Albula valley, the amateur researcher **Rico Stecher** found traces of **sauropods** on an almost vertical rock face. They are about 200 to 210 million years old. There are such tracks on **Piz Mitgel** too. The footprints are roundish and about 60 centimetres across. This is what the footprints of the heavy, four-legged long-necked dinosaurs typically look like.

gewusst: The trackways in the National Park lie in a place you are not allowed to enter, and yet you can see them.
Some dinosaur trackways in the Alps were discovered by walkers or amateur researchers, not by experts.

teile.einleitung: Domestication means that wild animals become domestic animals over many generations. Sheep and goats were among the first farm animals of the early farmers. They provided meat, milk, skins and leather.
wichtigste: Sheep and goats were first tamed in the Near East.
This happened about 10,000 years ago.
The ancestor of the domestic sheep is the mouflon.
The ancestor of the domestic goat is the bezoar ibex.
Cheese was made from milk, and leather from skin.
A shepherd looks after the flock.

abschnitte.text: The domestic sheep descends from the **mouflon**, a wild sheep with large, curved horns. The domestic goat descends from the **bezoar ibex**, which still lives wild today in the mountains of western Asia. In the **Near East**, for example in present-day Iraq, Syria and Turkey, the animals were tamed about 10,000 years ago. From there, sheep and goats came to Europe with the farmers.

With their own animals, farmers no longer had to hunt for so long. **Meat**, milk and skins were always close at hand. Sheep and goats are **plant eaters** and eat mainly grass and leaves. Goats also like nibbling at bushes. A **shepherd** watches over the flock and leads the animals to good pastures.

Fresh milk quickly goes sour. So people made **cheese** from it, which keeps much longer. The animals' skins were tanned. This produced **leather** for clothes, shoes and bags. The wool of the sheep was later used for spinning and weaving.

A young sheep is called a **lamb**, and a young goat is called a kid. The **pile dwellers** on the Swiss lakes also kept sheep and goats in the New Stone Age. We know this from finds of bones in their settlements. For the early farmers, the animals were an important store of food that walked along on four legs.

gewusst: Mouflons also live wild today in some areas of Europe, where people released them.
Goats are very good climbers and sometimes even stand on the branches of trees.

teile.einleitung: Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania is one of the most important find sites for the history of humankind. In its rock layers, fossils of early human ancestors and some of the oldest stone tools in the world were found.
wichtigste: Olduvai Gorge lies in northern Tanzania near the Ngorongoro Crater.
It is up to about 100 metres deep.
Wilhelm Kattwinkel found the first fossils there in 1911.
Hans Reck recovered a skeleton of a modern human in 1913.
The Oldowan culture is named after the gorge.
Because of the many finds, it is often called the “cradle of humankind”.

abschnitte.text: Olduvai Gorge lies in the north of **Tanzania** at the edge of the **Serengeti**. It is located about 20 kilometres north-west of the **Ngorongoro Crater** and belongs to the **East African Rift**. At its deepest points it is about 100 metres deep. In its walls you can see rock layers from almost two million years. The name goes back to the Maasai word “Oldupai”, a sisal-like **plant** common there.

In **1911**, the German doctor and insect researcher **Wilhelm Kattwinkel** came across fossil bones, reportedly while chasing a butterfly. Among other things he found remains of an early horse. His find encouraged further expeditions. In **1913**, the geologist **Hans Reck** led the first larger expedition. He recovered parts of a skeleton of **Homo sapiens**. It is about 20,000 years old and bears the number **OH 1**.

Later, **Louis and Mary Leakey** carried out research in the gorge for many years. In **1959**, Mary Leakey found a skull with huge molars and powerful jaws. It belongs to **Paranthropus boisei**, an early human ancestor. Because of its teeth, it was jokingly called the **Nutcracker Man**. Shortly afterwards, remains of **Homo habilis**, an early human species, were also discovered.

In the gorge, very simple stone tools were found. For these, a few pieces were struck off a pebble so that a sharp edge was produced. These tools were first described here. That is why the culture is called **Oldowan**. It belongs to the **oldest known stone tools**. Because so many fossils and tools were found at Olduvai, the gorge is often called the **cradle of humankind**.

gewusst: In Tanzania the gorge is now officially called Oldupai, like the plant after which it is named.
Nearby, at Laetoli, fossilised footprints of early human ancestors more than 3 million years old were discovered.

teile.einleitung: The Helvetii were a Celtic people who lived in the 1st century BC mainly on the Swiss Plateau between the Jura and the Alps. They are known above all through the account of the Roman general Julius Caesar about their migration in 58 BC. To this day the Latin name of Switzerland, Confoederatio Helvetica, recalls them.
wichtigste: The Helvetii were a Celtic people on the Swiss Plateau.
Around 100 BC, according to ancient sources, they still lived in southern Germany between the Rhine, the Main and the Danube.
According to Caesar, they were divided into four sub-tribes, also called cantons.
The Tigurine Divico defeated the Romans at Agen in 107 BC.
In 58 BC, the Helvetii set out to reach the territory of the Santones on the Atlantic.
Caesar defeated them in the battle of Bibracte and sent them back.
The abbreviation CH stands for Confoederatio Helvetica.

abschnitte.text: The Helvetii belonged to the **Celts**, who inhabited large parts of Europe in the Iron Age. Around 100 BC, according to ancient sources, they lived in southern Germany between the Rhine, the Main and the Danube. Later they moved to the **Plateau** between the Jura and the Alps. According to Caesar, they were divided into four sub-tribes, so-called **cantons** (Gaue), to which the Tigurini belonged.

abschnitte.titel: Divico and the victory at Agen
abschnitte.text: At the end of the 2nd century BC, the **Tigurini** moved from the north to Gaul together with the Cimbri. In 107 BC, their leader **Divico** defeated a Roman army at Agen in south-western France. The Roman general Lucius Cassius Longinus was killed in the battle. The defeated Romans had to retreat in disgrace.

The rich Helvetian **Orgetorix**, according to Caesar, planned to emigrate with the whole people to Gaul. But he died in 60 BC, before the plan was carried out. In 58 BC, the Helvetii set out all the same and burned their villages so that nobody would want to turn back. Their goal was the territory of the **Santones** on the Atlantic coast.

At first the Helvetii wanted to cross the Rhone near **Geneva**, but Caesar had the bridge broken down. They chose another route, but Caesar pursued them. In the **battle of Bibracte** in present-day Burgundy, he defeated them in 58 BC. Afterwards he sent them back to their territory so that no Germanic tribes would occupy the empty land.

After the defeat, the Helvetii came under the influence of Rome. Their main town later became **Aventicum**, present-day Avenches in the canton of Vaud. A Roman city with a theatre and a city wall arose there. Little by little, the Helvetii adopted the Roman way of life and the Latin language.

Our knowledge of the Helvetii comes mainly from Caesar's book on the **Gallic War**. Archaeologists have also found fortified settlements of the Helvetii, for example on the Mont Vully and on the Engehalbinsel in Bern. The Latin name of Switzerland is **Confoederatio Helvetica**, hence the abbreviation CH. The figure of Helvetia on coins also recalls this people.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of peoples who lived in large parts of Europe in the Iron Age.
A sub-tribe of a people with its own territory.
A large, fortified, town-like settlement of the Celts.
The Latin name of Switzerland, abbreviated CH.

gewusst: The Helvetii could write and used Greek letters for it.
Caesar claimed that the Helvetii had set fire to twelve towns and about 400 villages themselves before the migration.
From 1798 to 1803, Switzerland was called the “Helvetic Republic”.

teile.einleitung: Einkorn is one of the oldest kinds of wheat that humans grew. It became a crop plant over 10,000 years ago in western Asia. The glacier mummy Ötzi also had einkorn in his stomach.
wichtigste: Einkorn was first grown in the Karacadağ mountains in south-eastern Turkey.
When it was cultivated it changed: the grains no longer fell off by themselves.
The wild form is called Triticum boeoticum.
Einkorn is diploid, meaning it has two sets of chromosomes.
Remains of einkorn were found in Ötzi's stomach.
Einkorn flour is yellowish because it contains many carotenoids such as lutein.

abschnitte.text: **Einkorn** is called Triticum monococcum in science. Its wild ancestor, **Triticum boeoticum**, still grows in western Asia today. Genetic studies show that cultivated einkorn is most closely related to wild plants from the **Karacadağ mountains** in south-eastern Turkey. It probably became a crop plant there over 10,000 years ago.

In wild cereals, the ripe grains fall off by themselves. This helps the plant to spread, but is bad for the harvest. The first farmers harvested mainly ears that kept their grains, and sowed these again. Over time this produced einkorn whose **grains no longer fell off by themselves**. This change is a typical sign of a cultivated plant.

Einkorn is **diploid**. That means it has only **two sets of chromosomes**, so two copies of the genetic information. This makes it the simplest cultivated wheat. Emmer and durum wheat have four sets of chromosomes, and today's bread wheat even six. Like spelt, einkorn is a **hulled cereal**: the grains are firmly enclosed in husks and have to be dehusked after threshing.

In the stomach of the glacier mummy **Ötzi**, remains of einkorn were found. This shows that his community practised farming. Einkorn also occurred in pile-dwelling settlements in Switzerland. Flour from einkorn is noticeably **yellowish**. It contains clearly more **carotenoids** than modern wheat, above all the pigment **lutein**.

gewusst: The name Einkorn (German for “one grain”) comes from the fact that there is usually only a single grain in each spikelet.
Einkorn is grown again today in small amounts, for example for bread and pasta.

teile.einleitung: An oppidum is a fortified settlement of the Celts. We know the term from the Romans, above all from Julius Caesar. In Switzerland too there were such Celtic centres, for example in Basel.
wichtigste: The Latin word “oppidum” means town in general.
Julius Caesar called Celtic towns oppida in his account of the Gallic War.
Typical is the “Murus gallicus” wall of wood, earth and stone.
Well-known oppida are Manching in Bavaria and Bibracte in Burgundy.
In Basel, an oppidum lay on the Münsterhügel.
Oppida were also centres of coin production.

abschnitte.text: The Latin word **oppidum** means town. By it the Romans meant smaller towns and fortified places. **Gaius Julius Caesar** described many Gallic places as oppida in his work **“De bello Gallico”**. That is where the technical term of today comes from. Archaeology uses it for the large Celtic centres of the late Iron Age. According to Caesar, before their migration in 58 BC the **Helvetii** burned 12 oppida and about 400 villages.

The typical Celtic wall is called **Murus gallicus**, “Gallic wall”. It consisted of a framework of wooden beams joined with long **iron nails**. Between them lay earth and stones. The wood made the wall elastic against battering rams, and the stone front protected against fire. Caesar described this method of construction at the siege of **Avaricum**, present-day Bourges. Another type is the **Pfostenschlitzmauer** (post-slot wall) with vertical posts in the front, as at Kelheim.

One of the largest oppida lay at **Manching** near Ingolstadt in Bavaria. Its wall was about seven kilometres long. A gold treasure with hundreds of coins was found there. On **Mont Beuvray** in Burgundy lay **Bibracte**, the main settlement of the Aedui. Today a large museum of Celtic culture stands there. In Switzerland there were oppida, for example, on the **Münsterhügel** in Basel, on the Engehalbinsel in Bern and on the Mont Vully.

Oppida were not only fortresses. Craftsmen, traders and farmers lived there. Iron was forged, jewellery and pottery were made, and trade was carried on with far-off regions. In many oppida, **dimpled clay plates** were found. In their small hollows, metal was melted into blanks for **coins**. So oppida were also centres of **coin minting**.

gewusst: Caesar praised the Gallic wall because it could not be destroyed easily either by fire or by battering rams.
The Münsterhügel in Basel was easy to defend because it lies raised above the Rhine; the Celts secured it further with a rampart and ditch.

teile.einleitung: Göbekli Tepe is an ancient site in south-eastern Turkey. There, about 11,500 years ago, people put up huge stone pillars, long before there were cities, writing or farming.
wichtigste: The oldest structures date from around 9500 BC.
The builders were hunters and gatherers.
The pillars are T-shaped and probably represent human-like beings.
Wild animals can be seen in relief on many pillars.
From 1995, the archaeologist Klaus Schmidt led the excavations.
Since 2018, Göbekli Tepe has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: The Turkish name **Göbekli Tepe** means roughly “potbelly hill”. “Tepe” means hill, and “göbek” means belly or navel. The site lies on a hill near the city of Şanlıurfa. From 1995, the German archaeologist **Klaus Schmidt** of the German Archaeological Institute dug there. He recognised the great importance of the place and carried out research there until his death in 2014.

The large **stone pillars** look like a big T. The builders chiselled them out of the **limestone** in the surrounding area, and traces of the quarries can still be seen today. On some pillars, arms, hands, belts and loincloths are carved. That is why they are interpreted as greatly simplified **human figures**, perhaps ancestors or supernatural beings.

The pillars mostly stand in **circles or ovals** surrounded by walls. In the middle of each structure stand two especially large pillars. On many pillars, **reliefs** of wild animals can be seen: foxes, snakes, wild boar and birds. There was no writing at that time, so we do not know exactly what the pictures mean.

At the time of building, there was not yet any real **farming** there. The builders lived from hunting and from gathering wild plants. Even so, they managed to work and set up stones weighing tonnes. This surprised researchers. Göbekli Tepe is much older than the pyramids in Egypt. In 2018, **UNESCO** added the site to the World Heritage list.

gewusst: Göbekli Tepe is about 7000 years older than the great pyramids of Giza.
The builders had neither metal tools nor wheels, and yet moved pillars weighing tonnes.

teile.einleitung: Plesiosaurs were large marine reptiles that lived at the time of the dinosaurs. Many of them had a very long neck and four large flippers. They were not dinosaurs, however.
wichtigste: Plesiosaurs were marine reptiles, not dinosaurs.
Many had a very long neck and a small head.
They had four flippers that they moved like paddles.
They ate fish and squid.
They died out about 66 million years ago.
Elasmosaurus had over 70 neck vertebrae.

abschnitte.text: Plesiosaurs lived in the **sea**, at the same time as the dinosaurs on land. But they were **not dinosaurs**, they were a separate group of **reptiles**. They breathed with lungs and so had to come to the surface for air. At the end of the **Cretaceous**, about 66 million years ago, they died out. At that time the large dinosaurs also disappeared.

Many plesiosaurs had a very **long neck**. At the end sat a rather **small head** full of pointed teeth. The neck was especially long in **Elasmosaurus**: it had over 70 neck vertebrae, and the neck was longer than the whole rest of the body. But there were also plesiosaurs with a short neck and a very large head. They were dangerous hunters.

A plesiosaur had **four flippers**: two at the front and two at the back. It moved them like **paddles** or similar to wings under water. In this way it glided through the sea. Plesiosaurs were **predators**. They ate mainly **fish and squid**. With their pointed teeth, they held the slippery prey fast.

Many people think of **Nessie** when they hear plesiosaur, the legendary creature of **Loch Ness** in Scotland. Many imagine Nessie with a long neck and flippers. But there is no evidence for such an animal in the loch. One of the first researchers to find complete plesiosaurs was **Mary Anning** in England. She searched the coast for fossils about 200 years ago.

gewusst: The name plesiosaur means roughly “near lizard”.
In some plesiosaurs, stones were found in the stomach that they had probably swallowed.

teile.einleitung: Towards the end of the last Ice Age, groups lived in Europe that hunted mainly reindeer. In Switzerland too, for example at the Kesslerloch near Thayngen, these reindeer hunters left many traces.
wichtigste: In the 19th century, the late Old Stone Age was called the Reindeer Age.
The culture of the late reindeer hunters is called Magdalenian, after La Madeleine in France.
Reindeer sinews served as thread for sewing.
Batons with a hole, made of antler, probably served for straightening spear shafts.
Shed antlers could simply be collected.
At the end of the Ice Age, the reindeer moved north.

abschnitte.text: At many find sites of the late Old Stone Age, very many **reindeer bones** were found. That is why researchers in the 19th century spoke of the **Reindeer Age**. Today other technical terms are used. The culture of the late reindeer hunters is called the **Magdalenian**. The name comes from the rock shelter **La Madeleine** in the south-west of France. Many typical tools of this period were found there.

In Switzerland, the **Kesslerloch** near **Thayngen** in the canton of Schaffhausen is especially well known. Reindeer hunters left tools, bones and works of art there. Not far from it, in Germany, lies the **Petersfels** near **Engen** in the Hegau. There too, many traces of reindeer hunters of the Magdalenian were found. The groups probably moved back and forth between such places, depending on the season.

The hunters used the reindeer almost entirely. From **antler** they made spear points, harpoons and needles. A **baton with a hole** is a piece of antler with a large hole. Many researchers believe that it was used to straighten warmed **spear shafts**. Antler could also be obtained without hunting: reindeer **shed** their antlers every year and grow new ones. The shed antlers could be collected.

The **sinews** of the animals were valuable too. When dried, they are very **strong**. With them, clothes of fur and leather were sewn. In addition, points were tied to spears with sinews. Fine needles of bone or antler with an eye show how skilfully people could sew at that time. Warm clothing was vital in the cold of the Ice Age.

At the end of the Ice Age, the climate became **warmer**. Forests spread, and the open **cold steppe** disappeared. The reindeer no longer found suitable food here. They moved **north**, where it stayed cold. The people in Switzerland now hunted other animals of the forest, for example red deer and wild boar.

gewusst: In the Kesslerloch, a baton with a hole with an engraved reindeer was found, the “Grazing Reindeer”. It is among the best-known works of art of the Ice Age in Switzerland.
The reindeer hunters used needles with an eye, very similar to ours today.

teile.einleitung: All dinosaurs hatched from eggs. Fossilised dinosaur eggs and whole nests reveal a lot about how the animals raised their young. Some eggs even still contain tiny bones.
wichtigste: Newly hatched dinosaurs were much smaller than their parents.
Many dinosaurs laid their eggs in nests on the ground.
Often many eggs lay together in one nest.
Maiasaura means “good mother lizard”.
Oviraptor means “egg thief”, but it was sitting on its own eggs.
In 1923, famous nests were found in the Gobi Desert.
Even huge long-necked dinosaurs laid eggs only about the size of a grapefruit.

abschnitte.text: Many dinosaurs dug **nests** in the ground and laid their eggs in them. Often several eggs lay side by side, sometimes arranged in a circle. Researchers think that some dinosaurs covered their eggs with **plants and soil**. As the plants rotted, they gave off warmth and kept the eggs warm.

In 1923, a research expedition from New York found nests with fossilised eggs in the **Gobi Desert** in Mongolia. A dinosaur lay there too, which was named **Oviraptor**. That means “egg thief”, because people believed it had been trying to steal the eggs. Later, an Oviraptor was found sitting on a nest. They were its own eggs, which it was warming and protecting.

Even the huge **long-necked dinosaurs** laid only fairly small eggs, about the size of a **grapefruit**. A bigger egg would need a very thick shell, and the young one could hardly breathe or hatch out. That is why newly hatched dinosaurs were much smaller than their parents. They had to grow for many years until they were fully grown.

In North America, nests with young of a duck-billed dinosaur were discovered. It was given the name **Maiasaura**, which means “good mother lizard”. The parents probably brought food to their young in the nest. In some fossilised eggs there are tiny **bones** of unhatched babies. This is how we know which species laid the egg.

gewusst: Dinosaur eggs had a hard shell of lime, similar to the eggs of birds today.
Birds descend from dinosaurs, and sitting on a nest already existed among dinosaurs.

teile.einleitung: A harpoon is a spear with barbs that is used to catch fish. Even people of the Old Stone Age made harpoons from bone and antler and fished in rivers with them.
wichtigste: A harpoon has barbs at the tip.
The barbs hold the fish fast.
The point sits on a long wooden pole, the shaft.
Harpoons of the Old Stone Age had one or two rows of barbs.
People often caught salmon in the rivers with them.
In addition, they fished with fish hooks made of bone.

abschnitte.text: A harpoon consists of a point and a long pole made of wood, the **shaft**. At the tip sit **barbs**. These are small points that face backwards. They stop the fish from slipping off again. People carved the points from **bone** or **reindeer antler**. There are harpoons with barbs on one side and others with barbs on both sides.

People of the **Old Stone Age** often caught **salmon**. Salmon swim up the rivers in large groups to lay their eggs. Then there were very many fish at once. Fishing was mostly done in **shallow, clear water** at the bank. There you can see the fish well and can hit them.

Fish are easily startled. So the fisher had to **wait calmly** and stand still. At the right moment, he thrust the harpoon exactly at the fish. Water bends light, so a fish is not exactly where you see it. Good fishers knew this and aimed a little lower.

Besides the harpoon, people also used small **fish hooks**. They carved them from bone or shells, because there was no metal or plastic yet. Later, nets and fish traps were added. Fish was an important food, because it provides a lot of protein and fat.

gewusst: Many harpoon points of the Old Stone Age are carved from reindeer antler.
Some harpoons had barbs on both sides of the point.

teile.einleitung: A dolmen is a tomb made of huge slabs of stone from the New Stone Age. It looks like a big table made of stone. Dolmens are found in many parts of Europe, including Switzerland.
wichtigste: A dolmen is a tomb made of large slabs of stone.
The word dolmen means “stone table”.
On top lies a large, heavy capstone.
In German it is also called “Grosssteingrab” (large-stone tomb), and in northern Germany often “Hünengrab” (giants' tomb).
The huge stones of such structures are called megaliths.
In Sion, dolmens from the New Stone Age were found.

abschnitte.text: In a **dolmen**, several large stones stand upright. On top of them lies a heavy, flat **capstone**. The word comes from Breton and means “**stone table**”. Many dolmens were once covered by a **mound of earth** and stones. Today this mound has often disappeared, and you only see the stone frame.

Dolmens were **tombs**. Often many people were buried in them one after another. Researchers found **bones** of the dead in dolmens, and **grave goods** such as jewellery, tools or pots. So a dolmen was a kind of communal tomb for a community, used over a long time.

The huge stones of dolmens, menhirs and stone circles are called **megaliths**. In Greek that means “large stone”. In German a dolmen is also called a **Grosssteingrab**. In northern Germany people often say **Hünengrab**, because it used to be believed that only giants, called “Hünen”, could have moved such large stones. A special form is the **passage grave**: a long passage of stone slabs leads into the burial chamber.

In the **Petit-Chasseur** district of **Sion** in the canton of Valais, several dolmens from the New Stone Age were found. They belong to a large burial ground. There, stone slabs with human figures carved into them were also discovered. Later, the graves continued to be used in the Bell Beaker period.

gewusst: Some capstones of dolmens weigh several tonnes and were moved without machines.
Many dolmens are older than the Egyptian pyramids.

teile.einleitung: The hand axe is one of the oldest tools of humankind. It was knocked out of stone and held directly in the hand. A very old hand axe has been found in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: A hand axe is a tool made of stone.
It was often made of flint.
It was held in the hand without a handle.
It was used for cutting and scraping.
The first hand axe in Switzerland was found at Pratteln.
It is about 300,000 years old and was discovered by a schoolboy.
The culture whose typical tool is the hand axe is called the Acheulean.

abschnitte.text: A **hand axe** is a stone that has been struck sharp from both sides. Usually it has the shape of a **teardrop** or an almond: broad and round at the bottom, pointed at the top. It was often made of **flint**, which is also called **silex**. Flint gets very sharp edges when you break it.

abschnitte.titel: How to make a hand axe
abschnitte.text: Small pieces were struck off the raw piece with another stone. In this way the desired shape gradually emerged, until the edges were sharp. This needed a lot of practice and skill. The hand axe had no handle. It was held directly **in the hand**, which is where its name comes from.

The hand axe was an all-purpose tool. It was used for **cutting** and **scraping**. With it, people butchered animals they had killed, scraped skins and worked wood. The first hand axes were made well over a million years ago in **Africa**. The culture whose typical form is the hand axe is called the **Acheulean**, after the site of Saint-Acheul in France.

The first hand axe in Switzerland was found in **1974** at **Pratteln** in the canton of Basel-Landschaft. It was discovered by a **schoolboy**, Christoph Hauser, in a sunken lane. Researchers estimate its age at about **300,000 years**. This makes it one of the oldest tools known in Switzerland.

gewusst: The hand axe was made for over a million years, which makes it one of the longest-used tools in history.
Some hand axes are so carefully and evenly made that researchers marvel at their makers' sense of beauty.

teile.einleitung: Monte San Giorgio is a wooded mountain in the canton of Ticino on Lake Lugano. It is world famous for its fossils from the Triassic and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
wichtigste: Monte San Giorgio lies in the canton of Ticino on the southern shore of Lake Lugano.
About 240 million years ago, a warm sea lay there.
Very many well-preserved fish and marine reptiles were found.
Switzerland has shared the World Heritage Site with Italy since 2010.
In Meride there is a fossil museum.
Most of the finds are held at the University of Zurich.

abschnitte.text: Monte San Giorgio lies in the far south of Switzerland in the canton of **Ticino**. It rises on the southern shore of **Lake Lugano** and is over 1,000 metres high. Part of the mountain belongs to Italy. In 2003, the Swiss part was added to the **UNESCO World Heritage**. In 2010, the Italian part was added too. Since then the two countries have shared this World Heritage Site.

At the time of the **Triassic**, about 240 million years ago, a warm sea basin lay here. When animals died, they sank to the bottom. There fine mud covered them. Because there was little oxygen on the bottom, the bodies hardly decayed. In time, the mud became rock, and the animals became **fossils**. Many are so well preserved that even fine bones can be seen.

On Monte San Giorgio, mainly **fish** and **marine reptiles** were found. Very common is **Mixosaurus**, an ichthyosaur about one metre long. Several hundred finds of it are known. Especially strange is **Tanystropheus**: its neck was longer than trunk and tail together. It probably hunted fish and squid in coastal water. In addition there are many species of fish, crustaceans and other sea creatures.

In the village of **Meride** at the foot of the mountain stands a fossil museum. The well-known Ticino architect **Mario Botta** converted it, and it reopened in 2012. Most of the fossils, however, are kept at the **University of Zurich**. Researchers from Zurich dug on the mountain from the 1920s. Many finds are displayed in the Zurich museum and are studied to this day.

gewusst: So far, thousands of fossils have been recovered on Monte San Giorgio, including species known only from here.
Tanystropheus had such a long neck that researchers puzzled for a long time over how it could swim with it at all.

teile.einleitung: The find site La Tène lies in the canton of Neuchâtel, where the Thielle flows out of Lake Neuchâtel. Here weapons, tools, bridges and skeletons from the time of the Celts were found. What exactly happened at this place is still disputed.
wichtigste: The find site belongs to the canton of Neuchâtel.
It lies at the outflow of the Thielle from Lake Neuchâtel.
Colonel Friedrich Schwab of Biel had the first finds recovered.
Paul Vouga led large excavations from 1907 to 1917.
Skeletons of people and animals were also found.
Since 2009, the municipality there has also been called La Tène.

abschnitte.text: The find site lies near **Marin-Epagnier** at the eastern end of Lake Neuchâtel. There the **Thielle** flows out of the lake. It connects Lake Neuchâtel with Lake Biel. Its course was later straightened in the Jura water correction. That is why the area looks different today from the time of the Celts.

The first finds were recovered by Colonel **Friedrich Schwab** of Biel. A fisherman pulled weapons out of the shallow water on his behalf. Schwab put together a large collection of antiquities. From 1907 to 1917, the Neuchâtel archaeologist **Paul Vouga** led systematic excavations. He published the results in 1923. One of the wooden bridges now bears his name.

Besides weapons and implements, **skeletons of people and animals** were also found. Whether the dead died in battle, perished in an accident such as a flood, or were sacrificed is unclear. Some researchers see La Tène as a holy place where gifts were laid in the water. Others think rather of a bridge with a trading post. The **interpretation** remains disputed.

In **2009**, the municipalities of **Marin-Epagnier** and **Thielle-Wavre** merged. The new municipality chose the name of the famous find site. In this way it recalls the Celtic past. Many finds are displayed in the **Laténium** museum in Hauterive very close by.

gewusst: The whole later Iron Age of Europe is named after the find site La Tène.
Only when the lake level was lowered did the find site lie dry enough for large excavations.

teile.einleitung: **Archaeogenetics** studies genetic material from old bones, teeth and even from layers of soil. This tells us where people came from, what illnesses they had and how they were related. In recent decades the method has greatly changed research into prehistory.
wichtigste: The best-preserved ancient DNA is usually found in the petrous bone of the skull.
Ancient DNA shows typical damage, above all changes from cytosine to thymine.
Samples are handled in clean rooms so that no modern DNA gets in.
The plague bacterium Yersinia pestis has been detected in skeletons about 5000 years old.
The first farmers of central Europe came mainly from Anatolia and the Aegean.
With sediment DNA, humans and animals can be detected even without finds of bones.

abschnitte.text: Every cell contains **DNA**, the genetic material. After death it slowly breaks down into ever smaller fragments. But remains often survive in old bones and teeth. It is especially well protected in the **petrous bone**, a very dense bone in the skull that surrounds the inner ear. For his research into the genetic material of Neanderthals, the researcher **Svante Pääbo** received the Nobel Prize in 2022.

abschnitte.titel: Traces of time and clean laboratories
abschnitte.text: Ancient DNA has typical damage. At the ends of the fragments, **cytosine** is often changed into uracil, which shows up as **thymine** when it is read. This process is called **deamination**. The damage pattern is even useful, because it shows that a sequence is really old. Because old samples contain only a little DNA of their own, researchers work in **clean rooms** with protective suits, positive air pressure and UV light. This keeps modern human DNA out of the samples.

Genome studies show that **farming** did not come to central Europe just as an idea. Farming families from **Anatolia** and the **Aegean** moved in across the Balkans. The local hunters and gatherers were partly pushed out, and partly mixed with the newcomers. The ability to digest milk well as an adult was still very rare among these first farmers. It only became common in Europe thousands of years later, from the Bronze Age.

Germs leave genetic material too. In teeth from the New Stone Age and the Bronze Age, DNA of the plague bacterium **Yersinia pestis** has been found. The oldest evidence comes from skeletons about 5000 years old. So plague troubled people long before the **Black Death** in the Middle Ages. With ancient DNA you can also work out whether a skeleton belonged to a man or a woman, even in children.

Humans and animals leave traces of genetic material in the ground, for example through hair, droppings or skin cells. These remains are called **sediment DNA**, or sedaDNA for short. It is recovered directly from layers of soil. In this way, **Neanderthals** could be detected in caves, for example, without any bones having been found there.

gewusst: Part of the genetic material of people today outside Africa comes from Neanderthals.
Often a tiny amount of bone powder is enough for a study.

teile.einleitung: Dinosaur tracks are fossilised footprints of dinosaurs. Unlike bones, they show how living animals moved. There are famous sites in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: A dinosaur track is a fossilised imprint in rock.
The animals left their tracks in soft mud.
From the spacing of the tracks you can tell how fast an animal was moving.
Many parallel tracks show that animals travelled in groups.
Meat-eating dinosaurs mostly left tracks with three toes.
The Lommiswil quarry with many tracks is in the canton of Solothurn.

abschnitte.titel: How a track turns to stone
abschnitte.text: A dinosaur stepped into **soft mud** on the shore of a body of water. The print dried and was then covered by sand or mud. Over a very long time the layers turned to rock. This is how the **print in the stone** was preserved. Only when the rock above is worn away does the track come to light again.

Bones come from dead animals, but tracks come from **living animals**. If the prints lie far apart, the animal was running fast. Short gaps show slow walking. If many trails run **parallel** in the same direction, several animals walked together. So some dinosaurs probably lived in herds.

**Meat-eating dinosaurs** walked on two legs. Their tracks usually show **three toes**, like a bird's. This fits with the fact that **birds** descend from dinosaurs. Very large, round prints, on the other hand, often come from huge long-necked dinosaurs. They walked on four thick legs and were very **heavy**.

In the quarry at **Lommiswil** in the **canton of Solothurn**, you can see many dinosaur tracks on a tilted slab of rock. The tracks date from the **Jurassic**. At that time, a flat coastal landscape lay here. Today the slab stands at an angle because the layers of rock were bent when the Jura mountains formed.
