gewusst: From the size of a footprint, researchers can roughly estimate how long the animal's legs were.
In some places in the world, thousands of dinosaur tracks have been found on a single surface of rock.

teile.einleitung: In the village of **Frick** in the canton of Aargau, many dinosaur bones have been found. The **Frick Dinosaur Museum** shows these finds. Most come from **Plateosaurus**, a large plant eater from the Triassic.
wichtigste: The Frick Dinosaur Museum is in the Fricktal in the canton of Aargau.
The bones were found in a clay pit.
The clay is quarried for bricks.
Plateosaurus lived in the Triassic and ate plants.
A fully grown Plateosaurus could grow up to 10 metres long.
According to present knowledge, it walked on two legs.
The showpiece of the museum is a whole Plateosaurus skeleton.

abschnitte.text: Frick lies in the **Fricktal** in the canton of **Aargau**, not far from the Rhine. On the edge of the village there is a **clay pit**. There clay is quarried from which **bricks** for roofs and walls are made. During quarrying, workers came across fossilised bones again and again.

Almost all finds come from **Plateosaurus**. It lived in the **Triassic**, about 210 million years ago. A fully grown animal grew to about **10 metres** long. It had a long neck, a small head and a long tail. Plateosaurus ate **plants** and was one of the early large dinosaurs.

In the past, Plateosaurus was imagined on four legs. According to present knowledge, however, it walked on **two legs**. Its forelegs were shorter and could not turn so that the palms faced downwards. With its hands it probably grasped at plants.

In the Frick Dinosaur Museum you see bones, footprints and models. The **showpiece** is a whole **Plateosaurus skeleton** that was found in Frick. Whole skeletons are very rare, which is why this find is especially valuable. The museum also explains what the landscape of Switzerland looked like at the time of the dinosaurs.

gewusst: The clay pit of Frick is among the richest find sites of Plateosaurus in Europe.
At the time of Plateosaurus, all continents were still joined into one great primeval continent.

teile.einleitung: Emmer is a very old kind of wheat that was already being grown in the New Stone Age. Important cereals of today, such as durum wheat, came from it. In ancient Egypt, emmer was the most important bread grain.
wichtigste: Emmer is tetraploid, meaning it has four sets of chromosomes.
It arose from a natural cross between two wild grasses, including Triticum urartu.
Durum wheat came directly from emmer.
Spelt arose from a cross between emmer and a wild grass.
In ancient Egypt, bread and beer were made from emmer.
In Italy, emmer is called “farro”.

abschnitte.text: **Emmer** arose from the natural cross between **Triticum urartu** and a grass related to Aegilops speltoides. The so-called A genome comes from Triticum urartu. That is why emmer has **four sets of chromosomes** and is **tetraploid**. The wild ancestor, wild emmer, was found by the agronomist **Aaron Aaronsohn** in 1906 in Galilee, in the north of present-day Israel. The find helped to show where wheat comes from.

abschnitte.titel: Bread and beer on the Nile
abschnitte.text: In **ancient Egypt**, people in the Nile valley grew mainly **emmer** and barley. From emmer they baked bread and brewed beer. Emmer was also grown in the Fertile Crescent and later in large parts of Europe. The pile dwellers in Switzerland knew it too.

From cultivated emmer came **durum wheat** directly. From its semolina, spaghetti and other **pasta** is made. **Spelt** arose through a natural cross of emmer with another wild grass. Spelt has six sets of chromosomes and is still widely grown in Switzerland today. Today's bread wheat also belongs to this family.

In **Italy**, emmer is still grown and eaten today. There it is called “**farro**”, or more precisely “farro medio”. The grains are cooked, for example, in soups and salads. In other countries too, emmer is being grown more again, because it is regarded as robust.

gewusst: Grains of emmer have also been found as grave goods in Egyptian tombs.
Another German name for emmer is Zweikorn (“two grain”), because there are usually two grains in each spikelet.

teile.einleitung: Human evolution describes how humans developed over millions of years from ape-like ancestors. In 1859, in his book “On the Origin of Species”, Charles Darwin explained how living things change through natural selection. Fossils from Africa such as the skeleton “Lucy” show how this long path ran.
wichtigste: Charles Darwin published the book “On the Origin of Species” in 1859.
Natural selection means that better adapted living things have more offspring.
The chimpanzee and the bonobo are the closest living relatives of humans.
Very early on, our ancestors developed upright walking, even before the brain grew a lot.
Homo habilis means “handy human”.
Homo erectus was one of the first kinds of human to leave Africa.
Modern humans, Homo sapiens, arose about 300,000 years ago in Africa.

abschnitte.text: The English researcher **Charles Darwin** published the book “On the Origin of Species” in 1859. In it he explained **natural selection**. Living things that are better adapted to their environment are more likely to survive and have more offspring. In this way, species change over a very long time.

Humans do not descend from the chimpanzee, but both have common ancestors. These lived about 6 to 7 million years ago in Africa. The **chimpanzee** and the **bonobo** are the closest living relatives of humans. Our genetic material matches theirs by almost 99 per cent.

One of the first changes was **upright walking** on two legs, even before the brain grew a lot. This is shown by the **footprints of Laetoli** in Tanzania, about 3.6 million years old. **Lucy**, whose skeleton was found in Ethiopia in 1974, also already walked upright. But her brain was still hardly larger than a chimpanzee's.

About 2.5 million years ago, the first members of the genus **Homo** appeared. **Homo habilis**, the “handy human”, made simple stone tools. The **Leakey** family of researchers became famous through such finds in the Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania. In time the brain grew larger, and the tools got better.

**Homo erectus** was one of the first kinds of human to leave Africa, and spread as far as Asia. Closely linked with it is the **hand axe**, a carefully shaped stone tool. It probably already used fire too. Fire brought warmth, protection and cooked food that was easier to digest.

Modern humans, **Homo sapiens**, arose about 300,000 years ago in Africa. For a time it lived at the same time as other kinds of human such as the **Neanderthal** in Europe. The oldest and longest period of this story, which began with the first stone tools, is called the Old Stone Age or Palaeolithic. Today Homo sapiens is the only kind of human still alive.

begriffe.erklaerung: The slow change of living things over many generations.
Better adapted living things are more likely to survive and have more offspring.
A fossilised remain of a living thing.
The genus to which present-day humans and their close ancestors belong.

gewusst: The Swedish researcher Svante Pääbo received the Nobel Prize in 2022 for decoding the genetic material of Neanderthals.
For a long time, several kinds of human lived on Earth at the same time.
The footprints at Laetoli were preserved because early human ancestors walked over fresh, wet volcanic ash.

teile.einleitung: Pile dwellings are villages from prehistory whose houses stood on wooden piles on the shores of lakes and in bogs. People lived there from about 5000 to 500 BC. Because a lot has been preserved under water, we know astonishingly precisely today how they lived.
wichtigste: The houses of the pile dwellers stood on wooden piles on the shores of lakes.
The wooden piles have survived to this day because they lay in water and mud.
Since 2011, the “Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps” have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Of the 111 sites of the World Heritage Site, 56 lie in Switzerland, more than in any other country.
The settlements date from the period 5000 to 500 BC.
The pile dwellers lived mainly from arable farming and animals.
On the lake they travelled in dugout canoes.

abschnitte.text: The pile dwellers built their houses on **wooden piles** that they drove into the soft ground on the shores of lakes. The walls consisted of wattle with clay, the roofs of reed, straw or bark. A village often had a few dozen houses, sometimes protected by a fence. Today we know that some houses stood over the water, others on the damp shore ground that was only sometimes flooded.

In the very dry winter of 1853/54, the water level of **Lake Zurich** fell sharply. At Meilen, many piles and finds came to light. The Zurich scholar **Ferdinand Keller** explained them as remains of villages from prehistory. After that, a real pile-dwelling fever began in Switzerland, and searches were made on many lakes.

Because the remains lay in water and mud without air, they did not rot. Archaeologists found pots, tools, stone axes and jewellery, but also things that otherwise vanish, such as fabrics, baskets, wooden implements and food remains. Even **dugout canoes** are preserved, that is, boats made from a single hollowed-out tree trunk. With **dendrochronology**, the counting of tree rings, the age of the piles can often be determined to the exact year.

The pile dwellers lived mainly from **arable farming** and livestock. They planted cereals such as emmer, einkorn and barley, and flax for cloth. They kept cattle, pigs, goats and sheep and in addition went fishing, hunting and gathering. Their villages often lasted only a few decades, then they moved on or built anew.

Since 2011, the **Prehistoric Pile Dwellings around the Alps** have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. It comprises 111 sites in six countries: Switzerland, Germany, Austria, France, Italy and Slovenia. With 56 sites, about half of them lie in Switzerland, for example on Lake Zurich, Lake Biel, Lake Neuchâtel and Lake Constance. Most sites lie invisible today under water or in the ground.

In the **Pile Dwelling Museum Unteruhldingen** on the German shore of Lake Constance, reconstructed pile-dwelling houses stand. In Switzerland, for example the Laténium in Hauterive NE and the National Museum in Zurich show many finds. In Gletterens FR on Lake Neuchâtel, too, there is a reconstructed pile-dwelling village. There you can try out how people at that time made fire, cooked and made tools.

begriffe.erklaerung: A house that stands on wooden piles driven into the ground.
A boat made from a single, hollowed-out tree trunk.
A method of determining the age of wood with the help of tree rings.
A researcher who digs up and studies old remains from the ground.
Places that are so valuable for all humankind that they are especially protected.

gewusst: On Lake Biel at Twann, a piece of bread about 5,500 years old was found.
Switzerland has more World Heritage pile-dwelling sites than all five other countries together.
Many pile-dwelling settlements were discovered because the water level of the lakes had fallen sharply in dry winters.

teile.einleitung: The Chauvet Cave is a cave in southern France with some of the oldest cave paintings in the world. Its walls show lions, rhinoceroses, horses and many other animals of the Ice Age.
wichtigste: The Chauvet Cave lies in the Ardèche valley in southern France.
Three cave explorers discovered it in December 1994.
It is named after its discoverer Jean-Marie Chauvet.
The oldest pictures are over 30,000 years old.
Among the animals painted are cave lions and woolly rhinoceroses.
Since 2014, the cave has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: In December 1994, three **cave explorers** were exploring a rock face in the valley of the **Ardèche**. They found a hidden entrance and, behind it, huge halls full of pictures. One of them was called **Jean-Marie Chauvet**, and the cave is named after him. Because the old entrance was buried long ago, the cave remained almost untouched.

The painters showed many dangerous animals. You can see whole groups of **cave lions** that look as if they are hunting. Several **woolly rhinoceroses**, which lived in Europe at that time, are also painted. There are also horses, mammoths, bears and bison. The animals are often drawn in charcoal and look very lifelike.

abschnitte.titel: Traces of bears and a child
abschnitte.text: On the floor lie many bones and skulls of **cave bears**. They hibernated in the cave. Even paw prints and scratch marks were found. In the clay floor, a **trail** over 70 metres long, made by a child about eight years old, was also preserved.

Measurements on the **charcoal** show that the oldest pictures are over 30,000 years old. This makes them among the oldest known cave paintings. To stop the pictures being damaged, the cave is closed to visitors. Nearby, a large replica was built. In 2014, **UNESCO** added the Chauvet Cave to the World Heritage list.

gewusst: Thousands of years ago, a child walked over 70 metres through the cave, and the footprints are still there.
In the Chauvet Cave, especially many dangerous predators such as lions and bears are painted.

teile.einleitung: The giant deer was a mighty deer of the Ice Age. It is famous for its huge **antlers**, the largest of any known deer. Because many skeletons were found in Ireland, it is also called the **Irish elk**.
wichtigste: The giant deer had the largest antlers of any known deer.
The antlers could be up to about 3.6 metres wide.
Only the males carried antlers.
Every year it shed the antlers, and then a new set grew.
It ate grass, leaves and other plants.
It is also called the Irish elk, but was not an elk.
Its close relative today is the fallow deer.

abschnitte.text: The **antlers** of the giant deer were up to about 3.6 metres wide from one tip to the other. That is wider than a car and much wider than in any deer today. The antler beams were broad like shovels. Despite this weight on its head, the deer carried it with a powerful neck and strong shoulders.

abschnitte.titel: A new set of antlers every year
abschnitte.text: As in most deer, only the **males** carried antlers. Deer **shed** their antlers every year. After that, a new set grows in a few months. For the giant deer this was a huge achievement, because for so much bone the body needs many minerals from its food.

The giant deer was a **plant eater** like all deer. It ate grass, leaves and twigs. It lived in open landscapes with grass and single trees, from Europe to Asia. A dense forest would have been unfavourable for such huge antlers.

abschnitte.titel: Irish elk, but not an elk
abschnitte.text: In the **bogs of Ireland**, many well-preserved skeletons were found. That is why it is also called the **Irish elk**. Despite the name, it was not an elk. Studies show that it is closely related to today's **fallow deer**. At the end of the Ice Age, it became ever rarer and finally died out.

gewusst: The males of the giant deer reached a shoulder height of about two metres.
A giant deer has nothing to do with the elk, although it is often called that.

teile.einleitung: The Erstfeld gold hoard is one of the most valuable finds from Celtic times in Switzerland. It consists of seven gold rings that were discovered by chance in 1962 in the canton of Uri.
wichtigste: The hoard consists of neck rings and arm rings made of gold.
Building workers found it in 1962 on the slope above Erstfeld in the canton of Uri.
The rings were made around 300 BC in the Celtic La Tène period.
They are hollow and made of thin, soldered shells of gold.
The neck rings show intertwined hybrid creatures of human and animal.
The rings show hardly any signs of wear and were probably deposited soon after being made.

abschnitte.text: In 1962, Italian building workers were clearing **scree** from a slope above Erstfeld. Between large boulders they came across seven gold rings stacked inside one another. Unfortunately, the large boulder was blasted and the ground levelled before experts could examine the find spot precisely. That is why today we no longer know exactly how the hoard lay there.

The goldsmiths formed thin shells of **hammered gold** and soldered them together. That is why the rings are hollow inside. The gold is very pure, up to 95 per cent. X-ray images from 1994 showed **folded inserts of sheet gold** in three neck rings. These contain more silver and less gold. Probably they were meant to increase the value of the offering still further.

On the neck rings, **mythical creatures**, birds and snakes wind around one another. They are hybrid creatures of human and animal, including a so-called “Lord of the Animals”. The arm rings bear a wave pattern called the **running dog**. Such decoration is typical of Celtic art.

Judging by style and decoration, the rings date from the **La Tène period**, around 300 BC. So they are over 2000 years old. Because they look almost new, they were probably hardly ever worn. Many experts think of an **offering** or a hiding place. Erstfeld lies on the way to the Gotthard, which was used early on as a crossing over the Alps. Today the hoard is among the best-known pieces of the Swiss National Museum.

gewusst: The rings lay stacked inside one another, as if someone had carefully hidden them.
In some rings there is hidden sheet gold that can only be seen with X-rays.

teile.einleitung: The dog is humans' oldest domestic animal. It descends from the wolf and was already living with people in the Old Stone Age. Finds of bones and studies of genetic material show how this long friendship began.
wichtigste: Domestication means that wild forms become domestic animals over generations.
The dog descends from the wolf.
At Oberkassel near Bonn, a grave about 14,000 years old was found with two people and a dog.
Early dogs had a shorter snout and smaller teeth than wolves.
Dogs can digest starch better than wolves.
In Siberia, there were sled dogs as early as about 9500 years ago.

abschnitte.text: **Domestication** means that animals or plants change over many generations because humans choose which ones breed. So a single tamed wolf is not yet a dog. Only over a very long time did wolves that lived near people become **dogs**. The dog was the first animal that humans domesticated, long before there were farmers.

At **Oberkassel** near Bonn, a double grave about **14,000 years** old was found. In it lay a man, a woman and a dog. The find shows a close relationship between humans and dogs. Studies showed that the young dog had been seriously ill and was probably cared for by the people.

How can you recognise a dog from old bones? Early dogs usually had a **shorter snout** and smaller, more closely set **teeth** than wolves. Today, **genetic analyses** also help with identification. They show, for example, that dogs often have more copies of a gene for digesting **starch**. This fits with the fact that they ate leftover grain from farmers.

On the Siberian island of **Zhokhov**, dog bones and parts of sleds were found that are about **9500 years** old. Evidently the dogs were already being bred as draught animals back then. The **dingo** in Australia descends from domestic dogs that came there with people a few thousand years ago. After that, they lived wild again.

gewusst: All dog breeds today, from the Chihuahua to the St Bernard, belong to the same species.
The dingo is an example of a domestic animal that has gone wild again.

teile.einleitung: A menhir is a large stone that people of the New Stone Age set upright in the ground. Many menhirs are several metres tall. They are found all over Europe, especially many in Brittany, but also in Switzerland.
wichtigste: A menhir is a large, upright stone.
The word comes from Breton and means “long stone”.
At Carnac in Brittany, over 3,000 menhirs stand in rows.
In Switzerland stand the menhirs of Clendy near Yverdon-les-Bains.
In Falera in Graubünden there is a site with many stones.
Why menhirs were set up, nobody knows exactly.

abschnitte.text: The word **menhir** comes from **Breton**. This language is spoken in **Brittany** in France. “Men” means stone and “hir” means long. So a menhir is a **long stone**. People of the New Stone Age set up such stones without machines, only with ropes, wood and a great deal of strength.

When many menhirs stand in a line, this is called a **stone row**. At **Carnac** in Brittany, over 3,000 menhirs stand in long rows. It is one of the largest stone settings in the world. At Locmariaquer lies the **Grand Menhir Brisé**, the largest known menhir in Europe. Today it is broken into four pieces that together are about 20 metres long.

On the shore of Lake Neuchâtel near **Yverdon-les-Bains** stand the **menhirs of Clendy**. They are over 5,000 years old. In **Falera** in Graubünden, numerous stones stand in rows in the Parc la Mutta. Some researchers suspect a link there to the course of the sun. On Lake Geneva near Lutry, too, a row of menhirs was found.

Nobody knows exactly, because there is **no writing** from this time. Researchers suspect that menhirs were important for **celebrations** and **belief**. Perhaps they also marked special places or boundaries. Some stone rows could have something to do with the course of the sun and moon.

Many children know menhirs from the comics about **Asterix**. His friend **Obelix** is a stonemason and often carries a menhir on his back. In the German comic, the stones are called **Hinkelsteine**. The stories are set among the Gauls, that is, long after the time when the real menhirs were set up.

gewusst: The menhirs of Clendy were set upright again in the 20th century after they had fallen over.
The Grand Menhir Brisé probably weighed several hundred tonnes, as much as many lorries.

teile.einleitung: Radiocarbon dating is a method for determining the age of finds. It uses the radioactive carbon-14 that is found in all living things. For archaeology it was one of the most important discoveries of the 20th century.
wichtigste: The method uses the isotope carbon-14.
Willard Libby developed it in the late 1940s.
For this he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960.
The half-life of C-14 is about 5,730 years.
Only material from living things can be dated, such as charcoal.
The method reaches back to about 50,000 years.
“BP” refers to the year 1950.

abschnitte.text: In the upper **atmosphere**, neutrons from **cosmic radiation** hit nitrogen atoms. In the process, **nitrogen-14** is converted into **carbon-14**, C-14 for short. This isotope combines with oxygen to form CO2. Plants take it up in photosynthesis, animals and humans through food. So every living thing constantly has a little C-14 in it.

C-14 is **radioactive** and decays slowly. After the death of a living thing, no new C-14 is added. The **half-life** is about **5,730 years**. After this time, half of the atoms have decayed. After two half-lives, only **a quarter** is left, because 1/2 times 1/2 gives 1/4. If you measure how much C-14 is still there, you can calculate the age. With samples older than about **50,000 years**, almost nothing is left, and then the method no longer works reliably.

The American chemist **Willard Libby** developed the method in the late 1940s at the **University of Chicago**. For this he received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** in **1960**, which is awarded in Stockholm. Libby calculated a half-life of **5,568 years**. Later it turned out that about 5,730 years is more accurate. So that all results stay comparable, conventional radiocarbon ages are nevertheless still calculated with the Libby value.

Only material that comes from **living things** and contains carbon can be dated. This includes **charcoal**, wood, bone, seeds and textiles. A stone tool or a piece of pottery cannot be dated directly in this way. Archaeologists then take charcoal from the same layer. In Switzerland, for example, the age of many **pile dwellings** was determined in this way.

Radiocarbon dates are often given in **BP**. This means “before present”. In this, “present” always means the year **1950**. An age of 1000 BP therefore means about 1000 radiocarbon years before 1950. Because the C-14 content of the air was not always the same, the values have to be **calibrated**. For this they are compared, for example, with **tree rings** whose age is known exactly.

gewusst: With modern measuring instruments, a few milligrams of material are often enough today for a dating.
With radiocarbon dating, the age of the glacier mummy Ötzi was also determined: about 5,300 years.

teile.einleitung: The Cambrian explosion is a stretch of Earth's history about 540 million years ago. In a geologically short time, almost all the large animal groups that exist today appeared in the sea.
wichtigste: The Cambrian began about 540 million years ago.
At that time almost all of today's animal phyla appeared.
All animals of this time lived in the sea.
The Burgess Shale in Canada is a famous find site.
Soft body parts were preserved there too.
The Cambrian is named after Wales.

abschnitte.text: By **Cambrian explosion** people do not mean a loud event. What is meant is that at the beginning of the **Cambrian**, in a geologically short time, very many new animal groups appeared. Almost all of today's **animal phyla** can be traced back to this time. The Cambrian marks the start of the **Palaeozoic era**. The name comes from “Cambria”, the Latin name for **Wales**. Rocks from this period were first described there.

In the Cambrian there were still no animals on land. All animals lived in the **sea**. Many got **hard shells** or armour for the first time. These include the **trilobites**, distant relatives of today's crustaceans and insects. Hard parts fossilise well, so suddenly many more fossils are found from this time.

The **Burgess Shale** lies in the Rocky Mountains in **Canada**. Charles Walcott discovered the site in 1909. Normally only hard parts such as shells fossilise. In the Burgess Shale, however, **soft parts** were preserved too, for example of worms. That is why this site is especially valuable for research.

Some animals of the Cambrian looked very strange. **Opabinia** had five eyes on stalks and a long trunk with a grasping claw. **Anomalocaris** was a large **predator** and was among the largest animals of its time. It caught its prey with grasping appendages on its head.

gewusst: The animal Opabinia had five eyes.
In the Cambrian there were still no animals on land.

teile.einleitung: Parasaurolophus was a dinosaur with a long, hollow crest on its head. It lived in the Cretaceous in North America and ate plants.
wichtigste: Parasaurolophus had a long, hollow bone crest on its head.
With the crest, it could probably produce loud sounds.
It was a plant eater.
It belongs to the duck-billed dinosaurs.
It lived about 76 to 73 million years ago in North America.
It was about 9 to 10 metres long.

abschnitte.text: The most striking feature of Parasaurolophus is its **head crest**. It was long, curved backwards and made of bone. Inside it was **hollow**. A fully grown animal was about **9 to 10 metres** long. Parasaurolophus lived in the **Cretaceous**, about 76 to 73 million years ago. Fossils were found in **Canada** and in the **USA**, so in North America.

In the hollow crest ran long **tubes** connected to the nose. Researchers suspect that Parasaurolophus could produce loud, deep **sounds** with it, similar to a trombone. In this way the animals could perhaps communicate over long distances. In addition, the crest probably helped animals of the same species to recognise one another. This is not known for certain, however.

Parasaurolophus belongs to the **hadrosaurs**. They are also called **duck-billed dinosaurs**, because their mouth was broad and flat at the front. Parasaurolophus was a **plant eater**. Further back in the mouth it had very many teeth. With them it ground up leaves and twigs. Worn teeth were constantly replaced by new ones.

Parasaurolophus could walk on **all fours**, for example when feeding on the ground. For running fast, it probably reared up onto its strong **hind legs**. Its long tail helped it to keep its balance. Probably it lived in groups, which gave it protection from predatory dinosaurs.

gewusst: Researchers have reconstructed on the computer how the crest might have sounded: like a deep hum.
The name Parasaurolophus means roughly “beside Saurolophus”, because it was compared with this related dinosaur.

teile.einleitung: The Mont Vully is a hill in the Three Lakes region between Lake Murten and Lake Neuchâtel. Over 2,000 years ago, the Celtic Helvetii had a fortified main settlement there, a so-called oppidum.
wichtigste: The Mont Vully lies between Lake Murten and Lake Neuchâtel.
It is about 653 metres high and belongs to the canton of Fribourg.
On the hill lay an oppidum of the Helvetii.
The younger rampart was built around 120 BC and was about 600 metres long.
It protected an area of about 50 hectares.
For Expo.02, a piece of the Celtic wall was rebuilt.
On the south slope, wine is grown today.

abschnitte.text: The Mont Vully rises between **Lake Murten** and **Lake Neuchâtel**. Its highest point lies about 653 metres above sea level in the Fribourg municipality of Mont-Vully. This means it towers a good 200 metres above the lakes. The hill belongs to the **Lake District** in the canton of Fribourg, near Murten. In the area, German and French are spoken. In clear weather you can see from the summit over both lakes and as far as the Alps.

In the 1st century BC, the **Helvetii**, a Celtic people, lived on the Plateau. On the Mont Vully they had one of their fortified main settlements. The Romans called such places **oppidum**, which means town. A long rampart closed off the hill on the accessible side. The other sides were protected by the steep slopes. At about 50 hectares, the site was among the larger ones in the territory of the Helvetii.

abschnitte.titel: A wall of wood, stone and earth
abschnitte.text: The younger rampart was about 600 metres long and was built around 120 BC. It was a **Pfostenschlitzmauer** (post-slot wall). This means: in the front, vertical **oak posts** stood at intervals, with stones between them. Behind the front, earth was heaped up. This produced a wide and solid wall. Through gates you reached the inside.

From **1978 to 1987**, archaeologists studied the rampart closely. They found remains of gates and towers. Thanks to the finds, they could determine when the wall was built. For the national exhibition **Expo.02**, which in 2002 also took place in Murten, a piece of the wall was rebuilt. Today you can visit it on the hill and imagine well what the fortification once looked like.

Today the Mont Vully is known above all for its **wine growing**. The slopes above Lake Murten get a lot of sun. That is why vines thrive especially well there. The wine from the area bears the name **Vully**. Walking trails lead through the vineyards up to the summit and to the remains of the oppidum.

gewusst: The rampart of the oppidum was about as long as six football pitches one behind the other.
With the help of the finds, the building of the younger rampart could be narrowed down to the years around 124 to 120 BC.

teile.einleitung: A **smith** is a craftsman who works metal. He heats the metal in the fire and shapes it with the hammer. Even thousands of years ago, people learned to melt and shape copper and bronze.
wichtigste: A smith works metal.
He lays the hot metal on a heavy block, the anvil.
With tongs he holds the glowing metal fast.
A bellows blows air into the fire so that it gets hotter.
In the smelting furnace, charcoal was burned.
Copper only becomes liquid above 1,000 degrees.
Liquid bronze was poured into a mould.

abschnitte.text: For the work, the smith needs a very hot fire. In the past, **charcoal** was burned for this, which gets much hotter than ordinary wood. With a **bellows**, air is blown into the fire. The oxygen in the air makes the embers burn even brighter and hotter.

The smith holds the glowing metal with **tongs**, because it is far too hot to touch. He lays it on the **anvil**, a heavy block of metal. Then he strikes it with the **hammer** and **shapes** the soft, hot metal. In this way knives, nails, tools or horseshoes are made.

Copper only becomes liquid at **over 1,000 degrees**. The early metalworkers melted it in a **crucible**, a small vessel of fired clay. If you mix copper with a little tin, **bronze** is produced. The liquid bronze was poured into a **mould** of stone or clay. After cooling, axes, jewellery or swords were taken out.

With metal a new age began: the Stone Age was followed by the **Bronze Age** and later the **Iron Age**. Whoever could work metal was highly valued. In Switzerland too, moulds and bronze objects from this time were found. To this day there are smiths, such as farriers, who fit horseshoes to horses.

gewusst: The family name Schmid or Schmidt is one of the most common in the German-speaking world and comes from the trade of the smith.
Iron melts at an even higher temperature than copper, so people only learned later to work it.

teile.einleitung: The continents do not stand still, they move very slowly across the Earth. This idea is called continental drift. Alfred Wegener presented it in detail in 1915, but many researchers did not believe him at first.
wichtigste: Alfred Wegener presented the theory in a book in 1915.
Wegener was a meteorologist and polar explorer.
The coasts of Africa and South America fit together like pieces of a puzzle.
Fossils of Mesosaurus were found on both continents.
Today, plate tectonics explains the movement of the continents.
The Atlantic grows wider by about 2 to 3 centimetres every year.

abschnitte.text: **Alfred Wegener** was a meteorologist, so he studied the weather. He was also a polar explorer and travelled to Greenland several times. In 1915, he published the book “The Origin of Continents and Oceans”. Many experts rejected his idea at first. Wegener died in 1930 on an expedition in Greenland.

Wegener noticed that the east coast of **South America** and the west coast of **Africa** fit together like pieces of a puzzle. In addition, fossils of **Mesosaurus** were found on both continents. This small reptile lived in fresh water and could not cross an ocean. Rocks too match up on both sides. Wegener concluded from this that the continents once formed one great primeval continent, which he called **Pangaea**.

Since the 1960s, **plate tectonics** has explained how the continents move. The outer shell of the Earth consists of large **plates**. They float on the viscous, hot rock beneath. At the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge**, two plates move away from each other. As a result, the Atlantic grows by about 2 to 3 centimetres a year, roughly as fast as fingernails grow.

Where plates collide, mountains fold up. The **Indian Plate** broke away from the southern continent Gondwana, moved north and collided with Asia. In the process the **Himalayas** piled up. The **Alps** also arose in this way: the African Plate presses against Europe from the south. That is why Switzerland has high mountains and now and then earthquakes.

In **Iceland**, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge comes to the surface. The island lies on two plates that are drifting apart. That is why there are many volcanoes, hot springs and long cracks in the ground there. In some places you can stand between the two plates.

gewusst: Wegener's idea was only generally accepted decades after his death.
In many millions of years, the continents will be distributed quite differently on the Earth again.

teile.einleitung: The Iguanodon was a large plant-eating dinosaur. It is famous because it was one of the first dinosaurs ever to receive a scientific name.
wichtigste: The name Iguanodon means “iguana tooth”.
The first teeth were found in southern England.
Gideon Mantell gave the animal its name in 1825.
On its thumb it had a pointed spike.
In 1878, about 30 skeletons were found at Bernissart in Belgium.
A large Iguanodon was about 8 to 10 metres long.

abschnitte.text: The teeth of the Iguanodon look like very large teeth of an **iguana**. That is why it was given the name **Iguanodon**, which means “iguana tooth”. The first teeth were found in **southern England**. The doctor **Gideon Mantell** gave the animal its name in 1825. This made the Iguanodon the second dinosaur ever to receive a scientific name.

The thumb of the Iguanodon was a pointed **spike**. At first researchers thought the spike was a horn on the **nose**. That is how the Iguanodon was drawn at first. Only later skeleton finds showed that the spike belonged to the thumb. Perhaps the animal used it for defence.

In 1878, miners in a coal mine at **Bernissart** in Belgium found the skeletons of about 30 animals. This was a sensation, because now the build of the body was known exactly. Many of these skeletons now stand in the museum in **Brussels**. A large Iguanodon was about 8 to 10 metres long and weighed several tonnes.

The Iguanodon was a **plant eater**. With its toothless **beak** at the front of the mouth, it bit off plants. With the teeth further back, it chewed them. It could probably walk on four legs, but could also rear up onto its hind legs.

gewusst: For a long time, pictures showed the Iguanodon with a horn on its nose, when it was really its thumb.
In a single mine in Belgium, about 30 Iguanodon skeletons were found.

teile.einleitung: Meganeura was a giant dragonfly of prehistory. Its wings together were about 70 centimetres across. It lived about 300 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs.
wichtigste: Meganeura was a giant insect that looked like a dragonfly.
The wingspan was about 66 to 70 centimetres.
It lived about 300 million years ago in the Carboniferous.
It hunted other insects in flight.
The first fossils were found at Commentry in France.
Like all insects, it had six legs, plus four wings.

abschnitte.titel: An insect as wide as a pigeon
abschnitte.text: **Meganeura** is among the largest insects of all time. It looked like a **dragonfly** today, but was much bigger. Its wings together were about **66 to 70 centimetres** across. That is about as wide as with a pigeon. Like dragonflies today, it had **two pairs of wings**, so four wings, and, as an insect, **six legs**.

Meganeura lived about **300 million years ago** in the **Carboniferous**. In this period, huge swamp forests grew with tree-high ferns and horsetails. From these forests, much hard coal later formed. The **dinosaurs** only came onto the Earth much later. So Meganeura lived long before them.

Like dragonflies today, Meganeura was a **hunter**. It caught **other insects** in flight. For this it probably had large eyes and strong legs for grasping. There were no birds yet at that time. So in the air it had hardly any enemies.

Researchers suspect that the air in the Carboniferous contained more **oxygen** than today. Insects breathe through fine tubes in their bodies. With more oxygen in the air, even large insects could get enough air. The first fossils of Meganeura were found in the 1880s at **Commentry** in **France**.

gewusst: The largest dragonfly today has a wingspan of only just under 20 centimetres.
Strictly speaking, Meganeura was not a true dragonfly, but a close relative of their ancestors.

teile.einleitung: Ichthyosaurs were marine reptiles that lived at the time of the dinosaurs. They looked similar to dolphins today and spent their whole lives in the water.
wichtigste: Ichthyosaurs lived entirely in the sea.
The name means “fish lizard”.
They looked similar to dolphins.
Instead of legs they had flippers.
They breathed with lungs and had to surface to breathe.
Their young were born alive in the water.

abschnitte.text: The name **ichthyosaur** comes from Greek: “ichthys” means fish and “sauros” means lizard. So it means **fish lizard**. But ichthyosaurs were not fish, they were **reptiles**. They had a long snout, a streamlined body and a dorsal fin. Dolphins look similar too, although they are not related at all.

Their legs had turned into **flippers**. They used them to steer in the water. The drive came mainly from the powerful **tail fin**, similar to a fish. So ichthyosaurs could swim fast. They never came onto land.

Ichthyosaurs had very large **eyes**. With them they could see well even in dark, deep water. They hunted fish and squid. Because they had **lungs** and no gills, they had to come to the surface of the water to breathe.

Fossils of females have been found with young still lying inside their bodies. This shows that the young were **born alive**, directly in the water. So they did not have to hatch from eggs. Many well-preserved fossils come from **Holzmaden** in Baden-Württemberg. Remains of ichthyosaurs have also been found in Switzerland.

gewusst: Ichthyosaurs and dolphins look similar, although one is a reptile and the other a mammal.
Some ichthyosaurs had eyes more than 20 centimetres across.

teile.einleitung: In the Old Stone Age, people lived together in small groups. Such a group of relatives is called a **clan**. Together they hunted, gathered and lived, because surviving was easier together.
wichtigste: A clan is a group of relatives.
A clan was a small group of people.
Surviving was easier together.
The spoils of a hunt were shared.
In the evening the clan often sat by the fire.
Children learned from adults and elders by watching and joining in.

abschnitte.text: A **clan** is a group of **relatives**: parents, children, grandparents, aunts, uncles and other family members. In the Old Stone Age, people wandered about as hunters and gatherers. A clan was a **small group**, probably only a few dozen people. In this way everyone could find enough food.

Alone, life in the wild was very hard. **Together**, people could hunt large animals, fend off enemies and gather food. After a successful hunt, the clan **shared** the spoils. If someone was **injured** or ill, the others probably cared for them. Researchers have found bones of people who lived on for a long time with serious injuries.

abschnitte.titel: In the evening by the fire
abschnitte.text: In the evening the clan often sat **by the fire**. It gave warmth and light and kept wild animals away. By the fire, meat was roasted, and people surely told each other stories. In this way experiences and knowledge were passed on.

There were no schools. Children learned **by watching and joining in**. The **adults and the elders** passed on their knowledge: where to find edible plants, how to make tools, how to read tracks. The elders were important because they had a lot of experience.

gewusst: A clan also included people who could no longer hunt themselves, and they were still looked after.
The German word Sippe is very old and originally meant roughly the same as kinship.

teile.einleitung: The history of the Earth is about 4.6 billion years long. To put it in order, geologists divide it into eras and smaller periods. Many of these names tell where the rocks were first studied, like the Jurassic, which is named after the Jura mountains.
wichtigste: The Precambrian covers by far the largest part of Earth's history.
After it come the Palaeozoic, the Mesozoic and the Cenozoic.
The Mesozoic is called Erdmittelalter in German, the Cenozoic Erdneuzeit.
We live today in the Cenozoic.
The Jurassic is named after the Jura mountains, the Devonian after a county in England.
At the end of the Permian about 252 million years ago, there was the greatest mass extinction.
The crater of the asteroid that contributed to the extinction of the dinosaurs lies in Mexico.

abschnitte.text: The **Precambrian** stretches from the formation of the Earth to about 540 million years ago. That is almost nine tenths of the whole of Earth's history. For a long time there were only tiny living things, mainly in the sea. Only towards the end of the Precambrian did larger, many-celled living things appear.

After the Precambrian comes the **Palaeozoic** (in German, Erdaltertum, “Earth's ancient age”). One of its periods is the **Devonian**, named after the county of Devon in south-west England, where rocks from this time were studied early on. The **Carboniferous** is named after coal, because “carbo” means coal in Latin. From huge swamp forests of this time, many coal deposits formed. At the end of the **Permian**, about 252 million years ago, most of all species of sea animals died out. It was the worst **mass extinction** in Earth's history.

The **Mesozoic** is called **Erdmittelalter** (“Earth's middle age”) in German. It consists of the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous and is the time of the dinosaurs. The **Jurassic** is named after the **Jura mountains** in Switzerland and France, where many limestone rocks from this time are found. The Cretaceous ended about 66 million years ago with an asteroid impact. Its **Chicxulub crater** lies on the Yucatán Peninsula in **Mexico**.

After the extinction of the dinosaurs began the **Cenozoic**, in German the **Erdneuzeit** (“Earth's new age”). It continues to this day. During this time, mammals spread widely. The Alps, too, were folded up into a high mountain range in the Cenozoic. The Ice Ages and the appearance of humans also belong to this period.

gewusst: The Permian is named after the city of Perm in Russia.
If the whole of Earth's history were a single day, humans would have existed only for the last few seconds before midnight.

teile.einleitung: **Ötzi** is a man from the Stone Age who died in the Alps about 5300 years ago. He was found in the ice in 1991, together with his clothing and many objects. His **equipment** shows how skilful people were back then.
wichtigste: Ötzi wore a cap made of bear fur and a jacket made from the skins of goats and sheep.
His shoes were stuffed with grass on the inside, which kept his feet warm.
His bow of yew wood was about 1.80 metres long and not yet finished.
There were 14 arrows in his quiver.
The blade of his dagger was made of flint.
In a container made of birch bark he carried embers for a fire.
He also had a copper axe, a back frame and two pieces of birch polypore.

abschnitte.text: In September 1991, walkers in the **Ötztal Alps** discovered a dead man in the ice. The site lies just on the Italian side of the border with Austria, in South Tyrol. It soon became clear that the man was over **5000 years** old. Because the ice had covered him for so long, his clothes and tools were preserved too. Today Ötzi lies in the Archaeological Museum in **Bolzano**.

On his head Ötzi wore a **cap made of bear fur** with a strap under the chin. His **jacket** was sewn together from the skins of **goats and sheep** and had light and dark stripes. He also wore leggings made of fur. His **shoes** were stuffed with **grass** on the inside. The grass kept his feet warm, a bit like a sock.

Ötzi's **bow** was made of the hard wood of the **yew**. It was about **1.80 metres** long, so longer than Ötzi himself. But the bow was not quite finished yet. He carried his arrows in a **quiver**, a bag made of fur. It held **14 arrows**, of which only a few were ready to shoot.

Ötzi had a small **dagger** with him. The blade was made of **flint**, a very hard stone, and the handle of **ash wood**. Especially valuable was his **axe** with a blade made of **copper**. On his back he carried a **back frame** made of hazel wood, a frame for his belongings. Cords, nets and small tools for resharpening stone blades were also found.

In a **container made of birch bark**, Ötzi carried **embers** wrapped in leaves. This let him make a fire quickly. On a cord he had two pieces of **birch polypore**, a fungus that grows on birches. Researchers think he used it as a **medicine**. He also carried a tinder fungus for lighting fires.

gewusst: Ötzi's copper axe shows that people could already work metal at that time.
On Ötzi's skin, many small tattoos made of lines and crosses were found.

teile.einleitung: In an **excavation**, researchers carefully take fossils out of the ground. This takes a lot of patience, the right tools and precise notes. Every find should reach the museum undamaged.
wichtigste: The place where people dig is called the dig site.
With a shovel you move large amounts of soil, and with a brush you uncover the fossil.
Before it is taken out, the fossil is photographed so that its position is known.
Large bones are wrapped in plaster for transport.
Every find gets a number so that it can be found again.
In the museum, a preparator frees the fossil from the rock.

abschnitte.text: The place where people dig for fossils is called the **dig site**. There, the ground is removed **layer by layer**. A dig often lasts several weeks or comes back every summer. People dig **slowly**, because fossils are often brittle. Anyone who works too fast can destroy valuable finds.

First, larger amounts of soil and rock are removed with the **shovel**. Close to the fossil, people switch to finer tools such as hammer, chisel and trowel. Right at the end, dust and soil are brushed away with a fine **brush**. When you tap at stone, splinters can fly off. That is why people wear **safety glasses**.

Before a fossil is taken out, **photos** and **drawings** are made. They show how the bones lay in the ground. This helps later with putting them together and understanding them. Every find gets a **number**. Each number comes with notes about where it was found and which layer of rock it came from. This way the information is never lost.

Large bones are heavy and fragile. So they are wrapped in strips of cloth and **plaster**. The hard shell protects them like a plaster cast on a broken arm. This way they can be transported without damage. Small finds go into boxes or bags with labels.

abschnitte.titel: In the laboratory and the museum
abschnitte.text: The finds usually go to a **museum**. There, a **preparator** works on them. With fine tools and a lot of patience, the preparator frees the fossil from the rock. After that it is studied, stored and sometimes put on display. In Switzerland, for example, you can see dinosaur bones found in a clay pit at the **Saurier Museum Frick** (dinosaur museum) in canton Aargau.

gewusst: Preparing a large fossil can take months or even years.
Monte San Giorgio in Ticino is a UNESCO World Heritage Site because of its fossils.

teile.einleitung: The Mesozoic is the era of the dinosaurs. It consists of three periods: Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous. It began about 252 million years ago and ended about 66 million years ago.
wichtigste: The Mesozoic is called “Erdmittelalter” (Earth's middle age) in German.
It consists of the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous, in that order.
The Triassic began about 252 million years ago.
Stegosaurus lived in the Jurassic, Tyrannosaurus at the end of the Cretaceous.
About 66 million years ago, a huge meteorite probably ended the time of the dinosaurs.
Humans never lived at the same time as the dinosaurs.

abschnitte.text: The **Triassic** began about **252 million years ago**. At that time the continents were still united in the supercontinent Pangaea. In the Triassic, the first **dinosaurs** appeared. In Switzerland there are famous finds from this time: at **Frick** in the canton of Aargau, many skeletons of the plant eater Plateosaurus were found. On **Monte San Giorgio** in Ticino lie fossils of fish and marine reptiles, and the site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The Triassic was followed by the **Jurassic**. This period is named after the **Jura Mountains**, because many rocks from this time lie there. In the Jurassic lived huge plant eaters with long necks. **Stegosaurus**, with its bony plates on its back, also lived in the late Jurassic, about 150 million years ago. The first birds also appeared in the Jurassic.

The last period is the **Cretaceous**. It gets its name from thick layers of white chalk, a **limestone**. It consists of tiny shells of marine organisms. Right at the end of the Cretaceous lived **Tyrannosaurus**, one of the last large dinosaurs. In this period the first **flowering plants** also appeared.

About **66 million years ago**, a huge **meteorite** hit the Earth, in the area of present-day Mexico. Dust darkened the sky, and the climate changed greatly. The large dinosaurs died out. Only the birds survived, and they are regarded as the descendants of the dinosaurs today. After that the Cenozoic began.

Dinosaurs existed for over **150 million years**. Humans have existed for only a few hundred thousand years. That is only a tiny fraction of this time. Between the last Tyrannosaurus and the first human, there were many millions of years. In films, humans and dinosaurs meet, but in reality that was never so.

gewusst: The word Jurassic for a period of Earth's history comes from the Jura Mountains, which also lie in Switzerland.
The impact crater of the meteorite lies on the Yucatán Peninsula and is called Chicxulub.

teile.einleitung: An **abri** is an overhanging rock ledge. In the Stone Age, hunters and gatherers sought shelter under rock ledges like this. Archaeologists still find many traces of their lives there today.
wichtigste: An abri is a place where a rock face juts out far above.
The word comes from French and means shelter or refuge.
A rock overhang protected people from rain, snow and wind.
Unlike a deep cave, an abri was bright, and the smoke could drift away.
A well-known site in Switzerland is the Schweizersbild near Schaffhausen.
People often stayed only for a while and then moved on.

abschnitte.text: On some rock faces the stone juts out far at the top. Underneath, a sheltered place forms, a **rock overhang**. In French, a place like this is called an **abri**, which means shelter or refuge. Experts use the word in German too. An abri is not as deep as a cave, but open at the front.

The rock above your head kept off **rain and snow**, and the wall at your back slowed the **wind**. Because the overhang is open at the front, **daylight** came in. The smoke from the fire could drift away, unlike deep inside a cave. An abri on the **sunny side** was especially pleasant. There, the sun warmed the rock in winter.

People in the Stone Age lived as **hunters and gatherers**. They followed the animals and looked for plants, in different places depending on the season. So they usually did not live under the same rock overhang all year round. When food ran short, they moved on. But they returned to some places again and again.

In the ground under rock overhangs there are often **fireplaces, bones and tools**. People simply left rubbish and broken tools lying around. Soil and stones built up on top, and so the traces were preserved for many thousands of years. Archaeologists dig layer by layer and read from them when and how people lived there.

A well-known living site under a rock overhang is the **Schweizersbild** near Schaffhausen. Hunters lived there at the end of the last **Ice Age**. During excavations, very many tools made of flint were found, along with bones of animals they had hunted. Nearby is also the Kesslerloch cave, another important site from this time.

gewusst: Under an abri, layers of finds from many thousands of years can lie on top of each other.
Even today, walkers sometimes shelter under a rock overhang during a thunderstorm.

teile.einleitung: The reindeer is a deer that lives in the cold north. In the Ice Age there were reindeer also in the area of present-day Switzerland, and they were very important for the hunters of the Stone Age.
wichtigste: The reindeer belongs to the deer family.
In reindeer, both males and females carry antlers.
In North America, wild reindeer are called caribou.
In winter, reindeer often eat lichens.
Their broad hooves carry them in the snow like snowshoes.
Today many reindeer live in Finland, Norway and Sweden.
Stone Age hunters used almost everything from the reindeer.

abschnitte.text: The reindeer belongs to the family of **deer**. That is why it carries **antlers**. But in the reindeer, the **females** also have antlers, whereas in other deer usually only the males have them. Reindeer and **caribou** are the same species. In North America, the wild reindeer are called caribou. Today many reindeer live in the cold north, for example in **Finland**, **Norway** and **Sweden**.

Reindeer have a dense **coat** that protects them from icy cold. Their **hooves** are broad and splayed. They carry the animals in the snow like **snowshoes**, so they hardly sink in. In winter, reindeer paw away the snow with their hooves. Underneath they find **lichens**, which are also called **reindeer lichen**. In summer they eat grasses, herbs and leaves.

Reindeer live in **herds** and migrate long distances every year between summer and winter areas. In doing so, they often have to swim across **rivers**. There they make progress only slowly. Hunters of the Stone Age therefore liked to lie in wait for the herds at river crossings. In the **Ice Age**, reindeer also lived in the area of Switzerland. When it became warmer, they moved north.

For the people of the Stone Age, the reindeer was very valuable. They used **almost everything** from it. The **meat** was eaten, and from the **pelt** clothes and tents were made. **Antler** and **bones** were made into tools and weapons. The **sinews** served as strong threads for sewing. Even today some peoples in the north, such as the Sámi, keep large herds of reindeer.

gewusst: When reindeer walk, you can hear a soft clicking from their feet with every step.
Reindeer shed their antlers every year and then grow new ones.

teile.einleitung: According to what we know today, life on Earth began in the water at least about 3.5 billion years ago. The first living things were tiny single-celled organisms such as bacteria. From them, over an unimaginably long time, all plants, animals and also humans developed.
wichtigste: There was life at least about 3.5 billion years ago.
The first living things were single-celled organisms such as bacteria.
Stromatolites are among the oldest traces of life.
Cyanobacteria were the first to put large amounts of oxygen into the air.
For a long time, all living things lived only in the water.
About 540 million years ago, many animal groups arose in the Cambrian explosion.
Monte San Giorgio in Ticino has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2003 because of its fossils.

abschnitte.text: Exactly how dead matter became life is still not fully understood. In the famous **Miller-Urey experiment** of 1952/53, Stanley Miller and Harold Urey let electric sparks like lightning flash through simple gases. This produced **amino acids**, the building blocks of living things. According to one well-known hypothesis, life might also have arisen at hot springs in the **deep sea**.

The first living things were **single-celled organisms** such as bacteria, which consisted of just one cell. Some formed thick mats in shallow water. These mats built up limestone structures layer by layer, the **stromatolites**. Such structures are still growing today, for example in Shark Bay in Australia.

The **cyanobacteria** could carry out photosynthesis using sunlight, as plants do today. In doing so, they gave off **oxygen**. About 2.4 billion years ago, this oxygen built up in the air. Without it, there would be no animals and no humans today.

Later, living things arose whose cells have a **nucleus**, the **eukaryotes**. In it, the genetic material is well protected. From them developed many-celled living things such as algae, fungi, plants and animals. Bacteria, by contrast, still have no nucleus today.

About 540 million years ago, very many animal groups arose in a short time, which is called the **Cambrian explosion**. At that time, many animals developed hard shells and armour, which were well preserved as **fossils**. Fossils are fossilised remains or traces of living things. For a long time all animals lived only in the water, until first plants and later early four-legged animals descended from fish conquered the land.

**Monte San Giorgio** lies in Ticino on Lake Lugano. In its rocks, wonderfully preserved fossils of fish and marine reptiles were found that lived in a sea bay about 240 million years ago. Since 2003 the mountain has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. In the fossil museum in Meride you can look at many finds.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that consists of just a single cell.
A process in which living things use sunlight to make food and give off oxygen.
A fossilised remain or trace of a living thing.
A living thing whose cells have a nucleus.
A layered limestone structure built up by bacterial mats.

gewusst: For more than three billion years, almost all life on Earth consisted only of single-celled organisms.
We owe the oxygen you breathe in originally to tiny bacteria.
There are more bacteria living in your body than you have body cells of your own, or at least about the same number.

teile.einleitung: In aerial archaeology, researchers search from the air for traces of past times. From above, ditches, walls and paths show up that cannot be seen on the ground. Today drones and lasers help with this too.
wichtigste: Over filled-in ditches, cereal often grows taller and greener.
Over hidden walls, the plant growth stays poorer and ripens earlier.
In long dry spells in summer, such traces show up especially clearly.
When the sun is low, shallow rises cast long shadows.
LIDAR measures the height of the terrain from the air with laser pulses.
With LIDAR you can even see through forests to the ground.

abschnitte.text: Under many fields lie the remains of old settlements. Ditches and pits are filled with loose, **humus-rich soil**. It stores more water and nutrients. The cereal above it grows taller and greener, a **positive crop mark**. Over a **wall**, the layer of soil is thin and dries out quickly. The plants stay smaller and change colour earlier, a **negative crop mark**.

Crop marks show up especially clearly in **long dry spells** in summer. Then the differences in the soil have a strong effect on the plants. The drought summer of 2018, for example, brought many new sites to light in Britain and Ireland. In the morning or evening, the sun stands low. Then even low ramparts and hollows cast **long shadows** that can be seen well from the air.

**LIDAR** is a measuring method using laser light. An aircraft or a drone sends hundreds of thousands of **laser pulses** per second to the ground. From the time until the light comes back, a computer calculates the height. This produces an exact **height model** of the landscape. Some pulses get through gaps in the leaf canopy to the forest floor. If you subtract the plants, you can see ramparts, ditches and old paths.

A large LIDAR survey in **Guatemala** showed in 2018 tens of thousands of previously unknown structures of the **Maya**. Under the rainforest, houses, dams, fields and roads came to light. In **Cambodia**, from 2012, researchers found roads, water works and settlements of the Khmer around the temple complex of **Angkor**. These finds changed the picture of how many people used to live there.

In Switzerland too, the cantonal archaeological services use aerial photographs and laser data. With these, for example, old paths, burial mounds or castle sites are found in the forest. Such methods have a great advantage: you do not have to dig to discover a site. The ground stays protected as a result.

gewusst: Some sites can only be seen from the air for a few days a year, depending on the weather and plants.
With LIDAR, areas can be studied in a short time that would take years on foot.

teile.einleitung: The La Tène period is the later pre-Roman Iron Age in central Europe. It lasted roughly from 450 BC to around the birth of Christ. During this time Celtic groups spread far across Europe.
wichtigste: The La Tène period lasted roughly from 450 BC to around the birth of Christ.
It is named after the find site La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel.
Celtic hordes attacked the sanctuary of Delphi in 279 BC.
The Galatians settled in Asia Minor in the 3rd century BC.
The art shows flowing tendrils, spirals and faces.
The period ended with the conquest of the Celtic territories by Rome.

abschnitte.text: The **La Tène period** follows the Hallstatt period. It begins around **450 BC** and ends around the **birth of Christ**. Its end came with the conquest of the Celtic territories by **Rome**. It is named after the find site La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel. In the area of Switzerland at that time lived, among others, the Celtic **Helvetii**.

Celtic groups moved into many parts of Europe. Around 387 BC, Celts even conquered the city of Rome. After an invasion of Macedonia, Celtic hordes advanced in **279 BC** as far as **Delphi**, the famous sanctuary of the Greeks. The attack was repelled. Other groups settled in the interior of Anatolia in **Asia Minor**. They were called **Galatians**.

Typical of La Tène art are **flowing tendrils**, **spirals** and **grotesque faces**. The artists took over motifs from the Mediterranean region and shaped them into interlaced patterns. Human and animal faces merge with plants. An early style is named after the princess's grave of **Waldalgesheim** near Bingen on the Rhine. It belongs to the 4th century BC.

At the **Glauberg** in Hesse, a life-size sandstone statue was found in 1996 beside a burial mound. It shows a warrior with a shield, neck ring and a leaf-shaped head covering. In southern Germany there are rectangular enclosures with a rampart and ditch, the **Viereckschanzen**. In the past they were mostly interpreted as cult sites, but today many are also seen as enclosed farmsteads.

In the late La Tène period, large fortified settlements arose, the **oppida**. Craftsmen and traders lived there, and **coins** were struck. In Switzerland there were oppida, for example, on the Engehalbinsel in Bern. In 58 BC, Julius Caesar defeated the Helvetii. After that the area came gradually under Roman rule.

gewusst: The Galatians are the same people to whom the Letter to the Galatians in the Bible was later addressed.
The statue from the Glauberg is one of the few almost completely preserved stone figures of the Celts.

teile.einleitung: The Lion Man is a small figure made of mammoth ivory with a lion's head and a human body. It is about 40,000 years old and is among the oldest works of art of humankind. It was found on the Swabian Jura in southern Germany.
wichtigste: The figure has a lion's head and an upright human body.
It is carved from mammoth ivory.
It was found in the Hohlenstein-Stadel cave in the Lone Valley.
The first fragments were excavated in 1939.
The figure is about 31 centimetres tall and about 40,000 years old.
Today the original stands in the Ulm Museum.

abschnitte.text: The figure combines **animal and human**. It has the head of a big cat, probably a cave lion, and an upright **human body**. Such a being does not exist in nature. So the figure shows that people at that time could already imagine things that do not exist. What it meant exactly, nobody knows.

The Lion Man was carved from the **tusk of a mammoth**. With stone tools this was very laborious work. The figure is **31.1 centimetres** tall. For an ivory figure of the Ice Age, that is very large. It is between about 35,000 and 41,000 years old.

abschnitte.titel: A find shortly before the war
abschnitte.text: The figure lay in the **Hohlenstein-Stadel** cave in the **Lone Valley** in Baden-Württemberg. In August **1939**, Otto Völzing found the first pieces. The excavation was led by **Robert Wetzel**. Soon afterwards the Second World War began, and the finds lay unnoticed in boxes for a long time.

The figure had been broken into **hundreds of fragments**. Only in 1969 did **Joachim Hahn** put together about 200 of the over 260 splinters. In doing so he recognised that the figure represents a hybrid creature. Later further pieces were found, and the figure was reassembled several times. Today it is much more complete than at the start.

Robert Wetzel gave his finds to the city of **Ulm**. That is why the original now stands in the **Ulm Museum**. Since **2017**, six caves of the Swabian Jura have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. The title is “Caves and Ice Age Art in the Swabian Jura”. In these caves, flutes and many further small figures were also found.

gewusst: The Lion Man is one of the oldest known figures showing an imaginary creature.
Researchers have tried out how long the carving takes: probably hundreds of hours of work.

teile.einleitung: A burial mound is a grave over which a hill of earth and stones was heaped. In Switzerland, many such graves from the Bronze Age and the Iron Age are found, often in forests.
wichtigste: A burial mound is a grave under a mound of earth.
From the outside it looks like a round hill.
The dead were given grave goods, such as jewellery, weapons or vessels.
Rich and important people received especially large burial mounds.
In Switzerland, many burial mounds are preserved in forests.
In 1851, a Greek bronze vessel was found at Grächwil in the canton of Bern.

abschnitte.text: For a **burial mound**, the dead person was laid in a pit or a chamber. Over it, earth and stones were heaped. This produced a round **hill**. Today trees grow on many burial mounds. To walkers they often look like perfectly ordinary small hills in the forest.

abschnitte.titel: Why in the forest in particular?
abschnitte.text: On fields, the **plough** levelled the hills over many centuries. In the forest there was no ploughing. That is why the burial mounds there can often still be seen well. In Switzerland there are many such graves, for example on the Plateau. They are protected, and you may not dig there yourself.

The dead were given things to take into the grave: **jewellery**, weapons, tools or **vessels**. These things are called **grave goods**. Rich and important people received especially large mounds and many grave goods. People then speak of **princely graves**. At **Grächwil** in the canton of Bern, a large bronze water jug was found in a burial mound in 1851. It came from Greece and shows that there was trade as far as the Mediterranean.

**Archaeologists** dig carefully and examine the finds closely. The people of that time could not write yet. So the grave goods tell us a lot about their everyday life. We learn what jewellery they wore, what tools they used and with whom they traded.

gewusst: The jug of Grächwil was made in Greece about 2,500 years ago and came as far as the area around Bern.
Some burial mounds in the forest are more than 3,000 years old.

teile.einleitung: Agriculture means growing plants in fields and keeping animals in order to obtain food. In the New Stone Age, people began doing this and gradually stopped only hunting and gathering. This invention changed people's lives like hardly any other.
wichtigste: The transition from hunting and gathering to arable farming and livestock breeding is called the Neolithic Revolution.
Agriculture began over 11,000 years ago in the Near East.
The first farmers grew emmer, einkorn and barley.
In the Near East they also planted peas and lentils.
With slash-and-burn, they turned forest into farmland.
Harvesting was done with sickles with flint blades.
The farmers of the New Stone Age in Europe did not yet know the potato.

abschnitte.text: The first farmers lived in the **Fertile Crescent**, an area in the Near East from Israel across Syria to Iraq. There arable farming began around 9500 BC. The great change from hunting and gathering to farming is called the **Neolithic Revolution**. From there the new way of life spread slowly and reached central Europe and Switzerland around 5500 BC.

The first farmers grew old kinds of cereal, namely **emmer**, einkorn and barley. Pulses such as peas and lentils were added. From **flax**, also called linseed, they obtained fibres for cloth and oil from the seeds. Plants such as potatoes or maize only came much later from America to Europe.

Besides arable farming, people kept animals, which is called **livestock breeding**. Goats and sheep were among the first domestic animals, and later cattle and pigs were added. The animals provided meat, pelts and leather, and later milk and wool too. The dog had become a companion of humans much earlier, among the hunter-gatherers.

Because central Europe at that time was almost entirely covered in forest, the farmers first had to make room. In **slash-and-burn**, they felled trees and burned down the forest, and the ash fertilised the soil. They loosened the soil with digging sticks and hoes, later with a simple wooden plough, the **ard**. Harvesting was done with sickles into which sharp blades of flint were set.

To make flour, the farmers ground the grains on a flat **grindstone** with a smaller rubbing stone. From this they baked simple flatbreads or cooked porridge. They stored the supplies in vessels of fired clay, **pottery**. In this way they had enough to eat in winter too.

Thanks to agriculture, there was more food, and the number of people grew strongly. People became **settled** and built permanent villages. Because not everyone any longer had to provide food, new trades arose, such as potter or craftsman. Almost everything we eat today comes from plants and animals that farmers have bred over many thousands of years.

begriffe.erklaerung: The transition from hunting and gathering to arable farming and livestock breeding in the New Stone Age.
Forest is felled and burned in order to make farmland from it.
A very old kind of wheat that the first farmers already grew.
A flat stone on which grains of cereal were ground to flour with a second stone.
The keeping and breeding of animals such as goats, sheep and cattle.

gewusst: Our wheat today descends from wild grasses that grew in the Near East.
Many adults of the New Stone Age could not digest milk well, and that changed only over thousands of years.
In the pile-dwelling settlements of Switzerland, charred grains of cereal and even remains of bread from the New Stone Age have been preserved.

teile.einleitung: Bone flutes are among the oldest musical instruments in the world. People of the Ice Age carved them about 40,000 years ago from hollow bird bones. The best-known finds come from caves of the Swabian Jura in southern Germany.
wichtigste: Bone flutes were made mainly from hollow bird bones.
The oldest are about 40,000 years old.
They come from caves of the Swabian Jura in Germany.
The flute from the Hohle Fels is made from the wing bone of a griffon vulture.
A flute from the Geissenklösterle is made from a swan bone.
A flute is a wind instrument.

abschnitte.text: Bird bones are **hollow** inside and so light. That is why they are well suited to flutes. People cut the bone to size and drilled **finger holes** into it. If you cover the holes with your fingers or open them, higher or lower notes are produced. Because you blow air into it, the flute is a **wind instrument**.

abschnitte.titel: The flute from the Hohle Fels
abschnitte.text: In the **Hohle Fels** cave, a flute made from the wing bone of a **griffon vulture** was found. A griffon vulture is a large bird of prey with very long wings. The flute is almost completely preserved. It is regarded as one of the oldest known musical instruments of humankind.

In the **Geissenklösterle** cave too, flutes came to light. One of them is made from the bone of a **whooper swan**. Other flutes are made of **mammoth ivory**. That was much harder: you had to split a piece of tusk lengthways, hollow it out and join it together again so that it was airtight.

abschnitte.titel: Music of the first modern humans
abschnitte.text: The flutes are about **35,000 to 43,000 years** old. They date from the time when modern humans came to Europe. In the same caves, small figures made of ivory were also found. The finds show that art and music were already part of life then. Since 2017, the caves of the Swabian Jura have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: Researchers have played replicas of the flutes: you can blow real melodies on them.
In the same area, the Lion Man, a famous ivory figure, was also found.

teile.einleitung: **Bronze** is a mixture of copper and tin. It was the first metal that people used to make hard tools and weapons in large quantities. A whole era is named after it, the **Bronze Age**.
wichtigste: A mixture of metals is called an alloy.
Classic tin bronze consists of about 90 per cent copper and 10 per cent tin.
Bronze is harder than pure copper.
In Switzerland, the Bronze Age began about 4200 years ago.
The Bronze Age was followed by the Iron Age.
Tin was rare and was brought from far away.
In competitions, bronze is awarded for third place.

abschnitte.text: When you melt different metals together, you get an **alloy**. **Bronze** is one of the oldest alloys. It consists of about nine parts **copper** to one part **tin**, so roughly **90 per cent copper and 10 per cent tin**. The tin makes the metal **harder**. More tin makes bronze harder still, but also more brittle.

Because bronze is harder than copper, tools made from it were much better. People made **axes**, knives, **swords**, pins and **bracelets**. To do this, the liquid bronze was poured into **moulds** made of stone or clay. Bronze shines **golden brown**, a little paler than pure copper. Over time, a greenish layer, the **patina**, often forms on the surface.

**Tin** was found in only a few places in Europe. That is why it was very **valuable**. Traders brought it over long distances. Copper too often came from other regions, for example from the Alps. In this way, wide **trade routes** arose across Europe in the Bronze Age.

In Switzerland, the **Bronze Age** began about **4200 years ago** and lasted until about 800 BC. During this time, many people lived in villages on the shores of the lakes. In these **lakeside settlements**, many objects made of bronze have been found. Later, people learned to make **iron**. That is why the Bronze Age was followed by the **Iron Age**.

Bronze is still used today, for example for **bells**, statues and medals. In sports competitions, you get **gold** for first place and **silver** for second. The **bronze medal** is for **third place**. Many monuments in Swiss towns and cities are cast in bronze.

gewusst: Church bells are usually made of a bronze with an especially large amount of tin, so that they sound beautiful.
Bronze is so durable that objects from the Bronze Age are still preserved after more than 3000 years.

teile.einleitung: The Magdalenian is a culture of the late Old Stone Age at the end of the last Ice Age. Its people hunted mainly reindeer and wild horses. They left behind harpoons, decorated antler batons and famous works of art.
wichtigste: The Magdalenian is named after the find site La Madeleine in France.
Before the Magdalenian came the Solutrean, after it the Azilian.
The main prey were reindeer and wild horses.
Typical are harpoons with barbs made of reindeer antler.
Batons with a hole are decorated pieces of antler with a large hole.
In Switzerland there are important find sites on Lake Neuchâtel and near Schaffhausen.

abschnitte.text: The **Magdalenian** is named after the rock shelter La Madeleine in the Dordogne in France. It arose after the **Solutrean** in **south-western France**.
