After that it spread to Spain and central Europe. At the end of the Ice Age, it was replaced in south-western France by the **Azilian**, which is named after Mas d'Azil in the Pyrenees. In Germany, with the warming of the Allerød, the **Federmesser groups** followed.

The hunters of the Magdalenian lived mainly on **reindeer** and **wild horses**. They followed the migrations of the herds and lay in wait for them at narrow points. That is why people also speak of the **Reindeer Age**. From reindeer antler they made **harpoons** with barbs on one or both sides. These were also suited to fishing.

Typical of the Magdalenian are **batons with a hole**. These are often decorated pieces of antler with a large hole. Their purpose is not entirely clear. Perhaps they were used for straightening **spear shafts**. A famous baton with a hole comes from the Kesslerloch near Thayngen.

Many works of art come from the Magdalenian. People engraved animals into bone, antler and stone. At **Gönnersdorf** on the Middle Rhine, slate slabs with greatly simplified **female figures** were found. This type of figure is named after the place. Many well-known cave paintings in France and Spain also belong to this period.

On **Lake Neuchâtel** lie the find sites **Monruz** and **Hauterive-Champréveyres**. They were excavated during the building of the A5 motorway. They are among the most important camp sites of this period in Switzerland. Also well known are the **Kesslerloch** and the Schweizersbild in the canton of Schaffhausen. There, tools, jewellery and works of art of the reindeer hunters were found.

gewusst: The engraved reindeer from the Kesslerloch is a masterpiece of the Magdalenian.
Harpoons with barbs stay stuck in the prey and do not come loose easily.

teile.einleitung: The wheel is one of the most important inventions of humankind. It was invented about 5,500 years ago. With wheel and wagon, heavy loads could be transported much more easily.
wichtigste: The wheel was invented about 5,500 years ago.
The first wheels were round discs of wood.
One of the oldest wheels was found in the Ljubljana Marsh in Slovenia.
A wheel needs an axle to turn on the wagon.
The first wagons were pulled by oxen.
Later, lighter spoked wheels appeared.

abschnitte.text: Before there was the wheel, it was very laborious to move heavy things. Loads were pulled on **sledges** or round tree trunks were laid underneath as **rollers**. The rollers had to be carried again and again from the back to the front. With the wheel, everything became easier. With a wagon, you could transport much more, for example wood, stones or the harvest.

The oldest wheels and wagons date from the time around **3500 BC**, so about 5,500 years ago. The first wheels were **disc wheels**. They were put together from wooden boards. In the **Ljubljana Marsh** in Slovenia, a wooden wheel was found that is over 5,000 years old. In the damp marsh, wood has been well preserved. In pile-dwelling settlements on **Lake Zurich** too, wooden wheels from the New Stone Age were found.

For a wheel to turn on a wagon, an **axle** is needed. This is a rod on which the wheels sit. Either the wheels turn around the axle, or the axle turns with them. The first wagons were heavy. Strong **oxen** pulled them. Horses were only harnessed to wagons later.

Later the **spoked wheels** appeared. They have rods, the spokes, instead of a full disc. That is why they are lighter and the wagon gets faster. The wheel was not only used for driving. **Potters** used a turning disc, the **potter's wheel**. On it the clay turns, and you can shape round vessels quickly and evenly.

gewusst: With the wheel from the Ljubljana Marsh there was also an axle made of wood.
In America the wheel was known as a toy, but for a long time was not used for wagons.

teile.einleitung: The Kesslerloch is a small cave near Thayngen in the canton of Schaffhausen. At the end of the last Ice Age, reindeer hunters sought shelter here. Their traces make the cave one of the most important find sites in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Kesslerloch lies near Thayngen in the canton of Schaffhausen.
Reindeer hunters of the Magdalenian culture used the cave about 15,000 to 11,000 years ago.
The secondary-school teacher Konrad Merk was the first to start an excavation in 1873.
In 1874, Albert Heim found a piece of antler with an engraved reindeer.
Bones of over 50 animal species were found, including mammoth and reindeer.
A piece of jaw is among the oldest evidence of domestic dogs in central Europe.
The cave has been protected since 1902.

abschnitte.text: The Kesslerloch is a short through-cave in a limestone rock. It takes its name from travelling **tinkers**, whom people used to call Kessler. They repaired pots and cooking utensils here. In December 1873, the secondary-school teacher **Konrad Merk** began an excavation. He published his results in 1875.

About 15,000 years ago, it was much colder in the area than today. People of the **Magdalenian culture** hunted mainly reindeer and wild horses. The cave served them as a shelter. Bones of **53 animal species** were found, for example of mammoth, reindeer, ibex and chamois. A piece of upper jaw of a **dog** is about 14,000 to 15,000 years old. It shows that dogs already lived with people then.

On 4 January 1874, **Albert Heim**, together with Jakob Messikommer, discovered a piece of antler with an engraved reindeer. Heim later became a well-known Alpine geologist. The picture is regarded as one of the most beautiful works of art of the Ice Age. Also famous is a decorated **baton with a hole**, an antler rod with a hole. Its original is in the Rosgarten Museum in **Konstanz**, and copies and further finds can be seen in Schaffhausen and Zurich.

Not all the finds were genuine. Two engraved drawings with a **fox** and a **bear** were made afterwards in 1875. A researcher noticed that they had been copied from a children's book. The forgery shows how carefully finds have to be checked. The genuine works of art from the cave did not lose any value because of it, however.

The reindeer hunters wore **pendants** made of shells, snail shells, animal teeth and jet. They did not yet know metal. Some shells came from far away, which points to trade or long journeys. In 1902, the cave, together with the forest and meadows around it, was placed under **state protection**. Today you can visit it.

gewusst: The engraved reindeer from the Kesslerloch is often called the “Grazing Reindeer”.
The dog jaw from the Kesslerloch is among the oldest dog finds in central Europe.

teile.einleitung: Pottery is fired clay. When people became settled in the New Stone Age, they began to make pots from clay. In them they stored supplies and cooked their food.
wichtigste: Pottery is fired clay.
Sand or small stones were mixed into the clay so that the pot would not crack.
A freshly shaped pot had to dry well before firing.
Many pots of the New Stone Age are brown to black.
Some pots were decorated with incised lines.
Fired clay hardly decays, so many shards are found.

abschnitte.text: Vessels and figures made of **fired clay** are called **pottery**. Plates and cups today are often made of pottery too. In the **New Stone Age**, people became settled and began to grow cereals. Now they needed vessels for their supplies. Pots made of clay were ideal for this.

Pure clay shrinks a great deal when drying and firing. So **sand** or small stones were mixed in so that the pot would not crack. Then **coils of clay** were rolled and laid on top of one another. With **wet fingers** or a wet stone, the wall was smoothed. After that the pot had to **dry** well, because a wet pot would burst in the fire.

The pots were fired in an **open fire**. The clay mostly turned brown, grey or black. Coloured **glazes** were not yet known. Into the soft clay, people incised or pressed **patterns**, for example lines. After firing they stayed visible. Some pots had small **lugs**. Through them a cord was threaded to carry or hang the pot.

In a pot with a lid, **mice** could not get at the grain, and damp did not get in so easily. Wood and cloth rot in the ground, but **fired clay** survives for thousands of years. That is why archaeologists find very many **shards**. Because every period had its own shapes and patterns, they can use them to date finds. In the pile dwellings of Switzerland too, many clay vessels were found.

gewusst: Some cultures of the Stone Age are named after their pots, for example the Linear Pottery culture.
Pottery shards survive in the ground much longer than wood or cloth.

teile.einleitung: The Nebra Sky Disc is a bronze disc with golden images of the sun, moon and stars. It comes from the Bronze Age and is regarded as one of the oldest concrete depictions of the sky.
wichtigste: The disc has a diameter of about 32 centimetres and weighs around 2 kilograms.
It is made of bronze with overlays of gold sheet.
Looters found it in 1999 with a metal detector on the Mittelberg near Nebra.
In 2002, the police recovered the disc in Basel.
Seven gold dots are usually interpreted as the star cluster of the Pleiades.
Since 2013, it has been part of the UNESCO Memory of the World.

abschnitte.text: The disc is cast and hammered from **bronze**. On it are laid the sun or full moon, a crescent moon and stars made of **gold sheet**. A group of seven dots close together is interpreted by many researchers as the **Pleiades**, a star cluster. It was important for the calendar of farmers. Later, two golden **edge arcs** were added. They each span about 82 degrees and, according to the usual interpretation, show where the sun rises and sets on the horizon over the course of the year.

The sky disc has a diameter of about **32 centimetres**, about as big as a vinyl record. It weighs around **2,050 grams**. In the middle it is about 4.5 millimetres thick and becomes thinner towards the edge. It is also slightly curved.

In 1999, two **looters** with a metal detector came across the disc on the **Mittelberg** near Wangen in Saxony-Anhalt. It lay there together with swords, axes and arm spirals. The looters damaged the find and sold it on illegally. In 2002, dealers in stolen goods wanted to sell the disc in a hotel in **Basel**. An archaeologist posed as a buyer, and the Swiss police made the arrest.

Since it was recovered, the disc has belonged to the state of **Saxony-Anhalt**. It is displayed in the **State Museum of Prehistory** in Halle an der Saale and is its best-known piece. In 2013, UNESCO added it to the **Memory of the World** register. This register collects especially important documents of humankind.

gewusst: The famous sky disc was recovered by the police in a hotel in Basel.
Over time, the disc was altered several times, for example the edge arcs were only added later.

teile.einleitung: La Tène is a famous find site at the end of Lake Neuchâtel. From 1857, thousands of objects of the Celts were found here, mainly of iron. A whole period is named after this place: the La Tène period.
wichtigste: The find site La Tène lies at the eastern end of Lake Neuchâtel.
In 1857, a fisherman there pulled many old iron objects out of the water.
Most of the finds are weapons and tools made of iron.
In all, about 2,500 objects came to light.
The remains of two wooden bridges were also found.
The La Tène period of the Celts is named after this place.
Many finds are now in the Laténium museum in Hauterive.

abschnitte.text: In **1857**, the fisherman **Hans Kopp** searched in the shallow water at the end of Lake Neuchâtel. He did so on behalf of Colonel **Friedrich Schwab**, a collector of antiquities. In a short time, Kopp found about 40 old weapons. This began the exploration of the find site. The name La Tène means roughly **shallows**, that is, a place with shallow water.

Most of the finds are made of **iron**. The Celts could already work iron very well. Especially often, **swords** and **lance points** were found, along with shields, tools, jewellery and coins. In all, about **2,500 objects** came to light. Many sword scabbards are artfully decorated.

Later, many more finds were discovered. The reason for this was the **Jura water correction**. In it, the lake level was lowered by more than 2 metres. So a large part of the find site suddenly lay dry. The remains of **two wooden bridges** were found, which led across an old arm of the Thielle.

The Neuchâtel scholar **Édouard Desor** recognised early how important the find site was. Others at first thought it of little significance. Today the later Iron Age of the Celts is called the **La Tène period** after this place. It began about 2,500 years ago. Many finds can be seen in the **Laténium**, a large archaeology museum in Hauterive on the lakeshore.

gewusst: A small place in Switzerland gave its name to a whole period in Europe.
Why so many weapons lay in the water is still not clearly settled.

teile.einleitung: In the Ice Age, people in eastern Europe built huts from mammoth bones. In the treeless steppe there was hardly any wood, but many bones. The best-known huts were found in Ukraine.
wichtigste: Mammoth bone huts had walls of many large mammoth bones.
In the cold steppe hardly any trees grew, so wood was lacking.
Pelts were laid over the bone framework.
Well-known find sites such as Mezhyrich lie in Ukraine.
The huts are about 15,000 years old.
Inside burned a hearth, often with bones as fuel.

abschnitte.text: In the Ice Age, eastern Europe was a cold **steppe**. Only few trees grew there. Mammoth bones, by contrast, were plentiful. So people built their huts from **mammoth bones**. The huts were round. Large bones, skulls and tusks together formed a stable framework.

Over the bone framework, **pelts** were laid. This made the huts tight against **wind and cold**. Inside burned a **hearth** that gave warmth and light. Because wood was lacking, **bones** were burned too. Bones contain fat and so can burn.

Many mammoth bone huts were found in **Ukraine**. A well-known find site is **Mezhyrich**. In some huts, the lower jaws of mammoths were stacked so that a regular pattern arose. The huts date from the last Ice Age, about **15,000 years ago**. At that time many mammoths lived there.

abschnitte.titel: Where did the bones come from?
abschnitte.text: For a hut, very many bones were needed. Not all mammoths were hunted. People also **collected** bones of animals that were already dead. Hunting a mammoth was dangerous and only succeeded in a group. The meat, the pelt and the bones of a killed animal were used completely.

gewusst: For a single mammoth bone hut, the bones of many mammoths were needed.
Mammoths were well adapted to the cold, they had a dense coat and small ears.

teile.einleitung: To settle down means no longer to wander about, but to live permanently in one place. People took this step in the New Stone Age, when they became farmers. This began a completely new way of life, from which villages, towns and states later arose.
wichtigste: “Settled” means living permanently in one place.
People settled down in the New Stone Age.
People first began farming in the Near East.
The first farmers had to stay near their fields to look after them.
Settled people built permanent houses instead of tents.
They could store supplies better than nomads.
With settling down, the number of people grew.

abschnitte.text: For tens of thousands of years, people lived as **hunters and gatherers**. They followed the animals and the ripe fruits and lived in tents, huts or caves. Such wandering people are called **nomads**. When they began to lay out fields, they had to stay near their fields to sow, weed and harvest.

People first settled down in the **Near East**, in the so-called Fertile Crescent. There, around 9500 BC, the first villages with farming and livestock rearing arose. Well-known early settlements are **Jericho** and Çatalhöyük in present-day Turkey, where around 7000 BC thousands of people lived close together. In central Europe and Switzerland, people settled down around 5500 BC.

Settled people built **permanent houses** instead of tents. In central Europe these were typically long houses made of wood and clay, which could be over 30 metres long. Large families lived in them, sometimes together with their animals. In Switzerland, pile-dwelling villages later arose on the shores of lakes too.

Whoever stays in one place can store **supplies** in pits and clay vessels. In this way people had enough to eat in winter too. At the same time, property became more important: fields, houses, animals and tools belonged to particular families. Later this also gave rise to quarrels over land and to differences between rich and poor.

Because farming and **livestock rearing** provided more food, more children could be fed, and the number of people grew. Not everyone had to provide food any more, so craftspeople such as potters and weavers appeared. But the new life also had drawbacks: field work was hard, and in the crowded villages diseases spread more easily. Even so, the settled way of life prevailed almost everywhere.

**Settling down** is regarded as one of the most important turning points in human history. In time, villages became towns, and writing, laws and states arose. Almost all people on Earth live settled lives today. Only a few groups, such as some herding peoples in deserts and steppes, still wander as nomads with their herds.

begriffe.erklaerung: Living permanently in one place.
A person who wanders about without a fixed home.
Growing plants in fields.
Keeping and breeding animals.
An area in the Near East where people first became farmers.

gewusst: The stone site of Göbekli Tepe in Turkey is over 11,000 years old and was built by people who were only just settling down.
In Çatalhöyük the houses had no doors at the side: people climbed in through an opening in the roof.
The house cat probably joined the first farmers because mice lived in their grain stores.

teile.einleitung: **Archaeopteryx** is one of the most famous fossils in the world. The animal had feathers like a bird, but also teeth and claws like a small dinosaur. That is why it is called the **first bird**.
wichtigste: In German, Archaeopteryx has the nickname “Urvogel”, meaning first bird.
It is regarded as one of the oldest known birds.
It had feathers, but also pointed teeth and claws on its wings.
Its tail was long and had bones in it.
It was about the size of a raven.
All the finds come from the platy limestone near Solnhofen in Bavaria.

abschnitte.text: In the stone slabs with Archaeopteryx you can clearly see **impressions of feathers**. Its wings had feathers too, as in a bird. Archaeopteryx was about the size of a **raven**, so a rather small animal. It lived about 150 million years ago in the **Jurassic**. Whether it could fly well is still debated by researchers today.

Birds today have no teeth. Archaeopteryx, however, still had small **pointed teeth**. On each wing it had three fingers with **claws**, which it could perhaps use to hold on. Its **tail** was long and had many vertebrae, with feathers growing on both sides. In birds today, the bony tail is very short.

Archaeopteryx shows features of **dinosaurs and birds** at the same time. That is why it is seen as a **link** between these groups of animals. It was discovered shortly after Charles Darwin's famous book on the origin of species. Many saw it as proof that animals change over time. Today we know that birds descend from small meat-eating dinosaurs.

All finds of Archaeopteryx come from **Bavaria** in Germany. They lay in the fine **platy limestone** of the area around **Solnhofen**. This **limestone** formed from fine mud in shallow lagoons. Because the mud was so fine, even the feathers remained clearly visible. Today, about a dozen skeletons are known. One of the most famous is in the Natural History Museum in Berlin.

gewusst: The first piece of Archaeopteryx to be found, in 1861, was a single feather.
The name Archaeopteryx means roughly “ancient wing”.

teile.einleitung: The **Acheulean** is a very old culture of the Old Stone Age. Its best-known tool is the **hand axe**. It lasted for a huge stretch of time in Africa, Europe and Asia.
wichtigste: The Acheulean is named after the site of Saint-Acheul near Amiens in France.
It stretches from almost 2 million to about 150,000 years ago.
This makes it part of the Lower Palaeolithic, the oldest part of the Old Stone Age.
Some of the oldest finds are hand axes from Kokiselei on Lake Turkana in Kenya.
Typical tools are hand axes and, in Africa, also cleavers with a straight cutting edge.
Jacques Boucher de Perthes recognised early on that hand axes were made by humans.

abschnitte.text: A **hand axe** is a stone that has been worked on both sides. It is usually almond-shaped or pointed and has sharp edges. You could cut, scrape or chop with it. Making one took skill and planning. Besides the hand axe, the **cleaver** is typical in Africa. Instead of a point, it has a broad, straight cutting edge.

The Acheulean began almost **2 million years ago** and ended about **150,000 years ago**. This makes it part of the **Lower Palaeolithic**, the oldest part of the Old Stone Age. One of the oldest sites is **Kokiselei** on the western shore of **Lake Turkana** in Kenya. There, early hand axes about 1.76 million years old were found. The tools were made by early forms of human, for example **Homo erectus**.

The culture is named after **Saint-Acheul**, a suburb of **Amiens** on the Somme in France. Many hand axes were found early on in the old river gravels there. From 1838, the researcher **Jacques Boucher de Perthes** found hand axes together with bones of extinct animals. He thought they were tools of very ancient humans, but was rejected for a long time. Only confirmation by the geologist **Joseph Prestwich** brought him recognition.

Hand axes of the Acheulean are found in **Africa**, the **Middle East**, parts of **Asia** and **Europe**. Early humans passed their knowledge on over many generations. Over time, the hand axes became finer and more regular. In Switzerland such finds are very rare. One well-known hand axe was found in **Pratteln** in the canton of Basel-Landschaft.

gewusst: The Acheulean lasted far longer than the whole time from the first farmers until today.
Some hand axes are so beautifully symmetrical that researchers marvel at their makers' sense of shape.

teile.einleitung: The **Schöningen spears** are very old hunting weapons made of wood. They were found at Schöningen in Lower Saxony in a lignite open-cast mine. They are among the oldest completely preserved hunting weapons in the world.
wichtigste: The spears were found at Schöningen in Lower Saxony.
The excavations were led by Hartmut Thieme.
Most of the spears are made of spruce wood.
According to a new dating from 2025, they are about 200,000 years old.
They therefore probably come from early Neanderthals.
Next to the spears lay many bones of wild horses.
Damp, oxygen-poor lake deposits protected the wood.

abschnitte.titel: A find in the open-cast mine
abschnitte.text: At Schöningen, lignite is mined. Before the diggers arrived, archaeologists examined the ground. Under the leadership of **Hartmut Thieme**, they found several wooden spears in the 1990s. That was a sensation, because wood this old almost never survives.

Most of the spears are carved from **spruce wood**. They are about two metres long. The point lies in the hardest part of the trunk, and the centre of gravity is at the front, much like in a modern javelin. So the makers knew exactly how to build a good weapon.

For a long time, their age was estimated at around 300,000 years. A new dating published in **2025** gave an age of about **200,000 years**. This means the spears probably come from **early Neanderthals**. They lay in **damp, oxygen-poor lake deposits**. Without oxygen, fungi and bacteria can hardly break down the wood.

Together with the spears, bones of many **wild horses** were found. Cut marks can be seen on the bones. The finds **prove** that people at that time hunted large game in a **targeted and planned** way. For this they had to agree on a plan and work together as a group. Today the spears are on display in the research museum at Schöningen.

gewusst: Before the find, many researchers thought such early humans mainly ate carrion and hardly hunted themselves.
Wood only survives this long under very special conditions, which is why the spears are unique worldwide.

teile.einleitung: Çatalhöyük is one of the oldest large settlements in the world. It lies in central Anatolia in present-day Turkey and existed from about 7400 to 6000 BC.
wichtigste: Çatalhöyük lies on the Konya plain in central Anatolia.
The houses were built of sun-dried mud bricks.
The dead were often buried under the floors of the houses.
In many rooms, bulls' horns hung on the walls.
James Mellaart dug there from 1961, Ian Hodder from 1993.
Since 2012, Çatalhöyük has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: The name **Çatalhöyük** means roughly **fork mound**: “çatal” means fork, “höyük” means mound. The site consists of an east mound and a west mound. The houses were built of **mud bricks** and stood close together. There were hardly any streets. People probably entered the houses through the **roof** by a ladder.

The inside walls were plastered with clay and often **painted**. In many rooms, **bulls' horns** set in clay were found. The bull was evidently an important symbol. The inhabitants often buried their dead **under the floor** of their houses. So the living lived directly above their ancestors.

An important raw material was **obsidian**, a black **volcanic glass** from central Anatolia. From it people made very sharp blades and even **mirrors**. A wall painting showing houses and a mountain with two peaks is famous. Many interpret it as the volcano **Hasan Dağı**, and so as one of the oldest depictions of a landscape.

A well-known clay figure shows a **seated woman** resting her hands on **two big cats**, probably leopards. Nobody knows for sure who she represents. The figure is now in a museum in **Ankara**. It is one of the best-known works of art of the New Stone Age.

The British archaeologist **James Mellaart** was the first to dig at Çatalhöyük, from **1961 to 1965**. From **1993**, **Ian Hodder** led new, very careful excavations. In **2012**, UNESCO added the settlement to the **World Heritage** list. It is regarded as an especially well-preserved early large settlement.

gewusst: At times, several thousand people lived in Çatalhöyük, a great many for the New Stone Age.
New houses were often built exactly on the remains of old ones, so the mounds grew higher.

teile.einleitung: With the grindstone, the farmers of the New Stone Age made flour from grains of cereal. It was hard work that took a lot of time every day. From the flour came porridge and flat breads.
wichtigste: A grindstone was made of hard rock, for example granite or sandstone.
A small stone was rubbed back and forth on a large, flat stone.
The small upper stone is called the rubber.
Fine grains of stone in the flour wore down people's teeth.
The first breads were flat loaves.
They were baked on hot stones or in the embers.

abschnitte.text: A grindstone consists of two parts. The lower, large stone lies firmly on the ground. On it the **grains** were laid. The upper, smaller stone is called the **rubber** (Läufer). With it, the grains were rubbed back and forth until **flour** was produced. Because the stone had to withstand a lot, **hard rock** such as granite or sandstone was used.

When grinding, tiny pieces came off the stone. These fine **grains of stone** got into the flour. When eating, they wore down the **teeth**. That is why the teeth of many people from this time are heavily worn. Researchers can recognise this on skeletons.

For a dough you need at least **flour and water**. From it, flat **loaves** were shaped. Because they were thin, they cooked quickly. They were baked on **hot stones** or directly in the embers. The farmers of the New Stone Age did not yet know metal pans. In pile-dwelling settlements on Swiss lakes, even charred remains of bread were found.

Besides bread, the farmers often ate **porridge**. For this, grains or coarse flour were cooked with water or milk. A porridge filled you up and was easy to make. The crops grown included old kinds of wheat such as **emmer** and **einkorn**, as well as barley.

Much later, in the time of the Celts, the **rotary quern** spread. In it, a round upper stone is turned on a lower one. This was much faster than rubbing. Later still, water and wind drove large mills. The principle with two stones stayed the same for a long time, however.

gewusst: Rubbing flour took so long that probably several hours were needed for it every day.
The word rubber for the upper stone is also used for later mills.

teile.einleitung: The first humans lived millions of years ago in Africa. They could walk upright on two legs, made tools from stone and learned to use fire. They lived as hunters and gatherers and followed the animals and the food.
wichtigste: The first humans and their ancestors lived in Africa.
They could walk upright on two legs better than apes.
The famous skeleton “Lucy” comes from Ethiopia.
They made their tools from stone, which is why this time is called the Stone Age.
The hand axe and tools made of flint were especially important.
People learned to use fire for warmth and cooking.
They hunted and gathered and lived in caves and tents.

abschnitte.text: The ancestors of humans lived in **Africa**, mainly in the east and south of the continent. The oldest bones of early human ancestors were found there. Very well known is **Lucy**, the skeleton of a female early human ancestor from Ethiopia. She lived about 3.2 million years ago and was only about a metre tall.

Early humans could walk **upright** on two legs better than apes. This left their hands free to carry things and use tools. They could also look over tall grass. Over long distances, upright walking also saved energy.

The first humans made their tools from **stone**. That is why the time is called the Stone Age. A large tool held in one hand is the **hand axe**. **Flint** was especially popular, because it gets very sharp edges when struck.

A huge innovation was **fire**. Early humans used it to keep warm and cook food. It gave light at night and kept wild animals away. People sat together at the fire, which strengthened life together in the group.

The first humans got their food by hunting and gathering. They looked for berries, nuts, roots and fruit and hunted animals. Because they followed the animals and the food, they often moved on. They lived in **caves** and tents and made their clothes from **animal skins**.

In the course of time, different kinds of humans left Africa. First **Homo erectus** travelled as far as Asia. Much later, about 60,000 years ago, modern humans, Homo sapiens, spread across the whole world. It came to Europe about 45,000 years ago.

begriffe.erklaerung: An early ancestor of humans that already walked upright.
A large stone tool that was held in one hand.
A hard stone that forms sharp edges when struck.
People who live from hunting and gathered plants.

gewusst: Lucy got her name from a Beatles song that the researchers heard in the camp.
The oldest known stone tools are over three million years old and so older than the genus Homo.
All people alive today have common ancestors in Africa.

teile.einleitung: Our Solar System formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a rotating cloud of gas and dust. In its middle the Sun formed, and in the disc around it the planets, moons, asteroids and comets grew. Researchers can follow this story today using telescopes, space probes and meteorites.
wichtigste: The Solar System formed about 4.6 billion years ago.
It formed from a rotating cloud of gas and dust.
The Sun contains about 99.8 per cent of the total mass of the Solar System.
The planets grew together from planetesimals in a protoplanetary disc.
The inner planets are rocky planets, because near the Sun it was too hot for ice and much gas.
In the 18th century, Immanuel Kant and Pierre-Simon Laplace developed the idea of formation from a nebula.
Meteorites are important because many have stayed almost unchanged since the formation.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning there was a huge, cold **cloud of gas and dust**, made up mainly of hydrogen and helium. Part of it began to collapse under its own gravity. As it did so, the cloud spun faster and faster, like an ice skater drawing in her arms. The spinning flattened it into a disc.

Almost all the material, about 99.8 per cent of the mass, gathered in the middle of the disc. There it became so dense and hot that **nuclear fusion** set in. In this, hydrogen fuses into helium, and a huge amount of energy is released. This is how the **Sun** began to shine, and it still does so today.

In the **protoplanetary disc** around the young Sun, grains of dust stuck together. This produced lumps of rock kilometres across, the **planetesimals**. They collided and grew into ever larger bodies. Near the Sun it was too hot for ice, so the rocky planets Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars formed there, and further out the giant planets Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Not all the material became planets. Between Mars and Jupiter orbits the **asteroid belt** with countless lumps of rock. Beyond Neptune lies the **Kuiper belt** with many icy small bodies such as Pluto. Comets consist mainly of ice, dust and rock and come from these distant regions.

As early as the 18th century, **Immanuel Kant** and Pierre-Simon Laplace suspected that the Solar System arose from a nebula. Today, telescopes can see such discs of dust around young stars directly. **Meteorites** are especially valuable, because many have remained almost unchanged since the formation of the Solar System. Their age shows when the first solid bodies formed.

The University of Bern built a measuring instrument for the European space probe **Rosetta**, which reached the comet Churyumov-Gerasimenko in 2014. It studied the comet's gases and helped to show what the primeval nebula was made of. In 1995, the Geneva astronomers Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz discovered the first planet around a star like the Sun. For this they received the **Nobel Prize** in Physics in 2019.

begriffe.erklaerung: A flat disc of gas and dust around a young star, in which planets form.
A lump kilometres across from which planets grow together.
The fusing of atomic nuclei, by which stars produce energy.
A piece of rock from space that has fallen to Earth.

gewusst: The Sun is so big that about a million Earths would fit inside it.
Jupiter is so heavy that it probably prevented a planet of its own from forming in the asteroid belt.
Some meteorites that fall to Earth are older than the Earth itself.

teile.einleitung: The necropolis of Le Petit-Chasseur is a large burial ground from the Stone Age in Sion in the canton of Valais. Its burial chambers and the engraved stone stelae, which show simplified people, are famous.
wichtigste: The necropolis was discovered in 1961 during building work for houses.
Necropolis means city of the dead, that is, a large burial ground.
The graves date from the end of the New Stone Age and the Copper Age.
Over 30 engraved stone stelae were found.
Two dolmens are surrounded by triangular stone bases.
In 2019, six further stelae came to light during building work.

abschnitte.text: In **1961**, houses were being built in **Sion** in Valais. In doing so, workers came across large stone slabs. After that, archaeological **excavations** began that lasted many years. The word **necropolis** comes from Greek: “nekros” means dead, “polis” means city. What is meant is a large burial ground. The name Le Petit-Chasseur comes from the street where the site lies.

In the necropolis stand several **dolmens**. A dolmen is a burial chamber made of large stone slabs. Two of these burial chambers are surrounded by a large, **triangular base** of stones. This form of construction is typical of Le Petit-Chasseur. The site was used from about **2900 to 2200 BC**, that is, at the end of the New Stone Age and in the **Copper Age**. Later, people of the **Bell Beaker culture** also buried their dead here.

A **stele** is an upright stone slab. In Le Petit-Chasseur, **over 30** decorated stelae were found. They show greatly simplified **human figures**. Belts, decorated clothes and weapons are engraved. On the older stelae you often see a **dagger** at the belt, on younger ones rather a **bow and arrow**. Many stelae were later broken and used as building material for new graves.

Even decades after the discovery, the ground still gives up surprises. In **2019**, during a new building nearby, **six stelae** came to light that stood in a row. Some of them had been broken on purpose. Such finds help us to understand how people at that time honoured their dead. Many pieces from Le Petit-Chasseur can now be seen in the History Museum in Sion.

gewusst: The stelae of Le Petit-Chasseur probably show what clothes people wore about 4,500 years ago.
Similar human stelae are also known from the Aosta Valley in Italy, just across the Alps.

teile.einleitung: The Fertile Crescent is an arc-shaped region in the Near East. Here, about 11,000 to 12,000 years ago, people began farming and herding animals. This change altered people's lives for ever.
wichtigste: On the map, the region has the shape of a sickle.
The term comes from the American archaeologist James Henry Breasted, around 1916.
Mesopotamia lies between the Euphrates and the Tigris.
Here, farming and herding began about 11,000 to 12,000 years ago.
Vere Gordon Childe called this change the Neolithic Revolution.
Among the first crops is the lentil, and among the first farm animals the goat and the sheep.

abschnitte.text: The region stretches in an arc from the **Levant** on the Mediterranean across south-eastern Anatolia to the Persian Gulf. On the map it looks like a **crescent moon**. The American Egyptologist and archaeologist **James Henry Breasted** introduced the term around 1916 in a school textbook. The name caught on worldwide.

The western part on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean is called the **Levant**. It covers roughly the area of today's countries of Israel, Palestine, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria. In the east lies **Mesopotamia**, the “land between the rivers”. This means the **Euphrates** and the **Tigris** in present-day Iraq. Later, some of the first cities arose here too.

Even before farming, the people of the **Natufian** culture in the Levant were partly settled. From about 12,500 BC they harvested wild cereals. They are regarded as forerunners of the first farmers. Later, people in the Fertile Crescent began to grow plants deliberately and keep animals. The archaeologist **Vere Gordon Childe** called this change the **Neolithic Revolution**.

Among the first **crops** are cereals such as einkorn, emmer and barley, and pulses such as the **lentil**, the pea and the chickpea. Among the first **farm animals** were the **goat** and the **sheep**. They provided meat, milk and skins. From here, the farming way of life spread over thousands of years to Europe too, as far as the area of present-day Switzerland.

gewusst: Many foods that we eat every day today, such as wheat and lentils, come originally from the Fertile Crescent.
Mesopotamia is a Greek word and literally means “between the rivers”.

teile.einleitung: The bow and arrow are among the most important inventions of the Stone Age. With them, hunters could hit animals from a safe distance. Today archery is also a sport.
wichtigste: The stretched string on the bow is called the bowstring.
In the Stone Age, the bow was made of wood.
Feathers at the end of the arrow keep the arrow steady in flight.
Arrowheads were glued on with birch pitch.
Arrows are carried in a quiver.
Today the most commonly found items are the arrowheads of stone.

abschnitte.text: A bow consists of a flexible stave and a stretched string, the **bowstring**. You place the arrow against the string and pull it back. The bow bends and stores energy. When you let go, the string snaps forward and shoots the arrow away. In the Stone Age, the bow was made of **wood**, because it is flexible and strong. The wood of the **yew** was especially popular.

An arrow consists of a straight **shaft**, a **point** and **feathers** at the rear end. The feathers keep the arrow steady in flight, so it hits better. The point was often made of flint. It was fixed with **birch pitch**. This adhesive is obtained by heating birch bark strongly. The arrows were carried in a **quiver**, mostly on the back or at the side.

The bow and arrow had advantages over the **spear**. A hunter could take many arrows with him and shoot them quickly one after another. At **Stellmoor** in northern Germany, very old wooden arrows were found. At the end of the Ice Age, the place was a hunting ground. There people hunted mainly **reindeer**, of which very many bones were found. Someone who shoots with a bow is called an **archer**.

Wood, feathers and leather mostly decay in the ground. So of Stone Age arrows, the **stone arrowheads** are most often found. Only under special conditions is more preserved, for example in a bog or in ice. The glacier mummy **Ötzi**, found in 1991 in the Ötztal Alps, had a bow and a quiver with arrows with him. On the **Schnidejoch** in the Bernese Alps too, the melting ice released parts of Stone Age archery equipment.

gewusst: Ötzi's bow was not finished: it was not yet fully carved and had no bowstring.
The arrows of Stellmoor are over 12,000 years old and are among the oldest certainly known arrows.

teile.einleitung: Metalworking means obtaining metals from ore and making tools, weapons and jewellery from them. In prehistory, people learned first to work copper, then bronze and finally iron. These advances were so important that whole ages are named after the metals.
wichtigste: After the Stone Age, the Bronze Age and the Iron Age followed in Europe.
Bronze is a mixture of copper and about 10 per cent tin.
Bronze is harder than pure copper.
Bronze axes were mostly cast by pouring liquid bronze into moulds.
In the Iron Age, iron was obtained in a bloomery furnace with charcoal.
In the bloomery furnace, a lump of iron and slag formed, the bloom.
The smith had to clean and shape the bloom by hammering.

abschnitte.text: For a long time, people made their tools from stone, wood and bone. Towards the end of the New Stone Age, they began to work **copper**, at first for jewellery and small axes. Ötzi, who lived around 3300 BC, was already carrying an axe with a copper blade. In central Europe, the **Bronze Age** began around 2200 BC and the **Iron Age** around 800 BC.

**Bronze** is an alloy, that is, a mixture of metals. It usually consists of copper and about 10 per cent **tin**. Copper melts at about 1085 °C, tin already at about 232 °C. Together they make a metal that is harder than pure copper and casts well.

Bronze axes, sickles and swords were mostly **cast**. The metal was melted in a crucible and poured into a mould of stone or clay. For artistic pieces, **lost-wax casting** was used: first a model was shaped from wax and covered with clay. When heated, the wax melted out, and the liquid bronze flowed into the hollow.

Iron was obtained from **iron ore** in a bloomery furnace made of clay that was fired with charcoal. In the furnace it was about 1100 to 1350 °C, but iron only melts at about 1538 °C, so it did not become completely liquid. The liquid slag ran out of the furnace, which is where the German name **Rennofen** (“running furnace”) comes from. What remained was a spongy lump of iron and slag, the **bloom**.

The **smith** heated the bloom again and again and struck it with a hammer on the anvil. In this way he pressed out the slag and shaped the iron into bars, tools or weapons. Iron ore was much more common than copper and tin, for example as bean ore in the Jura. So tools of iron soon became affordable for many people.

Metals were valuable, and so a wide **trade** arose right across Europe, for example with tin from Cornwall in England. Whoever owned metal had power, so some families became rich and respected. With axes, ploughshares and sickles of iron, farmers could cultivate more land. Even today we make metals in blast furnaces and foundries, with similar basic ideas to those of back then.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mixture of two or more metals, for example bronze from copper and tin.
Rock containing so much metal that it can be extracted.
A furnace of clay in which iron was formerly obtained from ore with charcoal.
A lump of iron and slag that forms in the bloomery furnace.
The remains of rock that are separated from the metal when smelting.

gewusst: A bloomery furnace had to be supplied with air by bellows for many hours so that it stayed hot enough.
For a single kilogram of iron, a multiple of that amount of charcoal was needed in the bloomery furnace.
The famous Nebra Sky Disc from Germany is made of bronze with inlays of gold.

teile.einleitung: **Archaeobotany** studies plant remains from archaeological sites. Seeds, charcoal or pollen reveal what people used to eat and grow, and what the landscape looked like. In Switzerland, the lakeside settlements provide particularly many finds.
wichtigste: Macroremains such as seeds and charcoal are distinguished from microremains such as pollen.
In permanently wet ground without air, even plant remains that have not been charred are preserved.
Flotation is used to recover charred remains from soil samples.
Pollen analysis studies pollen in bogs and lake sediments.
Phytoliths are tiny bodies of silica from plant cells.
The study of charcoal is called anthracology.
Weed seeds in grain reveal how fields were farmed.

abschnitte.text: Archaeobotany divides its finds roughly into two groups. **Macroremains** can be seen with the naked eye or with a magnifying glass, such as grains, seeds, fruit shells and **charcoal**. **Microremains** such as **pollen**, spores or **phytoliths** can only be seen under the microscope. Phytoliths are tiny bodies of **silica** that many plants, especially grasses, deposit in their cells. They survive even where other plant remains vanished long ago.

Plants usually decay quickly. Bacteria and fungi break them down. But in **permanently wet ground with no air**, the oxygen these living things need is missing. That is why even fruits, mosses and remains of bread have been preserved in **bogs** and **lakeside settlements**. The prehistoric pile dwellings around the Alps, many of them in Switzerland, have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since 2011. Otherwise, plant parts survive mainly when they are **charred**.

Charred seeds are found by **flotation**. The soil is stirred up in water. Light charred seeds and charcoal float to the top and are skimmed off with fine sieves. The study of charcoal is called **anthracology**. Under the microscope, charcoal still shows the cell structure of the wood. This shows which kinds of wood were used as firewood or building material.

abschnitte.titel: Pollen tells the history of the landscape
abschnitte.text: Pollen has a very tough shell. In bogs and lake sediments it survives for **thousands of years**. In **pollen analysis**, experts count how much pollen from which plants is found in each layer. A **pollen diagram** then shows how forests, meadows and fields in a region have changed. For example, you can see when the first farmers cleared woodland.

Among old grain there are often **seeds of arable weeds**. Each weed has its own needs in terms of soil, moisture and cultivation. Their mix shows what kind of soil the grain grew on. You can even tell whether fields were manured or hoed, and whether the grain was harvested high up or close to the ground.

gewusst: In Swiss lakeside settlements, remains of bread baked over 5000 years ago have been found.
The wind can carry tree pollen many kilometres.

teile.einleitung: Druids were priests and scholars among the Celts. They knew about gods, stars and plants and were very highly respected. What we know about them comes mainly from accounts by Roman writers.
wichtigste: A druid was a priest and scholar among the Celts.
Druids often held ceremonies in sacred groves in the forest.
The oak was an especially important tree for them.
According to Pliny, they cut mistletoe with a golden sickle and wore white robes.
They learned their knowledge by heart instead of writing it down.
According to Caesar, druids did not have to go to war.

abschnitte.text: Among the **Celts**, the **druids** were priests, judges and wise teachers. They knew about the gods and the stars. The **Helvetii**, who lived in the area of present-day Switzerland, were Celts too. The druids were held in great esteem. The Roman **Julius Caesar** wrote that they did not have to go to war or pay taxes.

The Celts had **sacred groves**. These are stretches of woodland where the druids held their ceremonies. The **oak** was a sacred tree. A **mistletoe** growing on an oak was regarded as very special. The Roman scholar **Pliny the Elder** described in his “Natural History” how druids cut the mistletoe with a **golden sickle**, wearing **white** robes as they did so.

The druids did not write their knowledge down. Their pupils had to learn everything **by heart**, many songs and verses. According to Caesar, this training took many years for some. Druids also knew many **plants** and their effects. With them they tried to heal the sick.

Because the druids wrote nothing down, much of the information comes from **Romans** such as Caesar and Pliny. They wrote about foreign peoples, often from their own point of view. So much remains uncertain. Today many children know the druid **Getafix** (called Miraculix in German) from the Asterix comics. In them he brews the magic potion for the Gauls.

gewusst: Pliny the Elder died in AD 79 during the eruption of Vesuvius.
Mistletoe grows on trees as a partial parasite and is rather rare on oaks, which is why it was regarded as special there.

teile.einleitung: The Denisovan is a form of human from the Old Stone Age that has only been known since 2010. It was discovered not through a skeleton, but through the genetic material from a tiny bone. It was a close relative of the Neanderthal.
wichtigste: The Denisova Cave lies in the Altai Mountains in Siberia.
In 2008, a tiny piece of a finger bone was found there.
In 2010 its DNA revealed a previously unknown form of human.
It was decoded at the Max Planck Institute in Leipzig.
People in Melanesia and Papua New Guinea carry especially much Denisovan DNA.
Many Tibetans owe easier breathing at high altitude to a gene variant from the Denisovans.

abschnitte.text: The **Denisova Cave** lies in the **Altai Mountains** in southern Siberia, not far from the border with Kazakhstan. Its name means roughly “Denis's cave”. According to tradition, a hermit of that name once lived there. The cave has been studied by archaeologists for decades and contains traces from very many thousands of years.

In 2008, Russian archaeologists found a small piece of a **finger bone**. Researchers at the **Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology** in Leipzig recovered **DNA**, that is, genetic material, from it. It matched neither modern humans nor Neanderthals. The results appeared in 2010 in the journal “Nature”. This is how a completely new form of human became known.

Denisovans and **Neanderthals** were closely related. They also met: in 2018, the genetic material of a piece of bone from the cave showed a girl whose mother was a Neanderthal and whose father was a Denisovan. Ancestors of people today also met the Denisovans. That is why some people today still carry something of their genetic material.

People in **Melanesia** and **Papua New Guinea** have especially much Denisovan DNA, around 4 to 5 per cent. Many **Tibetans** have a variant of the gene **EPAS1** that helps with breathing at high altitude, where there is little oxygen. This variant probably passed from Denisovans to their ancestors. A lower jaw from a limestone cave at about 3280 metres on the **Tibetan Plateau** was recognised as Denisovan in 2019.

gewusst: The lower jaw from Tibet was found by a monk as early as 1980, but only almost 40 years later did anyone know who it belonged to.
Of the Denisovans, only very few bones and teeth are known to this day, but their genetic material is known very precisely.

teile.einleitung: The bone needle was an important invention of the Old Stone Age. With it, people could sew furs together precisely. This produced warm clothes, shoes, bags and tent covers.
wichtigste: A bone needle has an eye, like a sewing needle today.
Dried animal sinews were used as thread.
The eye was drilled with a pointed flint.
The needle became smooth and pointed by grinding on a rough stone.
Most needles are about as long as a finger.
With needle and thread, close-fitting, warm clothes were made.

abschnitte.text: The hole in a sewing needle is called the **eye**. The thread is passed through the eye. Even the needles of the Old Stone Age had such a hole. Most needles found are only a few centimetres long, that is, about **finger length**, and very fine.

First a thin sliver was cut from a bone or antler. Then it was rubbed back and forth on a **rough stone** until it was smooth, thin and pointed. The eye was drilled with a pointed **flint**. Flint is hard enough to drill a hole in bone. Metal was not yet known at that time.

**Animal sinews** served as thread. In the body, sinews connect the muscles to the bones. When dried, they can be split into thin threads that are very **strong**. With thick leather, holes were first pierced with an **awl**. An awl is a pointed tool. After that, the thread was easier to pull through.

With needle and thread, pieces of fur could be sewn together precisely. This produced clothes that **fit closely to the body**. They keep you much warmer than furs hung loosely about you. Besides clothes, people also sewed shoes, bags and large **covers for tents** from many pelts. This helped people to survive the cold of the Ice Age.

gewusst: The shape of the sewing needle with an eye has hardly changed since the Stone Age.
Sinew threads shrink as they dry and so make a seam especially strong.

teile.einleitung: In the Stone Age there were no clothes shops. People made their clothes themselves, mainly from the fur and leather of animals. That was a lot of work, but it protected well against cold and wet.
wichtigste: In the Old Stone Age, clothes consisted mainly of fur and leather.
A fresh pelt first had to be freed of meat and fat.
For this, a stone scraper was used.
In tanning, animal skin is made durable, and this produces leather.
Clothes were held together with leather straps.
The loom only appeared in the New Stone Age.

abschnitte.text: The people of the Ice Age lived in a cold climate. Warm pelts came above all from animals of cold regions, for example **reindeer** and **foxes**. Their fur is especially dense. The hunters used almost everything from an animal: meat to eat, bones for tools and the pelt for clothes.

On a fresh pelt, **meat and fat** still stuck. These remains were scraped off with a **scraper**, a stone tool with a round, sharp edge. Otherwise the pelt would have rotted. Then came **tanning**: the skin is treated so that it does not rot and stays soft. This produces **leather**, which is strong and lasts a long time.

With needles made of bone and threads made of animal sinews, pieces of fur were sewn together. This produced coats, trousers and caps. There were no zips or buttons made of metal. Clothes were tied shut with **leather straps**. On their feet, people probably wore soft **shoes made of fur and leather**.

A great deal about old clothes is known thanks to **Ötzi**, who died in the Alps about 5,300 years ago. The ice preserved his clothes. He wore a cap of bearskin and shoes lined with hay inside. Ötzi, however, lived after the Old Stone Age already, in the Copper Age.

In the **New Stone Age**, farmers learned to spin threads from flax and later from wool. With the **loom** they made fabrics. In the pile-dwelling settlements on Swiss lakes, even remains of weaves and cords were preserved, because they lay in the damp ground. From the Old Stone Age, by contrast, hardly any clothes are found: fur and leather have long since **rotted** in the ground.

gewusst: Stone tools survive for many thousands of years, clothes made of fur almost never.
Ötzi's shoes were lined with hay, which warmed like an insole.

teile.einleitung: The **Aurignacian** is a culture of the later Old Stone Age. It belongs to the first modern humans in Europe. Some of the oldest works of art in the world come from this time.
wichtigste: The Aurignacian is named after Aurignac in the department of Haute-Garonne in southern France.
The people of this culture were anatomically modern humans, Homo sapiens.
Typical are keeled scrapers and bone points with a split base.
The ivory figures of the Swabian Jura belong to the Aurignacian.
The Aurignacian was followed by the Gravettian.
Édouard Lartet, Gabriel de Mortillet and Henri Breuil shaped its study.

abschnitte.text: The Aurignacian began about **40,000 years ago**. It is the first culture of the **Upper Palaeolithic** in Europe. It was carried by **Homo sapiens**, the anatomically modern human. This is shown by teeth and skulls from sites such as **Mladeč** in the Czech Republic and **Brassempouy** in France. In the past, some researchers also thought of Neanderthals.

A guide tool is the **keeled scraper**. It has a high, narrowing working edge that recalls the keel of a ship. Also typical of the early Aurignacian are **bone points with a split base**. The lower end of these projectile points made of bone or antler was split so that they could be fixed to a shaft. They are also called **Aurignac points**.

Some of the oldest works of art come from the Aurignacian. In caves of the **Swabian Jura** in southern Germany, small **ivory figures** were found, such as animals and the famous **lion-man**. Flutes made of bone and ivory were also discovered there. The first radiocarbon dates from the **Chauvet Cave** in France, with its cave paintings, also gave over 30,000 years and fit the Aurignacian.

The culture is named after a rock shelter near **Aurignac** in the department of Haute-Garonne. There, in 1860, **Édouard Lartet** linked stone tools with the bones of Ice Age animals. This showed that humans lived at the same time as extinct animals. **Gabriel de Mortillet** introduced the term in 1867, but later struck it from his system. From 1906, **Henri Breuil** argued for recognising the Aurignacian again. He showed that it comes before the Solutrean, and in 1912 divided it into three stages.

The Aurignacian was followed by the **Gravettian**. Many of the well-known **Venus figurines** come from this time. The Solutrean and the Magdalenian followed later. This sequence of cultures helps archaeologists to date finds from the Old Stone Age.

gewusst: The caves with Ice Age art on the Swabian Jura have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2017.
The flutes from the Aurignacian are among the oldest known musical instruments.

teile.einleitung: The Iron Age is the part of prehistory in which people learned to make tools and weapons from iron. In central Europe it began around 800 BC and is divided into the Hallstatt period and the La Tène period. It is especially important for Switzerland, because the site of La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel gave its name to a whole era.
wichtigste: In the Near East, the Iron Age is said to begin around 1200 BC with the fall of the Hittite Empire.
In central Europe it began around 800 BC.
The earlier Iron Age is called the Hallstatt period, after the village of Hallstatt in Austria.
The later Iron Age is called the La Tène period and began around 450 BC.
The site of La Tène lies on Lake Neuchâtel, and the first finds came to light in 1857.
Typical of this time are rich princely graves such as those at Vix and Hochdorf.
In the area of Switzerland, the Iron Age ended with the conquest by the Romans.

abschnitte.text: The Iron Age followed the **Bronze Age**. Iron is harder than bronze, and iron ore is found in many more places than copper and tin. So more people could own tools such as axes, knives and ploughshares. In the Near East, the Iron Age began around 1200 BC, when the **Hittite Empire** fell.

The earlier Iron Age in central Europe lasted from about 800 to 450 BC. It is named after **Hallstatt** in Austria, where people grew rich by mining **salt**. From 1846, the mine master Johann Georg Ramsauer led the excavations in the large burial ground. He opened almost a thousand graves with precious grave goods.

In the Hallstatt period, powerful leaders were buried in splendid graves. In the grave of the **Lady of Vix** in France, around 500 BC, lay a huge bronze mixing vessel from Greece, the Vix krater. It is over a metre and a half tall. In the **princely grave of Hochdorf** in Baden-Württemberg, the dead man lay on a couch made of bronze.

Around 450 BC, the later Iron Age began, the **La Tène period**. It is named after the site of **La Tène** on Lake Neuchâtel, where the first finds were discovered in 1857. Especially many weapons such as swords, lances and shields came to light there. The playful style of the decoration on these finds is now called the La Tène style.

In the Iron Age, **Celtic** peoples such as the **Helvetii** lived in the area of Switzerland. They built fortified settlements, for example on the Mont Vully or on the Engehalbinsel in Bern. They minted coins and traded as far as the Mediterranean. With the conquest by the Romans in the 1st century BC, the Iron Age ended here.

To this day, most tools and machines are made of iron or **steel**. Many place names in Switzerland come from Celtic times. The **Laténium** museum in Hauterive in canton Neuchâtel shows many finds from La Tène. So you can still get to know the Iron Age well today.

begriffe.erklaerung: The earlier Iron Age in central Europe, about 800 to 450 BC.
The later Iron Age, from about 450 BC, named after La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel.
A rich grave of a powerful leader with precious grave goods.
An object that was placed in the grave with a dead person.

gewusst: The Vix krater holds over 1000 litres and is one of the largest bronze vessels of antiquity.
In the salt mine at Hallstatt, thanks to the salt, even remains of clothing and tools from the Iron Age have been preserved.
Because La Tène is in Switzerland, finds all over Europe bear the name of a Swiss place.

teile.einleitung: The **spear** is one of humankind's oldest weapons. It is a long shaft with a point. It could be thrown or used to thrust, above all for hunting.
wichtigste: A spear is a long shaft with a point.
The oldest spears found are made of wood.
With a spear you could throw or thrust.
Later, points of stone, bone or metal were fitted.
Spears were used mainly for hunting.

abschnitte.text: The oldest spears were made entirely of **wood**. People carved a straight stem and sharpened the point. Sometimes the point was hardened in the fire. Wood normally rots quickly, so such spears are found only rarely. Famous are the **Schöningen spears** from Germany, which are about 200,000 years old.

With a spear you could **throw** or **thrust**. A throwing spear is rather light and flies far. A thrusting spear is heavier and more powerful. With it, however, hunters had to get close to the animal, which was dangerous.

Later, people tied **stone points** to the wood, for example of flint. Points of **bone** or antler were common too. With them the spear penetrated better. In the Bronze Age and the Iron Age there were then spearheads of **metal**.

Today nobody uses a spear for hunting any more. But it lives on in sport: in the **javelin throw** in athletics, a spear is thrown as far as possible. The sporting javelin is built much like the old spears, with the centre of gravity in the front part.

gewusst: A yew spear found at Lehringen in Lower Saxony between elephant bones is over 100,000 years old.

teile.einleitung: Coal is a black rock that can burn. It arose from plants that grew in swamp forests many millions of years ago. For a long time, coal was the most important fuel in the world.
wichtigste: Hard coal arose from the plants of huge swamp forests.
The transformation took millions of years.
The geological period of the great coal forests is called the Carboniferous.
In the coal forests grew tree-high ferns, horsetails and clubmosses.
Coal consists mainly of carbon and is black.
Coal is mined in mines.
In bogs today, peat forms, a precursor of coal.

abschnitte.text: About 300 million years ago, in the **Carboniferous**, huge swamp forests grew. There stood tree-high **ferns**, **horsetails** and **clubmosses**. There were no flowers yet at that time. The word Carboniferous comes from the Latin word for coal, because much hard coal dates from this time.

Fallen trees dropped into the water of the swamps. There they did not rot completely, because hardly any air reached them. In time, sand and mud settled over them. Under the great pressure and the heat in the depths, the plant remains slowly became **brown coal** and later **hard coal**. In bogs today, **peat** forms, a precursor of it.

Hard coal is **black** and often shines a little. It consists mainly of **carbon**. In the coal and in the rock next to it, you often find **leaf impressions** of ferns. Such fossils show what the plants of prehistory looked like.

Coal is taken out of the ground in a **mine**, either underground or in large pits. The workers are called **miners**. Coal burns for a long time and gives a lot of heat. With it, people heated houses and ran **steam engines** and railways. In Switzerland there is only little coal. An old brown coal mine at Käpfnach near Horgen can be visited today as a museum.

When coal is burned, **carbon dioxide** is produced. This gas increases the warming of the Earth. That is why many countries want to burn less coal. They rely more on water, sun and wind. Switzerland gets most of its electricity from hydropower and nuclear power, not from coal.

gewusst: The coal we burn today is solar energy that plants stored millions of years ago.
From many metres of plant remains, only a much thinner layer of coal forms.

teile.einleitung: Flax is a plant whose stem provides fibres for cloth. It is also called linseed plant and is among the oldest crops. The pile dwellers in Switzerland already grew flax.
wichtigste: Flax is also called lin or linseed plant.
Its flowers are mostly blue.
The plant grows to about 1 metre tall.
The fibres are obtained from the stem.
Flax was laid in water or on damp meadows so that the fibres came loose.
Oil is obtained from the seeds.
The pile dwellers grew flax to make cloth.

abschnitte.text: **Flax** is a slender plant with a thin stem. It grows to about **one metre** tall. A flowering field of flax glows light blue, because the small flowers are mostly **blue**. They each bloom only briefly. Another name for flax is **linseed plant**.

The **fibres** are in the long **stem**. After the harvest, the flax was laid in water or on damp meadows. The wet makes the soft parts of the stem rot, and the fibres come loose. After that the stems were broken and combed to separate the fibres from the woody inside. From the fibres, thread was spun.

From the threads, cloth is made by **weaving**. In this, threads are crossed lengthways and crossways. Cloth made from flax is called **linen**. It is cool and very durable. The **pile dwellers** in Switzerland planted flax beside their cereals. From its fibres they made cloth, cords and nets. Such remains have been found in pile-dwelling settlements, because they were preserved in the wet ground.

The small brown **seeds** are called **linseeds**. You can eat them, for example in bread or in muesli. **Linseed oil** is also pressed from them. It is used as cooking oil and for paints and for caring for wood. So a single plant provided cloth and food at the same time.

gewusst: The English word “line” is connected with the Latin word for flax, because a cord made of flax drew a straight line.
The German word “Leinwand” (canvas) also comes from flax, because painters used to paint on linen.

teile.einleitung: The Megalithic culture comprises large structures made of huge stones in the New Stone Age. These include burial chambers, stone circles and temples. They are found from Malta to Scandinavia and even in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Megalith means “large stone”.
The cairn of Barnenez in Brittany is among the oldest megalithic structures in Europe.
The temples of Ġgantija on Gozo are among the oldest free-standing stone buildings in the world.
On the Orkney Islands stands the stone circle Ring of Brodgar.
In northern Germany, the Funnel Beaker culture built many megalithic tombs.
In Oberbipp in the canton of Bern, a dolmen was discovered in 2011.
The idea of megalithic structures probably spread from north-western France.

abschnitte.text: The word **megalith** comes from Greek and means “large stone”. People of the New Stone Age moved stones weighing tonnes without machines. With them they built **dolmens**, that is, burial chambers of stone slabs, and **passage graves**, to which a passage leads. In addition there are stone circles and single upright stones. A study of 2019 evaluated over 2,000 age determinations. According to it, the oldest megalithic tombs arose around 4500 BC in **north-western France**, and the idea probably spread across the sea.

The **cairn of Barnenez** is a large stone mound with eleven burial chambers. It arose around 4800 to 4500 BC and is among the oldest megalithic structures in Europe. In the Gulf of Morbihan lies the passage grave of **Gavrinis**. Most of its wall stones are decorated with arcs, spirals and lines. It arose around 4200 to 4000 BC.

On the Maltese island of **Gozo** stand the temples of **Ġgantija**. They arose around 3600 BC and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. On Malta there is also the **Hypogeum of Ħal Saflieni**, a multi-storey complex that was cut into the rock. The remains of thousands of people were found in it. On the Scottish **Orkney Islands** stands the stone circle **Ring of Brodgar**, which originally had about 60 stones.

In northern Germany and southern Scandinavia there are thousands of **megalithic tombs**. Most were built by the **Funnel Beaker culture**, mainly between about 3500 and 2800 BC. It is named after its vessels with a funnel-shaped rim. Many of these tombs were used again and again over a long time.

In **2011**, a New Stone Age **dolmen** was discovered in **Oberbipp** in the canton of Bern. It was built in the second half of the 4th millennium BC and used for a long time as a **collective grave**. Bones of about 30 people were found in it. Also well known are the dolmens of Sion in Valais and the standing stones of Clendy near Yverdon-les-Bains.

gewusst: Some megalithic structures are older than the pyramids in Egypt.
How people moved the huge stones, researchers try to find out with experiments.

teile.einleitung: Fossilisation is the name for the process in which the remains of living things turn to stone. It happens only rarely and takes a very long time. Thanks to fossils, we know today which animals and plants lived millions of years ago.
wichtigste: In fossilisation, the remains of living things turn to stone.
A dead animal must first be covered quickly.
Bones and teeth are most often fossilised.
It works especially well on the bed of bodies of water.
Fossilisation takes very many years.
Most dead animals rot away completely, so there are only a few fossils.

abschnitte.text: For an animal to be fossilised, it has to be **quickly covered by mud** or sand after death. Then scavengers cannot destroy it. Under the cover, oxygen is also missing, and decay slows down. This works especially well on the **bed of lakes and seas**. There, new mud is constantly being deposited.

**Bones** and **teeth** are most often fossilised, and so are the shells of mussels and snails. These hard parts last longest. Soft parts such as skin and muscles usually rot quickly. That is why for many animals only the skeleton is known.

Over the years, **ever new layers** of sand and mud settle over the buried animal. Under the pressure, these layers turn to rock. **Water** in the ground carries minerals into the bones. Little by little, the minerals replace or fill the remains, until the bones are as hard as **stone**. This usually takes thousands or millions of years.

Sometimes the living thing disappears completely, but its shape is preserved in the rock. Such an **impression** shows the shape of a living thing in the stone, for example in leaves and shells. Fossils come to the surface again when wind, water and ice **wear away** the rock. They also turn up during building work or in quarries. Because most animals are eaten or rot away, fossils are rare and valuable.

gewusst: Footprints, eggs and fossilised droppings also count as fossils.
In amber, that is, fossilised tree resin, tiny insects are sometimes preserved down to the finest details.

teile.einleitung: The cave of Altamira in northern Spain is famous for its coloured pictures of bison on the ceiling. It was one of the first caves in which paintings from the Stone Age were discovered.
wichtigste: Altamira lies near Santillana del Mar in Cantabria.
In 1868, a man found the entrance when he was looking for his hunting dog.
In 1879, little María discovered the pictures on the ceiling.
The coloured bison are especially famous.
For a long time, experts thought the pictures were fakes.
Since 1985, Altamira has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: Altamira lies near **Santillana del Mar** in **Cantabria**, close to the north coast of Spain. In 1868, **Modesto Cubillas** was looking for his missing hunting dog and came across the cave entrance. Later, **Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola** examined the floor of the cave. His little daughter **María** looked up in 1879 and discovered the animal pictures on the ceiling.

The ceiling shows a group of coloured **bison** in red and black. There are also deer, horses and wild boar. The painters cleverly placed the bison on natural **humps of rock**. This makes the bodies look almost three-dimensional. Because of this magnificent ceiling, Altamira is often called the “**Sistine Chapel of the Stone Age**”, after the famous chapel in Rome.

Many experts did not believe that people of the Stone Age could paint so beautifully. The Frenchman **Émile Cartailhac** declared the pictures to be fake. When similar pictures were found in France, he changed his mind. In 1902, he published the essay “**Mea culpa d'un sceptique**”, in English roughly “A sceptic's confession of guilt”. The text is regarded as a famous admission of a mistake in science.

In the past, very many visitors came to the cave. Their warm **breath** changed the climate, and **mould** formed on the pictures. That is why the original cave may no longer be freely visited today. In the museum next door there is an exact **replica**. In 1985, Altamira became a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and in 2008 further painted caves in northern Spain were added.

gewusst: A little girl discovered one of the most famous works of art of the Stone Age because she looked at the ceiling.
A researcher apologised publicly because he had taken the pictures for fakes.

teile.einleitung: Many of the first farmers in central Europe lived in longhouses. These large wooden houses had room for a whole family. They show that people were becoming settled and stayed near their fields.
wichtigste: Longhouses were long houses of the first farmers in central Europe.
Thick wooden posts in rows carried the roof.
The walls consisted of woven branches plastered with clay.
The roof was thatched with straw or reed.
Some longhouses were up to 40 metres long.
A hearth gave warmth and light.

abschnitte.text: In the **New Stone Age**, people began to grow cereals and keep animals. They had to tend and harvest their fields. So they stayed in one place and became **settled**. Instead of tents, they built permanent houses. The early farmers in central Europe built long wooden houses for this, which are called **longhouses**.

Thick **wooden posts** stood in several rows in the house. They carried the heavy roof. Between the posts of the walls, branches and rods were woven. Then **clay** was spread on top. This produced a firm, tight wall. The roof was thatched with **straw** or **reed**, which, tied densely, kept the rain out.

Some longhouses were up to **40 metres** long. That is longer than an ordinary gymnasium. Often several houses stood together and formed a small village. Of the houses, usually only dark discolourations in the ground remained where the posts had stood. From these, archaeologists can still recognise the floor plan today.

Many people lived together in a longhouse, often a **large family**. An open **hearth** warmed the house and gave light. There was no electricity or metal yet. In the house, people cooked, worked and slept. Supplies such as grain were also stored inside.

Longhouses were typical of the early farming culture that is called **Linear Pottery culture** after its decorated vessels. In Switzerland, traces of this culture are known mainly from the canton of Schaffhausen. Later, people on the Swiss lakes built mostly smaller houses in **pile-dwelling settlements**.

gewusst: The post holes of a longhouse can still be recognised in the ground after more than 7,000 years.
For a single longhouse, many large tree trunks were needed, which were felled with stone axes.

teile.einleitung: The Rauraci were a Celtic people at the Rhine bend around Basel. They were neighbours of the Helvetii and later gave the Roman city of Augusta Raurica its name.
wichtigste: The Rauraci lived at the Rhine bend around Basel, on the Upper Rhine and in the Jura.
In 58 BC, they moved with the Helvetii towards Gaul.
After the defeat at Bibracte, they had to return.
Lucius Munatius Plancus founded a colony in their territory in 44 BC.
The Roman city of Augusta Raurica bears their name.
An important settlement was Basel-Gasfabrik.

abschnitte.titel: A people at the Rhine bend
abschnitte.text: The **Rauraci** were a Celtic people. They settled on the **Upper Rhine**, at the Rhine bend around **Basel** and in the **Jura**. Several of their settlements lie in the present-day urban area of Basel. Their neighbours to the south were the **Helvetii**. Like other Celts, the Rauraci lived from arable farming, livestock, crafts and trade. The Rhine was an important route for traffic.

In the north of Basel lay a large, **unfortified settlement** of the Rauraci. Its remains were come across in **1911** during the building of a **gasworks**. That is why the find site is now called **Basel-Gasfabrik** (“Basel gasworks”). The settlement was an important **centre of trade and crafts**. Many pits, pottery, tools and coins were found there. Later a fortified place, an oppidum, arose on the **Münsterhügel**.
