In **58 BC**, the Helvetii wanted to leave their homeland and move to Gaul. The Rauraci joined them. The Roman general **Julius Caesar** stood against them. At **Bibracte** in Burgundy there was a battle, which the emigrants lost. Afterwards they had to return to their homeland. We know of these events mainly from Caesar's own account.

In **44 BC**, **Lucius Munatius Plancus** founded a Roman colony in the territory of the Rauraci. Plancus was an officer of Caesar and a governor in Gaul. His tomb stands in **Gaeta** in Italy. Later, the city of **Augusta Raurica** arose near **Augst** and **Kaiseraugst** on the Rhine. It bears the name of the Rauraci and is among the best-preserved Roman cities north of the Alps. Today you can visit a large theatre and many excavations there.

Almost 1,900 years later, the old name was used again. In the area of the **Prince-Bishopric of Basel**, the **Rauracian Republic** arose in **1792** under the influence of the French Revolution. It lasted only briefly. Already in **1793**, it was annexed to **France**. The name shows how long the memory of the Celtic people stayed alive.

gewusst: The inscription on the tomb of Plancus in Gaeta mentions the founding of the colony in the territory of the Rauraci.
In Augusta Raurica, a large silver treasure from late antiquity was found in 1961.

teile.einleitung: Nomads are people who have no fixed home and keep moving on. In the Old Stone Age, all people lived like this: they followed the animals they hunted and the plants they gathered.
wichtigste: Nomads move from place to place and do not stay long.
People of the Old Stone Age followed, for example, the reindeer herds.
They went everywhere on foot and carried their things themselves.
So they owned only few things.
When moving on, they took the pelts of their tents with them.
They used good camp sites again and again.

abschnitte.text: Reindeer travel long distances in **spring** and **autumn** between their summer and winter areas. The hunters of the Old Stone Age followed them. The herds took similar routes every year. The elders knew these routes from **experience** and told the younger ones about them. In this way the group knew where it could find animals at the right time. This way of life is called **nomadism**.

In the Old Stone Age there were still no wagons and no tamed horses. People went everywhere **on foot**. Everything they owned, they had to **carry** on their backs or in their arms. So nobody had many things. People owned only what they really needed: clothes, tools of stone and bone, weapons for hunting and pelts.

A **camp site** is a place where a group lives for a while. There it set up its **tents**. The tents consisted of a framework of poles over which **pelts** were stretched. When the group moved on, it took the pelts with it. They were valuable and light enough to carry. At the new place, a tent was built with them again.

Nomads did not simply wander aimlessly. Good places they used **again and again**, often at the same time of year. They came back when there were animals to hunt or berries and nuts to gather there. At such places, archaeologists find several layers with hearths and tools one above the other. From this you can see that people came here many times.

gewusst: Only with arable farming in the New Stone Age did people become settled and build permanent houses.
Even today there are still peoples who move around with their herds of animals, for example in Mongolia or in the north of Scandinavia.

teile.einleitung: **Brachiosaurus** was one of the largest dinosaurs. With its long neck, it could reach leaves high up in the trees. It lived in the Jurassic in North America.
wichtigste: The first skeleton was found in 1900 in the US state of Colorado.
The name means “arm lizard”.
Its front legs were longer than its back legs.
It was about 20 to 25 metres long.
With its head raised, it stood about 9 to 13 metres high.
It lived in the Jurassic, about 150 million years ago.
The huge skeleton in Berlin is now regarded as a separate species, Giraffatitan.

abschnitte.text: Brachiosaurus belonged to the **sauropods**, the large plant eaters with a long neck and a long tail. Its name comes from Greek: **brachion** means arm, **sauros** means lizard. So it is called the **arm lizard**. The name fits, because its **front legs** were longer than its back legs. That is why its back was higher at the front than at the back.

Like a **giraffe**, Brachiosaurus held its neck high. With its head raised, it was about **9 to 13 metres** tall. That is taller than a house with three storeys. Its length was about **20 to 25 metres**, as long as two buses one behind the other. So it could reach leaves at great height, which other animals could not get at.

Brachiosaurus lived in the **Jurassic**, about **150 million years ago**. It was a **plant eater**. Because it was so big, it had to eat a great deal every day. Its teeth were built for stripping off leaves, not for chewing. The food was digested in its huge belly.

The first skeleton was dug up in **1900** in the US state of **Colorado** in **North America**. Later, very similar bones were found in Tanzania in Africa. From these, one of the tallest dinosaur skeletons in the world was assembled in the **Natural History Museum in Berlin**. For a long time it was counted as Brachiosaurus. Today it is regarded as a separate species called **Giraffatitan**.

gewusst: To this day, no complete skeleton of the North American Brachiosaurus is known.
Brachiosaurus was described and named in 1903 by the American researcher Elmer Riggs.

teile.einleitung: At Laetoli in Tanzania, ancient footprints of early human ancestors have been found. They are about 3.7 million years old. The tracks show that these early human ancestors already walked upright on two legs.
wichtigste: Laetoli lies in the north of Tanzania in East Africa.
The footprints are about 3.7 million years old.
They were preserved in wet volcanic ash.
The large trail was excavated in 1978 and is about 25 metres long.
According to the usual interpretation, it comes from three individuals.
Today the tracks have been covered with soil again to protect them.

abschnitte.text: A volcanic eruption once covered the area of **Laetoli** with ash. Rain made the **volcanic ash** wet and soft. Early human ancestors and animals walked over it and left prints. After drying, the ash became as hard as cement, and new ash covered the tracks. The layers were dated to about **3.6 to 3.7 million years**.

In 1976, researchers at Laetoli had a **fun fight** with dried elephant dung. Andrew Hill dodged a lump of dung, fell over and noticed fossilised animal tracks in the ground. So the search for more tracks began. In 1978, the geochemist **Paul Abell** was the first to recognise a footprint of an early human ancestor. After that, the whole line of tracks was uncovered in **1978**.

The famous trail is about **25 metres** long, and depending on the measurement, 24 to 27 metres are given. You can see two tracks side by side. A third individual evidently stepped in the prints of another. That is why people usually assume **three** individuals. The prints show that the early human ancestors already walked **upright**. In 2015, tracks of the same age from two more individuals were found about 150 metres away. One of them was **clearly larger** than those known before.

Taking the tracks away would have been too expensive and too risky. So they were **covered with soil** again. That protects them best from wind, water and plant roots. For exhibitions, casts and precise recordings of the tracks are used.

gewusst: The excavations at Laetoli were led by the famous researcher Mary Leakey.
In the same layer of ash, tracks of many animals were also found, even of birds and raindrops.

teile.einleitung: Pangaea was a huge supercontinent in which almost all the land masses of the Earth were united. It existed about 300 to 200 million years ago and then slowly broke up into the continents we know today.
wichtigste: Pangaea was a supercontinent.
The name means “whole Earth”.
Pangaea existed about 300 to 200 million years ago.
The ocean around Pangaea was called Panthalassa.
Pangaea broke up first into Laurasia and Gondwana.
Many rocks of the Alps arose from deposits of the Tethys.

abschnitte.text: In **Pangaea**, almost all the land masses of the Earth were united into a single **supercontinent**. The name comes from Greek: “pan” means whole, “gaia” means Earth. Pangaea formed towards the end of the **Palaeozoic**, about 300 million years ago. All around lay a huge ocean, the **Panthalassa**. That means “whole sea”. In the interior of the continent it was often very dry, because the sea was far away.

The Earth's surface consists of large **plates** that move very slowly, only a few centimetres a year. In the **Jurassic**, about 200 million years ago, Pangaea began to break apart. First it divided into the northern continent **Laurasia** and the southern continent **Gondwana**. These later broke up further. From Laurasia came North America, Europe and Asia, and from Gondwana, among others, South America, Africa, Australia and Antarctica.

Between Laurasia and Gondwana lay a sea, the **Tethys**. On its floor, lime and clay were deposited, layer by layer. Later, Africa and Europe moved towards each other again. In the process these layers were pressed together and folded up high. This produced the **Alps**. That is why fossils of sea creatures are found today even in the Swiss mountains.

In the **Triassic**, when Pangaea was still joined together, the **first dinosaurs** appeared. Land animals could then spread over the whole supercontinent. That is why fossils of the same land animals are found today on widely separated continents. Such finds helped the researcher **Alfred Wegener** to support his idea of drifting continents. He also gave Pangaea its name.

gewusst: The coasts of South America and Africa fit together on the map almost like pieces of a puzzle.
The Atlantic still grows a few centimetres wider every year.

teile.einleitung: The Hallstatt culture is a culture of the earlier Iron Age in central Europe. It is named after the village of Hallstatt in Austria, where a large burial ground was discovered near the salt mine.
wichtigste: Hallstatt lies on Lake Hallstatt in the Salzkammergut in Austria.
The Hallstatt culture, as the earlier Iron Age, lasted from about 800 to 450 BC.
Paul Reinecke divided the Hallstatt period into stages A to D.
In the burial ground, the dead were buried partly unburnt and partly cremated.
Powerful families lived in fortified hilltop settlements, the princely seats.
Since 1997, the Hallstatt-Dachstein Salzkammergut region has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.titel: A place between lake and mountain
abschnitte.text: The village of **Hallstatt** lies squeezed between the shore of **Lake Hallstatt** and steep mountain slopes. The landscape is called the **Salzkammergut** and is named after its rich salt deposits. Even in prehistoric times, people mined salt here. Salt was very valuable, because it could be used to preserve meat and fish. In the high valley above the village lies the famous **burial ground**.

abschnitte.titel: The stages of the Hallstatt period
abschnitte.text: The German archaeologist **Paul Reinecke** divided the Hallstatt period into stages A to D, Ha A to Ha D for short. Stages A and B are now counted as part of the late **Bronze Age**. Stages C and D make up the Hallstatt period in the narrower sense, that is, the earlier **Iron Age** from about 800 to 450 BC. During this time, tools and weapons made of iron became established. After it came the **La Tène period**. The term “Hallstatt culture” was introduced in 1905 by the Viennese researcher **Moriz Hoernes**.

In the burial ground at Hallstatt, very many graves with rich grave goods were found. About half of the dead were buried **unburnt**, and the others were **cremated**. Both kinds of burial existed side by side. Experts distinguish a western and an **eastern Hallstatt zone** (Osthallstattkreis). In the east, for example in Slovenia and Styria, warriors were often given a **battle-axe** and parts of armour in the grave.

In the late Hallstatt period, powerful families lived on fortified hilltops. Experts call them **princely seats**. These families traded with the Mediterranean region and owned precious goods from the south. Nearby there are often rich **burial mounds**. Well-known examples are the Heuneburg on the Danube and Mont Lassois in France. In the area of present-day Switzerland too, there are traces of the Hallstatt culture.

gewusst: In the salt mine at Hallstatt, thanks to the salt, even remains of clothing and wooden tools were preserved.
A whole era of prehistory is named after a small village in Austria.

teile.einleitung: Experimental archaeology rebuilds old tools, houses or boats and tries them out. This makes it possible to test how people in earlier times might have worked and lived. There have been well-known experiments in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: Experimental archaeology tries out old techniques in practice.
An experiment shows that something was possible in a certain way.
In 1947, Thor Heyerdahl sailed the raft Kon-Tiki from Peru to Polynesia.
In 2007, two families lived like people in the New Stone Age in the programme “Pfahlbauer von Pfyn”.
Peter Reynolds founded the Butser Ancient Farm in England in 1972.
The Lejre centre in Denmark is one of the oldest of its kind.

abschnitte.text: In **experimental archaeology**, things from the past are rebuilt and used. A successful experiment shows that something was **possible** in a certain way. It does not prove that people back then really did it like that. For that, the results must be compared with real **finds** and evidence.

The Norwegian **Thor Heyerdahl** sailed in 1947 on the balsa raft **Kon-Tiki** from Peru to the Tuamotu Islands in Polynesia. He wanted to show that people from South America could have reached Polynesia by raft. The experiment proved that it was **feasible**. It did not prove that the islands were really settled that way.

abschnitte.titel: Living like in the Stone Age
abschnitte.text: In 2007, Swiss television showed the programme “**Pfahlbauer von Pfyn**” (“Pile dwellers of Pfyn”). Two families and two young men lived for several weeks in a rebuilt pile-dwelling village at the Hinderrietweiher near Pfyn in **Thurgau**. Archaeologists accompanied the project. In England, **Peter Reynolds** founded the **Butser Ancient Farm** in 1972. There, Iron Age houses are rebuilt, and long-term experiments test things such as harvest yields and the storage of grain in pits in the ground. In **Denmark**, the **Lejre** centre has existed since 1964, today called Sagnlandet Lejre.

To understand early iron production, **bloomery furnaces** are rebuilt. In them, iron ore is heated with charcoal so that iron forms without melting. A spongy **bloom** is produced, which has to be forged. **Stone tools** are also copied and used. Cutting wood, meat or grain leaves different **traces of use**. Comparison with originals shows what a find was used for.

gewusst: The voyage of the Kon-Tiki lasted over three months.
Failures are valuable in experiments too, because they show what probably did not work.

teile.einleitung: The dog is humankind's oldest domestic animal. It descends from the wolf and has lived with us for many thousands of years. It helped with hunting, herding and guarding.
wichtigste: All dogs descend from the wolf.
Tame dogs have existed for about 15,000 years, perhaps even longer.
Dogs helped hunters to track down animals.
Later they herded the flocks of shepherds.
A young dog is called a puppy.
In Swiss pile dwellings, bones of the small peat dog were found.

abschnitte.text: All dogs descend from the **wolf**. Probably wolves came close to humans because there were food scraps there. The tamest animals stayed and over time became dogs. The oldest certain **dog bones** are about 14,000 to 15,000 years old. But perhaps the dog has existed even longer.

The dog got **food and protection** from humans, for example food scraps and a place by the fire. In return, it helped humans. Dogs smell and hear very well. So they found wild animals faster than the hunters. At night the dog **barked** loudly when strangers or wild animals approached the camp.

When people became settled and kept animals, the dog got a new task. It **herded the flock**, kept the sheep and goats together and drove off predators. In the **pile dwellings** of Switzerland, bones of a small dog were found. Researchers called it the **peat dog**, because the bones lay in peat and lake mud.

Near **Bonn** in Germany, a grave about 14,000 years old was found. In it lay people and a dog. The dog had been buried like a member of the family. This shows how important dogs already were to people then. A young dog, by the way, is called a **puppy**. Puppies need a lot of sleep and care.

gewusst: The dog became a domestic animal long before people practised farming.
The dog from the grave near Bonn was ill and was cared for by the people.

teile.einleitung: In the salt mountain of **Hallstatt** in Austria, people have been mining salt for about 7,000 years. It is one of the oldest salt mines in the world. Because salt preserves things, many traces of the prehistoric miners were preserved there.
wichtigste: In Hallstatt, people have been obtaining salt for about 7,000 years.
Salt was needed mainly to preserve meat.
The salt preserved wood, leather and cloth in the mountain.
The waste layers of the ancient miners are called Heidengebirge.
A wooden staircase from the 14th century BC is regarded as the oldest wooden staircase in Europe.
In 1734, miners found a dead man preserved in the salt.
The tunnels were lit with burning wood splints.

abschnitte.text: Without a fridge, food spoils quickly. With **salt**, meat and fish can be **preserved**. That is why salt was very valuable in prehistory. Whoever owned salt could trade with it. As a result the settlement of Hallstatt became rich, and a whole period of the Iron Age is named after it, the **Hallstatt period**.

The miners drove tunnels deep into the mountain. There they struck off the salt rock with picks made of bronze. They had light from **burning wood splints** that they held in the hand or in the mouth. The remains of splints, tools, salt and clay still lie in the mountain today. Experts call these layers **Heidengebirge**.

abschnitte.titel: The oldest wooden staircase in Europe
abschnitte.text: In the salt mountain, a large wooden **staircase** was found. It was built in the **14th century BC** and is regarded as the oldest wooden staircase in Europe. Its steps could be adjusted and also taken apart again. That wood lasts so long is unusual: in salt, however, it is preserved, because salt prevents decay.

The salt **preserved** many things: wood, leather, scraps of cloth, fur caps and even food remains. So researchers today know fairly exactly how the miners worked, what they wore and what they ate. In **1734**, miners even came across a dead man who had been preserved in the salt. He is called the “Man in the Salt”.

The village of Hallstatt lies on a lake in the Salzkammergut. Since 1997, the landscape has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Salt is still obtained in the salt mountain today. Visitors can tour the mine and slide down into the depths on old chutes used by the miners.

gewusst: In Hallstatt, a large burial ground was also discovered, with many grave goods of bronze and iron.
A whole period of the Iron Age is named after the village of Hallstatt.

teile.einleitung: **Archaeozoology** studies animal bones from archaeological sites. From bones, teeth and fish bones, you can tell which animals people hunted, kept and ate. This builds up a picture of everyday life in earlier times.
wichtigste: The minimum number of individuals shows how many animals there must have been at least.
The age at slaughter is estimated from teeth and from the growth plates of the bones.
Many young male and old female cattle point to dairy farming.
Early domestic animals were usually smaller than their wild ancestors.
Cut marks show how animals were butchered.
Washing the soil through fine sieves stops small bones from being overlooked.
The dog is regarded as humans' oldest domestic animal.

abschnitte.text: At a dig, thousands of pieces of bone are often found. First you count how many pieces belong to each species. This number is called the **NISP**. But it does not say how many animals there were. For that there is the **minimum number of individuals**, or **MNI** for short. If you find three left thigh bones of cattle, for example, there must have been at least three cattle.

Experts estimate the **age at slaughter** mainly from the **teeth**. They come through at fixed ages and wear down over time. The **growth plates** at the ends of the long bones also help. They fuse in a known order. From many age estimates, a **slaughter-age profile** is built up. If you find many young bulls and old cows, the cattle were probably kept mainly for **milk**.

abschnitte.titel: From wild animal to domestic animal
abschnitte.text: Early **domestic animals** were usually **smaller** than their wild ancestors. Domestic cattle, for example, are much smaller than the **aurochs** they descend from. The reasons are changes in diet and keeping, and selection by humans. The oldest domestic animal is the **dog**. It was tamed from the wolf by hunters and gatherers in the Ice Age. Sheep, goats, cattle and pigs only came with settled life.

Fine **cut marks** on bones show that an animal was butchered and the meat cut off. Stone blades and metal knives leave typical notches. Their position reveals how people went about skinning and cutting up the animal. Traces of fire or bites from dogs can also be recognised.

By hand, it is mainly large bones of cattle or pigs that stand out. Bones of **fish**, **birds** and small mammals are tiny. That is why the soil is often **washed** with water through fine sieves. Otherwise you would get a wrong idea of what people ate. In the Swiss lakeside settlements, animal bones have been preserved in particularly large numbers.

gewusst: The aurochs, ancestor of our cattle, has been extinct since the 17th century.
From fish bones you can even tell which species of fish were caught in a lake.

teile.einleitung: The Bell Beaker culture is named after its clay vessels, which look like upside-down bells. It was widespread in large parts of Europe at the transition from the New Stone Age to the Bronze Age. It left traces in Valais too.
wichtigste: The Bell Beaker culture is dated to about 2600 to 2200 BC.
The bell beakers probably arose on the Iberian Peninsula.
Typical grave goods with men are wrist guards for archery.
Also typical are buttons with a V-shaped perforation.
Copper and gold spread with the culture.
In the necropolis of Petit-Chasseur in Sion, older dolmens were reused.

abschnitte.text: The culture is named after its **bell beakers**. These clay vessels look like upside-down bells and are often decorated with bands. The culture belongs to the end of the **New Stone Age** and the **Copper Age**. In central Europe it was widespread from about **2600 to 2200 BC**. According to the majority view today, the oldest beakers come from the **Iberian Peninsula**, probably from Portugal.

In men's graves you often find stone **wrist guards**. They protected the wrist from the snapping back of the bowstring and point to **archery**. There are also arrowheads and **copper daggers**. Also typical are **buttons with a V-shaped perforation** made of bone, amber or jet. In this way they could be sewn onto clothing.

With the Bell Beaker culture, **copper** and **gold** spread across large parts of Europe. Iron only appeared over a thousand years later. A famous find is the “**Amesbury Archer**”, buried near Stonehenge around 2300 BC. Isotopes in his tooth enamel show that he spent his childhood in the **Alpine region**. DNA analyses from 2018 showed that at this time the population of Britain was largely **replaced**.

In the necropolis of **Petit-Chasseur** in **Sion** in the canton of Valais, dolmens and decorated **statue menhirs** were found. These are stone slabs with human figures carved into them. The graves were older than the Bell Beaker culture. The Bell Beaker people went on using them and reworked some of the stelae.

gewusst: The grave of the Amesbury Archer was the richest of its time in Great Britain.
Bell beakers have been found from Portugal to Hungary and from North Africa to Britain.

teile.einleitung: **Seriation** is a method used in archaeology. With it, finds such as graves or vessels are put into a time order. It says what came earlier and what came later, but not in which year.
wichtigste: Seriation gives a relative sequence without calendar years.
Around 1899, Flinders Petrie ordered Egyptian graves using his “Sequence Dating”.
The popularity of a type often produces a battleship curve.
Closed finds such as single graves are especially suitable.
Today correspondence analysis is often used.

abschnitte.text: Things come into **fashion** and go out of fashion again. A new shape of vessel is at first rare, then becomes popular and finally disappears. If you draw this, the curve looks like a ship seen from above. It is called a **battleship curve**: first narrow, then wider and then narrow again. If you compare many such curves, you can put the finds in order.

**Closed finds** are especially suitable, for example **single graves**. All the grave goods in a grave went into the ground **at the same time**. Graves with similar grave goods therefore probably date from a similar time. In this way a series from old to young graves is produced.

abschnitte.titel: Petrie and the graves of Egypt
abschnitte.text: The British Egyptologist **Flinders Petrie** ordered hundreds of graves from Egypt around **1899**. He called his method **“Sequence Dating”**. Today computers work out the sequence, often with **correspondence analysis**, a statistical method. What remains important: seriation gives a **relative chronology**. For real dates in years, other methods are needed, such as radiocarbon dating.

gewusst: Seriation does not say which end of the series is the older one: that has to be found out with other clues.

teile.einleitung: Rice is one of the most important foods in the world. Its cultivation began many thousands of years ago in China on the Yangtze. From there it spread across the whole of Asia and beyond.
wichtigste: Asian cultivated rice descends from the wild rice Oryza rufipogon.
The Shangshan culture already used rice about 10,000 years ago.
The Hemudu culture in Zhejiang province is famous for rice finds and pile dwellings.
The Liangzhu culture built large water works and has been a World Heritage Site since 2019.
Japonica rice was first domesticated in China.
In Japan, wet-rice farming became established in the Yayoi period.

abschnitte.titel: From wild rice to cultivated rice
abschnitte.text: Asian rice is called **Oryza sativa** in science. It descends from the wild rice **Oryza rufipogon**. Over a long time, people chose plants whose grains did not fall off so easily and were larger. In this way a wild plant became a **crop**. This is called **domestication**. First **japonica rice** arose in southern China, later **indica rice** in South and South-East Asia. In Africa, independently of this, a different species was grown, African rice.

Among the oldest evidence is the **Shangshan culture** on the Yangtze in Zhejiang province. In its pottery, **rice husks** were found, that is, the casings of the grains. They had been mixed into the clay to make it stronger. These traces are about **10,000 years** old. They show that people used rice even then.

The **Hemudu culture** existed from about 5500 to 3300 BC. The find site lies near Yuyao in **Zhejiang** province, in the damp lowland on the lower Yangtze. Large quantities of **rice grains** and remains of wooden **pile dwellings** were found there. Already around 5000 BC, beams were joined with **mortise-and-tenon joints**: a tenon on one beam fitted exactly into a hole in the other. Iron was not yet known at that time.

The **Liangzhu culture** flourished from about 3300 to 2300 BC in the Yangtze delta. It built a large city with **dams and canals**. Its economy rested on intensive **wet-rice farming**. In this, the rice fields stand under water. Since **2019**, the ruins of Liangzhu have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

In Japan, the people of the **Jōmon period** lived mainly as hunters, gatherers and fishers. With the **Yayoi period**, **wet-rice farming** and metalworking came to Japan from the mainland. Rice became the most important food there. Even in Switzerland some rice grows today: in **Ticino** near Ascona, it is grown on fields by Lake Maggiore.

gewusst: Rice is a staple food for more than half of the people in the world.
The rice from Ticino is regarded as one of the northernmost rice-growing places in Europe.

teile.einleitung: Plateosaurus was one of the first large dinosaurs. It lived about 210 million years ago and ate plants. At Frick in the canton of Aargau, so many skeletons were found that a dinosaur museum of its own was created there.
wichtigste: Plateosaurus lived in the late Triassic about 210 million years ago.
It was a plant eater with a long neck.
It walked on its two hind legs.
At Frick in the canton of Aargau, the first bones were found in 1961.
In 1985, the first complete skeleton was discovered there.
The Frick Dinosaur Museum opened in 1991.

abschnitte.text: Plateosaurus lived in the **Upper Triassic**, the late Triassic, about 210 million years ago. It belongs to the **early large dinosaurs**. Adult animals could grow to several metres long. It had a small head, a **long neck** and a long tail. Plateosaurus was a **plant eater**. With its neck it reached leaves up high.

abschnitte.titel: On the move on two legs
abschnitte.text: In the past, people thought Plateosaurus walked on all fours. Today we know: it walked on its **two hind legs**. Its forelegs were shorter and could not be turned so that the palms faced downwards. They were used for **grasping**, for example to pull branches closer. On its hands it had powerful claws.

**Frick** lies in the Fricktal in the canton of **Aargau**. There, clay for bricks is quarried in a **clay pit**. In **1961**, dinosaur bones first came to light there. The first scientific excavation followed in **1976**. In **1985**, the first connected skeleton was discovered. Since then, remains of many dozens of Plateosaurs have been found at Frick. This makes Frick one of the most important sites of this dinosaur in Europe.

On **21 October 1991**, the **Frick Dinosaur Museum** opened. Its showpiece is the skeleton of 1985. But the museum shows further finds from the clay pit. These include the predatory dinosaur **Notatesseraeraptor**, which is known only from a single skeleton. It was excavated in 2006 and 2009, and in its stomach remains of its last prey were found. Also on display is **Proganochelys**, which is regarded as the oldest turtle of Switzerland.

gewusst: Many Plateosaurs at Frick probably got stuck in the mud and could not get out again; that is why so many skeletons lie there.
Plateosaurus is also known from Germany, for example from Trossingen in Baden-Württemberg.

teile.einleitung: The **Linear Pottery culture** (Linearbandkeramik) was the first large farming culture of central Europe. It gets its name from the decoration on its clay pots, which looks like bands. People lived in large longhouses and grew cereals.
wichtigste: The Linear Pottery culture lasted from about 5500 to 4900 BC.
It arose in western Hungary, in Transdanubia, and spread as far as the Paris Basin.
Typical are longhouses built with posts.
The typical stone tool is the shoe-last adze.
Wooden wells, for example at Erkelenz-Kückhoven, are among the oldest wooden structures in the world.
Sought-after jewellery was made from the spondylus shell from the Mediterranean.
Finds such as Talheim and Herxheim also show violence and puzzling customs.

abschnitte.text: The pots of this culture are decorated with incised lines that run round the pot like **bands**. That is why people speak of **Linear Pottery** or Linearbandkeramik. The culture arose around **5500 BC** in **Transdanubia** in western Hungary. One forerunner was the Starčevo-Körös culture, among others. From there it spread quickly westwards, as far as the **Paris Basin**, and lasted until about 4900 BC.

Typical are the **longhouses** built with **posts**. They were often 20 to over 30 metres long and stood on five rows of wooden posts. The walls were made of wickerwork smeared with clay. A house had room for a large family, for supplies and perhaps for animals. Several houses together formed a village.

The Linear Pottery people were **farmers**. They grew cereals such as emmer and einkorn and kept cattle, sheep, goats and pigs. For working wood they used the **shoe-last adze**, a polished stone axe whose shape recalls a shoe last. For water they dug **wells** with wooden walls. The well of **Erkelenz-Kückhoven** in the Rhineland dates from around 5100 BC and is among the oldest wooden structures in the world.

People exchanged goods over great distances. Especially sought after were shells of the **spondylus shell**, a thorny oyster from the Aegean or the Adriatic. From them people made **bracelets** and **beads**. Good stone for tools was also transported far. This shows that the villages were in contact with each other.

Not everything was peaceful. At **Talheim** near Heilbronn in Baden-Württemberg, a pit was found with 34 dead people who had died violently. The find shows that there were deadly conflicts around 5000 BC. At **Herxheim** in the Palatinate, cut-up bones of several hundred people were found. Whether this was a special **cult of the dead** or **cannibalism** is debated by researchers.

gewusst: Wood is only preserved for thousands of years if it lies permanently in wet groundwater, as with the well at Kückhoven.
The age of the well timber was worked out by dendrochronology, that is, from the tree rings.

teile.einleitung: Homo habilis is an early human species from Africa. It lived about 2.1 to 1.5 million years ago and is linked with simple stone tools.
wichtigste: Homo habilis was described in 1964 in the journal “Nature”.
The first describers were Louis Leakey, Phillip Tobias and John Napier.
Raymond Dart suggested the name “habilis”.
It lived about 2.1 to 1.5 million years ago.
Its brain was about 650 cubic centimetres in size.
The type specimen OH 7 is the lower jaw of a child.

abschnitte.text: The species name “habilis” was suggested by the anatomist **Raymond Dart**. He was already known for the find of the “Taung Child”. The name fits because simple **stone tools** lay in layers of the same age. It was assumed that this early human had made them. Fine notches on animal bones show **cut marks** from sharp stones. So Homo habilis cut meat off bones.

In April 1964, **Louis Leakey**, **Phillip Tobias** and **John Napier** presented the new species in the journal “Nature”. Tobias was a South African anatomist and studied above all the skulls and the brain volume. The basis was finds from the **Olduvai Gorge** in Tanzania. The description is regarded as a turning point in research on early humans.

The **type specimen** is the find on which the description of a species is based. For Homo habilis this is **OH 7**, an almost complete lower jaw with the teeth of a child. Jonathan Leakey found it in 1960. Another famous find is the skull **KNM-ER 1813** from Koobi Fora in Kenya. It is small, almost complete and about 1.9 million years old.

abschnitte.titel: Brain and lifespan of the species
abschnitte.text: The brain of Homo habilis was about **650 cubic centimetres** in size. That is about a third more than in the older **Australopithecines**. Humans today have about twice as much. All certain finds are about 2.1 to 1.5 million years old. Whether Homo habilis is a direct ancestor of modern humans is debated among experts.

gewusst: The most important find of Homo habilis is the lower jaw of a child.
The name “habilis” means “skilful” in Latin.

teile.einleitung: Palaeontology is the science of the living things of prehistory. Palaeontologists look for fossils in rock and find out which animals and plants once lived on the Earth.
wichtigste: Palaeontologists study living things of prehistory.
Fossilised remains of living things are called fossils.
The word fossil comes from the Latin “fossilis”, dug up.
Fossils are mostly found in rock.
For every find, the exact find spot is written down.
A coprolite is fossilised dung.
Tiny fossils are studied with the microscope.

abschnitte.text: **Fossils** are fossilised remains of living things of prehistory. They can be bones, teeth, shells or impressions of leaves. Traces belong too, such as footprints. The word comes from the Latin **“fossilis”**, which means dug up. Crystals and gemstones are not fossils, because they were never alive. The name palaeontology comes from Greek and means roughly “study of ancient living things”.

Fossils mostly lie in **rock layers**. These layers formed over a very long time, for example from mud on the floor of a sea. The deeper a layer lies, the older it usually is. In Switzerland, **ammonites** are often found. These were sea creatures with a shell coiled up like a snail. Famous find sites also include **Monte San Giorgio** in Ticino and the clay pit of **Frick** in Aargau.

In an excavation, researchers work very carefully with hammer, chisel and brush. Especially important is the **find spot**. It is written down exactly, measured and photographed. Only in this way do you know later from which rock layer and from which time a fossil comes. After that, the find is cleaned in the laboratory. Some fossils are so tiny that you can only look at them closely with a **microscope**.

Fossils tell a lot about life in prehistory. A fossilised **tooth** shows what an animal ate. Pointed teeth for tearing often belonged to meat eaters, while broad or leaf-shaped teeth mostly belonged to plant eaters. A **coprolite** is fossilised dung. In it you sometimes find remains of bones or plants. From many finds, palaeontologists put together a picture of what the Earth looked like millions of years ago.

gewusst: Some fossils are over 3 billion years old; they are traces of tiny living things.
Ammonites were so widespread that they can be used to determine the age of rock layers.

teile.einleitung: **Amber** looks like a golden stone, but is really ancient tree resin. Sometimes it contains insects that lived millions of years ago. Even in the Stone Age, people made jewellery from it.
wichtigste: Amber is fossilised tree resin that has become hard.
It is often millions of years old.
It is usually yellow to orange.
Insects, spiders and parts of plants can be trapped inside it.
Especially large amounts of amber are found on the Baltic Sea.
Amber is light, and it floats in very salty water.
Even in the Stone Age, amber was popular jewellery.

abschnitte.text: Many trees, for example conifers, produce **resin**. This is a sticky liquid that seals wounds in the bark. Millions of years ago, a lot of resin dripped from the trees in great forests. It was covered by soil and sand and became **hard** over a very long time. This is how **amber** formed. It is also called fossilised resin, although it is not a true stone.

Sometimes **insects** got stuck in the sticky resin. New resin flowed over them and enclosed them. Because they were sealed in airtight, they are **very well preserved**. You can even see fine legs, wings and tiny hairs. Besides insects, you also find **spiders**, leaves, flowers or seeds. Large animals do not fit inside. For research, such inclusions are a window into prehistoric times.

Especially large amounts of amber are found on the **Baltic Sea**. It comes from prehistoric forests of that area and is about 40 million years old. After storms, the sea washes pieces up onto the beaches. Amber is very light, only a little heavier than water. In very **salty water it floats** on top, while in fresh water it sinks slowly.

Most amber glows **honey-yellow to orange**. But there are also pale, almost white pieces and dark, reddish ones. In the hand, amber feels **light and warm**, not cold like a stone. If you rub it on a woollen cloth, it attracts small scraps of paper. It becomes electrically charged as you do so.

Even in the **Stone Age**, people wore amber as **jewellery**. It was traded over long distances, even as far as southern Europe. Necklaces, pendants and small figures are still made from it today. A famous work of art was the **Amber Room** in Russia, a whole room with walls made of amber. It was lost in the Second World War and later rebuilt.

gewusst: The Greek word for amber is “elektron”, which is where the word electricity comes from.
Amber can burn, and it smells of resin as it does.
